en: The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated from a Sanskrit manuscript brought from Central India by the Monk Fajie of the Great Tang Dynasty,
at the request of the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladāsa of Khotan.
Translated at Longxing Monastery in Beiting by Xuanzang. The Bodhisattva Stage of Supreme Joy, Part One of One. Thus have I heard:

At one time, not long after the Bhagavat had attained enlightenment, on the second seventh-day period, he was dwelling in the Palace of the Sovereign King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, within the Maṇi-jewel Treasury Hall, together with a vast assembly of immeasurable great bodhisattvas.

All those bodhisattvas had come together from various buddha-fields; they were all non-retrogressive regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, bound by only one more birth, and destined to realize true awakening.
That is to say:
having already attained stable abiding in the sphere of activity of all bodhisattva wisdom, they are able to enter the domain of activity of all Tathāgata wisdom without ceasing;
they are skillfully able to manifest various supernatural powers and all manner of deeds, acting at the appropriate time without obstruction to mature and subdue all sentient beings.

All activities for the benefit and happiness of others are never in vain; they give rise to all bodhisattva vows and practice for as many eons, worlds, and lands as there may be, without even a moment’s rest.
They have fully prepared the inexhaustible provisions of merit and wisdom of all bodhisattvas, making them available for the common enjoyment of all worlds.

Having reached the further shore of all bodhisattva wisdom and skillful means, they manifest entry into the gates of birth-and-death and nirvana, yet do not abandon the cultivation of the bodhisattva path.

They are skillfully able to sport with and understand all bodhisattva meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and clear wisdom; they have attained mastery in all such activities.

Having acquired the sovereign power of all bodhisattva supernormal faculties, they are able, through effortless mental instants, to travel to the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Tathāgatas and act as their leaders to request the Buddhas to teach the Dharma;
they uphold the wheel of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas and are extensively able to make offerings to and serve all Buddhas.
They constantly and diligently cultivate all the deeds and practices of bodhisattvas;

their bodies appear universally throughout all worlds, their speech and sounds are unimpeded, their mental wisdom is pure and penetrating throughout the dharma-realm without stagnation, and they universally perceive all realms of the three periods of time.

All the secret treasuries of merit and correct practice belonging to all bodhisattvas are already fully perfected; even if one were to praise their merits for immeasurable and ineffable eons, one could never exhaust them.
Their names were:

Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, Padmagarbha Bodhisattva, Guṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Padmaguṇagarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Jyotirgarbha Bodhisattva, and Dharaṇī... [Bodhisattva].
The Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Vimalacandragañja, the Bodhisattva Sarvavyūhaprabhāsa-garbha,
the Bodhisattva Jñānasamantāvabhāsagarbha, the Bodhisattva Candanaguṇagañja,
the Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣagañja, the Bodhisattva Puṣpaguṇagañja, the Bodhisattva Kusumaguṇagañja, the Bodhisattva Utpalaguṇagañja...
Bodhisattva Pāradharagarbha, Bodhisattva Devadharagarbha, Bodhisattva Puṇyadharagarbha,
Bodhisattva Asaṅgapariśuddhajñānagarbha, Bodhisattva Guṇavijayagarbha, Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇaguṇadharagarbha,
Bodhisattva Vimalagarbha, Bodhisattva Vigatamalapagarbha, and those adorned with various eloquences.
Gandhagarbha Bodhisattva, Mahāprabhājālaprabhāsagarbha Bodhisattva, Vimalatejaprabhāsarājagarbha Bodhisattva,
Asaṅgavicitrasvararutagarbha Bodhisattva, Sarvasattvapraṇidhānasaṃdhāraṇaguṇatārakagarbha Bodhisattva, Mahāsamudravyūhagarbha Bodhisattva, and Sumerugarbha Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Guṇagañja, Bodhisattva Sarvaguṇaviśuddhagañjasaṃdarśana, Tathāgataguṇagañja, Buddhaguṇagañja, Bodhisattva Suvarṇasūkṣmamahātejo-rājaprabhāsagañja,
Bodhisattva Sarvalakṣaṇavyūha-viśuddhagañja, and Vajrajvālā-hṛdayasvastika.
The Bodhisattva Lakṣaṇavyūha, the Bodhisattva Jyotirāja-prabhāsa-garbha, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja-anāvaraṇajñānagarbha,
and the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra— such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as these were immeasurable,
innumerable, inconceivable, unfathomable, incomparable, and boundless.
Boundless and without limit, beyond expression and beyond expression, they had all gathered from various and diverse buddha-fields,
with Vajragarbha Bodhisattva as their leader.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the bodhisattva samādhi called "Great Vehicle Radiance.

Having entered this concentration, immediately beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten koṭis of buddha-fields in each of the ten directions, there appeared ten koṭis of buddha-tathāgatas, each as numerous as the atoms in ten koṭis of buddha-fields, all sharing the same name, Vajragarbha;
they all manifested their faces and spoke these words together:
“Excellent, excellent, Son of the Buddha!
You are now able to enter this Mahāyāna Radiance Bodhisattva Samādhi.”
However, noble son!

Now, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions—each as numerous as the atoms within ten koṭis of Buddha-fields—collectively empower you. Because you are sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the original vows of the World-Honored One Vairocana, you shall enter into the path of all Bodhisattvas and be able to manifest the inconceivable light of the Buddha-dharma.

Within the various stages of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*), [this is practiced] in order to embrace all roots of goodness; to discern skillfulness regarding all Buddha-dharmas; to extensively know the Dharma; to correctly expound and well-establish the Dharma; to attain the purification of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); to remain unstained by any worldly dharmas; to attain the purity of supramundane roots of goodness; to realize the sphere of activity of inconceivable wisdom; and even to realize the sphere of the Buddha’s wisdom.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of the setting forth and attainment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of all bodhisattvas; for the sake of skillfully establishing the exposition of the various bodhisattva stages as they truly are; for the sake of correctly taking the sublime Dharma of the Buddhas as one's object of focus; for the sake of cultivating the distinctions of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas; for the sake of skill in the light of great wisdom that is well-selected and decisive; for the sake of entering the gateway of definitive knowledge; for the sake of obtaining fearless eloquence that reveals what is appropriate to each situation; for the sake of realizing the stage of vast and unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*); for the sake of not losing the mindfulness of the bodhicitta; for the sake of skillfully bringing the realm of all sentient beings to maturity; and for the sake of attaining everywhere the eloquence of decisive selection and penetration.
Nevertheless, son of good family!
You should skillfully explain this dharma-gate of the distinctions of the Dharma,
which is as follows:

Because they have received the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas; because they have been sustained by the light of wisdom of all Tathāgatas; because they have already perfectly purified their own roots of goodness; because they have already brilliantly adorned the true *dharmadhātu*; because they have already universally gathered and benefited all sentient beings; because they have already realized the basis for the wisdom of the *dharmakāya*; because they have already received empowerment from all Buddhas; because they have already manifested the greatest body that transcends all worlds; because they have already surpassed all worldly destinies; because they have already purified the worldly-transcending path of the True Dharma; and because they have already been able to fulfill the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).

At that time, those Tathāgatas of the ten directions bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha a body that cannot be eclipsed; they bestowed the eloquence of unimpeded exposition; they bestowed the entry into subtle, pure wisdom and discernment; they bestowed the empowerment of mindfulness free from forgetfulness; they bestowed the skill of well-determined wisdom; they bestowed the non-abandonment of all-pervasive cognitive activity; they bestowed the power of perfect enlightenment that can never be overcome; they bestowed the fearlessness of a Tathāgata to ensure he was not cowed; they bestowed the definitive establishment of the principles of the Dharma through the great unhindered analytical knowledge encompassed by the wisdom of omniscience; and they granted him the arousal of the adornments of the well-discriminated body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.

Why is this so? It is because this bodhisattva has attained the samādhi of the Radiance of the Mahāyāna; it is because such is the natural law (*dharmatā*); because it is brought forth by his original vows; because of his perfectly pure and superior sublime intention (*adhyāśaya*); because he has already well-polished the wheel of pure wisdom; because he has already well-accumulated all the provisions (*saṃbhāra*); because he has already well-refined the tasks to be performed; because he possesses immeasurable mindfulness as a vessel; because his brilliant resolve (*adhimukti*) has attained purity; because he has well-mastered the gateways of unadulterated dhāraṇīs; and because he is sealed by the seal of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.

At that time, those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, without rising from their seats, each extended their right hand through the power of spiritual penetrations and stroked the crown of the head of the Great Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.

Then the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having received the empowerment of the crowning touch from those Buddhas of the ten directions, arose from his meditative absorption and addressed the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

This vow of the bodhisattva is definitive and unadulterated; it cannot be fully illumined even by the vast dharma-realm that extends to the nature of empty space, reaching to the end of the future, and is able to rescue all classes of sentient beings.
O Sons of the Buddha!

Only when a bodhisattva is securely established in this vow can they enter the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past; they can enter the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the future; and they can also enter the ground of wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the present.
O Sons of the Buddha!

All Bodhisattvas have ten stages of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmi*). For this reason, the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have already taught, shall teach, and are now teaching them; it is with this underlying intention that I speak these words.

What are these ten? First is named the Ground of Supreme Joy; second, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement; third, the Ground of Radiant Light; fourth, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Ground Difficult to Conquer; sixth, the Ground of Manifestation; seventh, the Ground of Far-Going; eighth, the Ground of Immovability; ninth, the Ground of Excellent Wisdom; and tenth, the Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the Ten Stages of all Bodhisattvas.
It has been taught by the Buddhas of the past, will be taught by those of the future, and is being taught now by those of the present.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
I do not see any buddha-field where the Tathāgata therein does not praise and expound these ten stages of the bodhisattva. Why is this so?"

These bodhisattvas possess superior, sublime, and excellent qualities; they are able to purify the light of the dharma-gates of all bodhisattva paths, which refers precisely to the establishment and explanation of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
"O Sons of the Buddha!
You should know that this place is inconceivable; it refers to the wisdom personally realized within the established dharmas of the various stages.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, having designated these names of the ten stages, remained silent and did not further analyze or explain them.
At that time, when the entire assembly of bodhisattvas had heard the names of the ten bodhisattva stages but had not heard their explanation, they all felt a deep yearning and thought to themselves:
"For what cause and for what reason does this Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having merely stated the names of the ten bodhisattva stages, remain silent and provide no further explanation?"

At that time, within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there was a bodhisattva named Vimukticandra. Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great multitude, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in verse:
"Why does the Perfectly Awakened One, Endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and merit, Having designated these most sublime stages, Not explain them with sovereign ease?"
All are resolute, these Bodhisattvas of great renown;
for what reason do you speak of the names of the stages but not expound their meaning?
All the sons of the Buddhas, fearless and all desiring to hear it.
I pray that you will provide a correct analysis and explain the meaning and intent of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
This entire assembly is pure, free from indolence, dignified and composed,
dwelling in freshness and solidity, and fully endowed with merit and wisdom.
They gazed at one another with mutual reverence, all of them looking up with single-minded devotion;
they longed only for the nectar of the Dharma, just as bees yearn for pure honey.
When the Greatly Wise and Fearless One, Vajragarbha, heard this, he—
Desiring to gladden the great assembly, he replied to the Son of the Buddha in verse:
"Though you have performed what is most supreme and exceedingly rare, This has been able to manifest the conduct of a Bodhisattva;
The stage of Eloquence (*pratibhāna-bhūmi*) is most subtle and wondrous, For by means of it, the stages of a Buddha are cultivated and realized."
Subtle and difficult to see, free from conceptualization, Transcending the mind-ground and hard to realize;
The realm of the wise is purely untainted, And those in the world who hear of it are utterly bewildered.
With a mind as firm and immovable as a vajra, One’s faith and understanding of the Buddha’s wisdom are most supreme;
Thoroughly realizing that there is no self, only the ground of mind— Such a person can hear this subtle wisdom.
Just as one might paint the void with myriad colors, Or as the wind moves along the path of birds;
So too is the untainted wisdom of the Buddha— Though it is differentiated, it is difficult to perceive.
Therefore, I have now aroused such wisdom as this, which is difficult for anyone in the world to understand;
and since even those who can believe in this most supreme Dharma are so rare, I am not fit to provide a broad explanation.
At that time, having heard these words, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

This assembly is now entirely pure; these bodhisattvas possess well-purified intentions and well-cleansed thoughts, have skillfully cultivated all practices, have served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, have well accumulated the provisions for enlightenment, have accomplished immeasurable varieties of merit, are forever free from doubt and devoid of all defilements, are well-established in superior intention and resolute conviction, and regarding the Buddha-dharma, they do not follow the teachings of others."
"Excellent!
Son of the Buddha, you have expounded this meaning; these bodhisattvas dwell in direct realization within such a state.
Then, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Please explain the most peaceful and secure, the supreme conduct of the Bodhisattvas;
distinguish the various stages, whereby through the purity of wisdom one attains perfect enlightenment.
This assembly is free from all faults; their resolve and understanding are entirely clear and pure."
"Having served immeasurable Buddhas, one is able to know the meaning of this stage.
Then the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
"O Son of the Buddha!"

Although this assembly is entirely pure, these bodhisattvas possess well-purified intentions and well-cleansed thoughts; they have skillfully cultivated all practices and have already served immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of buddhas. Having well accumulated the provisions for enlightenment and accomplished immeasurable varieties of merit, they are forever free from doubt and devoid of all defilements or blemishes. They dwell securely in superior intention and resolute conviction, and within the Buddha-dharma, they do not follow the teachings of others.

However, there are other sentient beings of inferior understanding who, upon hearing this profound and inconceivable point, suddenly give rise to doubt and confusion; this will lead them through the long night to a multitude of sufferings that are meaningless and without benefit.
"I pity these people; therefore, I delight in silence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Though this assembly is pure and possesses vast wisdom, Profound, sharp, and capable of discernment;"
Their minds are as immovable as the king of mountains, Unshakeable like the great ocean.
Because their practice is not yet long-standing and they have not yet attained realization, They act according to consciousness rather than wisdom;
Hearing this, they would give rise to doubt and fall into evil realms— Out of compassion for such as these, I do not speak.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra again addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, saying: "Excellent,
O Son of the Buddha!
Please explain this without hesitation.
By the Buddha’s supernormal power and his protective mindfulness, such inconceivable matters as these can all be trusted. Why is this so?
O Son of the Buddha!

When this explanation of the ten stages is being spoken, it is the natural law that all Buddhas protect and keep it in mind, and all Bodhisattvas, desiring to guard and protect this ground of wisdom, rouse their courageous vigor.
Why is this? This is the primary correct practice of a bodhisattva, and it is also the cultivation and realization of all Buddha-dharmas.
O Son of the Buddha!

For example, in all enumeration and explanation of written characters, the alphabet is the beginning and the alphabet is the end; there is not even the slightest portion of the enumeration and explanation of written characters that is apart from the alphabet.
O Son of the Buddha!
All the Buddha-dharmas are likewise thus: they take the stages (*bhūmi*) as the beginning for initiating practice, and they take the stages as the end for realizing Buddha-wisdom.
"Therefore, Son of the Buddha!
We pray that you will expound this for us, sustained and protected by the power of all Buddhas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Excellent, Son of the Buddha! We pray that you will expound the practices of the stages for entering into awakening;
there is not one among all the Sovereign Honored Ones of the ten directions who does not protect and mindfully regard this root of wisdom.”
This begins with right practice and culminates in wisdom; all Buddha-dharmas arise from this.
Just as all scripts are subsumed within the alphabet, so too do the Buddha-dharmas rely upon the stages (*bhūmi*).
At that time, this assembly of great bodhisattvas, for the sake of this same meaning, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in verse:
"O you of supreme, stainless wisdom, With excellent speech and boundless eloquence;
Proclaiming beautiful words, The principles corresponding to the ultimate truth."
Maintaining pure wisdom in mind, with the intentionality of the Ten Powers,
and possessing unimpeded analytical discernment, he proclaims the supreme ten stages.
This assembly is free from arrogance, as well as the defilements of views and doubt.
With morality and concentration, and with a mind full of joy, I only wish to hear your excellent teaching.
Like one who thirsts for cool water, like one who hungers for fine food,
like one who is ill and longs for wholesome medicine, or like a swarm of bees craving honey.
This assembly is likewise; we pray to hear the Dharma of the Deathless.
Excellent, O One of Pure Wisdom! Please explain the stainless stages, revealing the path of the Sugata that accords with the Ten Powers and is unimpeded.

At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni emitted from the mark of the white tuft between his brows countless rays of light named "Illuminating the Power of Bodhisattvas. These countless rays of light formed a retinue, and their radiance shone universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, reaching everywhere without exception. They caused all sufferings of the evil realms to cease, eclipsed all the palaces of the Māras, and illuminated the assemblies of immeasurable Buddhas, manifesting the inconceivable spheres, modes of conduct, majestic powers, and playful manifestations of all Buddhas.

Having illuminated the worlds of the ten directions and all the assemblies of the Buddhas, and having empowered the bodies of the bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he remained suspended in the air above, having manifested a great cloud-net pavilion of light.

Those World-Honored Ones were likewise; from their white tuft marks (*ūrṇā-kośa*), they emitted countless rays of light, with innumerable beams of radiance as their retinue. These lights shone universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, reaching everywhere without exception, causing all suffering in the evil realms to cease. They eclipsed all the palaces of the Māras and illuminated the assemblies of immeasurable Buddhas, manifesting the inconceivable spheres, modes of conduct, majestic powers, and playful manifestations of all Buddhas.

It illuminated all the worlds throughout the ten directions as well as the assemblies of all Buddhas; through the empowerment of the Buddha’s spiritual power, it manifested the inconceivable playful displays of the Buddhas by means of the bodies of the Bodhisattvas who preach the Dharma. Having illuminated the assembly of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni and the body of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, it likewise formed a great cloud-net pavilion of radiant light in the sky above and remained there.

Thereupon, from the light streaming forth from the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the various worlds, the assemblies of those Buddhas, as well as the bodies of those Bodhisattvas and their Dharma-thrones, all appeared clearly and were seen here.

From the light rays streaming from the ūrṇā-kośa of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout those immeasurable Buddha-fields, this trichiliocosm, as well as the assembly of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s great gathering, along with the body and Dharma-seat of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, all appeared clearly and were seen by them.
At that time, from this cloud-net terrace of light, these verses issued forth:
"The Buddha is peerless and equal to space; With the ten powers, he is sovereign over boundless multitudes.
Within the wondrous Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas, The Supreme among Gods and Humans now bestows grace upon you."
Sons of the Buddha, you should now, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, Open this wondrous Dharma-treasury of the Dharma King;
Reveal the subtle, wondrous, and vast practices, And distinguish and establish the various stages of wisdom.
Whoever hears this supreme Dharma-gate shall likewise receive the protection of the Sugata;
all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions will entirely uphold and mindfully protect them.
One should be able to cultivate and accumulate all correct practices, Gradually fulfilling the stainless stages;
One will be able to realize the qualities such as the ten powers, And awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Though one dwell amidst the waters of the ocean or within the fires of the kalpa, if one is free from doubt, they are fit to hear this Dharma-gate;
whereas those who harbor doubts and lack faith shall never again hear such a teaching.
I shall now explain the path of knowledge regarding the most excellent stages, including their realization, entry, abiding, and advancement;
I shall describe the spheres of practice in their proper sequence for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha surveyed the ten directions and, wishing to increase the pure faith of the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"The path of the Great Sage is subtle and difficult to know; It is beyond conceptualization and free from discrimination.
It is difficult to realize; it is the domain of those with untainted wisdom, Whose nature is eternally tranquil, without arising or ceasing."
The emptiness of nature is quiescent, non-dual, and exhaustive; Transcending realms, it is equal and reaches nirvāṇa.
Without boundaries, center, or conditions, there is nothing to be realized; It transcends the three periods of time and is equal to empty space.
The tranquility and quiescence realized by the Buddhas are difficult to proclaim through any mode of speech;
this stage and its practice are likewise so—difficult even to explain, let alone to hear!
Far removed from discursive thought and the path of the mind, this wisdom is the domain of the Muni;
it is not revealed by the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases, nor can it be fathomed by the mind or conceived by the intellect.

Just as the tracks of birds in the sky cannot be described by the wise nor easily shown, so too are the stages of the Buddha-sons; it is extremely difficult even to explain them, let alone to hear them!
Now I shall speak of only this one portion, through the power of great compassion and aspiration;
though its gradual stages are beyond the scope of the ordinary mind, may wisdom fulfill all wishes as desired.
Thus, this realm is extremely difficult to perceive; it is ineffable and dwells solely within one's own intentionality.
Nevertheless, relying upon the power of the Buddha, I shall now speak; you all should listen with single-minded reverence.
Such gateways of wisdom and right practice could not be fully expounded even in billions of eons;
I shall now briefly explain them for you to hear, so that the true meaning of the Dharma may be understood entirely according to principle.
O Benevolent One, wait with single-minded reverence; I shall speak well, sustained by the Buddha’s power.
I will proclaim the sound of the subtle and wondrous True Dharma, With appropriate parables and harmonious, orderly words.
This is difficult to clarify through words alone, yet it is sustained by the spiritual power of immeasurable Buddhas;
as their light and forms enter my body, I am now able to expound this teaching.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If there are sentient beings who have well accumulated roots of virtue, well gathered the provisions, well cultivated all practices, served the Buddhas well, well amassed pure dharmas, been embraced by virtuous friends, possessed a well-purified intention, and followed along with a vast and superior resolve;

Possessing sublime resolve and manifesting compassion, they generate such a mind as follows: for the sake of seeking the wisdom of a Buddha; for the desire to realize the power of the ten powers; for the attainment of the great fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata; for the acquisition of the equal, unique qualities of a Buddha; for the purpose of rescuing and delivering all the world; for the purification of great compassion; for the realization of the exhaustive knowledge of the ten directions; for the unimpeded purification of all Buddha-fields; for the ability to know the three periods of time in a single kṣaṇa; and for the fearless turning of the great wheel of Dharma.

The Bodhisattva’s generation of the mind of awakening is preceded by great compassion; it is embraced by superior wisdom and skillful means, constantly sustained by both intention and resolute intention. Through the immeasurable power of the Buddhas, by the force of firm resolve and the power of wisdom, there arises unimpeded knowledge that is well-discriminated and certain. This accords with the spontaneous, wondrous wisdom that requires no teacher, enabling one to receive all Buddha-teachings through wisdom and insight—teachings and instructions that extend to the limit of the Dharma-realm, exhaust the nature of empty space, and reach the end of the future.

The initial arousal of this mind is itself the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), their realization and entry into the Bodhisattva’s state of right nature free from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*), and their birth into the family of the Tathāgatas. Their lineage is noble and beyond reproach; having already left behind the worldly realms, they enter the supramundane path, abide within the fundamental dharma-nature of Bodhisattvas, and are well-established in the station of Bodhisattvas. In accordance with the principle of equality throughout the three times, they succeed to the lineage of the Tathāgatas and are destined for unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas abide in such dharmas as these, they are said to be well-established in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), because they are immovable.
O Sons of the Buddha!"

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Extreme Joy, they experience extreme abundance of joy, abundant pure faith, abundant affection and delight, abundant serenity, abundant exultation, abundant leaping-forth, abundant valor, abundant freedom from contention, abundant freedom from malice, and abundant freedom from resentment.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva abides in the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they give rise to extreme joy when recollecting the Buddhas;

they give rise to joy when recollecting the Buddha-dharma, when recollecting the bodhisattvas, when recollecting the bodhisattva practices, when recollecting the purity of the perfections (*pāramitā*), when recollecting the excellence of the bodhisattva stages, when recollecting that other bodhisattvas cannot outshine them, when recollecting the instructions and admonitions of the Buddhas, when recollecting the bringing of benefit to sentient beings, and when recollecting their own entry into the application of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas. In all these instances, they experience great joy.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands: "I have now turned away from all worldly spheres; I am drawing near to the Buddhas and distancing myself from the stage of ordinary beings, while approaching the stage of wisdom. I shall forever sever all falling into the perilous evil destinies and serve as a place of refuge for all sentient beings."

Recently, I have seen all the Buddhas abiding in the realm of the Buddhas and entering into the state of equality of all bodhisattvas; having abandoned all fears that cause the hair on one's body to stand on end, I give rise to supreme joy.
Why is this so? O Sons of the Buddha!
As soon as a bodhisattva has realized the Stage of Supreme Joy, all fears—namely:
They are entirely free from the fear of lacking a livelihood, the fear of ill repute, the fear of death, the fear of rebirth in evil destinies, and the fear of timidity in assemblies. Why is this so?
Because this bodhisattva is free from the notion of a self, they have no attachment even to themselves, much less to any material requisites;
for this reason, they have no fear of being unable to sustain their life.
Because he has no expectations and gives rise only to the desire, "I should provide all the necessities of life for all sentient beings," for this reason, he has no fear of ill repute.
Because they have abandoned the view of a self, they harbor no notion of the destruction of a self; therefore, they have no fear of death.
Knowing for themselves that after death they will certainly not be separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in future lives, they consequently have no fear of the miserable realms.
Because of his intention, he perceives that in all the world there is not even one who is his equal, much less superior; therefore, he has no timidity or fear when among a multitude.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Thus, having already abandoned fear, arrogance, and horripilation, the bodhisattva takes great compassion as their precursor; free from aversion and devoid of worldly inclinations, they diligently apply themselves to spiritual practice in order to cultivate and realize all roots of goodness."

By means of the predominance of faith, by means of abundant verified purity, by means of pure resolute conviction, by means of abundant faith and understanding, by means of the elicitation of compassion,
by means of being endowed with great loving-kindness, by means of a mind free from weariness, by means of being adorned with shame and dread of blame,
by means of constant association with patience and gentleness, and by means of profound reverence, compliance, faith, respect, and veneration.
They hold the noble teaching of the Tathāgata dear; they accumulate all roots of goodness day and night without weariness;
they serve spiritual friends; they delight in the garden of the Dharma; they seek out extensive learning without satiety;
they investigate the teachings they have heard according to the principle; they possess a mind free from attachment; and they do not crave fame.
Seeking honor and respect; not longing for the necessities of life; drawing forth a mind of equanimity like a precious jewel through insatiable diligence;
single-mindedly aspiring to the stage of omniscience; taking as one's object the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-qualities; and seeking the unattached *pāramitās*.
Being free from flattery and deception; acting in accordance with what one says; constantly guarding truthful speech;
exhorting others without defiling the lineage of the Buddhas; not abandoning any of the trainings of the bodhisattvas;
remaining as immovable as the king of mountains regarding the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*; and being able to achieve the supramundane while not departing from worldly affairs.
In the intermediate path, one accumulates the provisions for the factors of enlightenment through tireless cultivation, constantly aspiring for ever more excellent dharmas.
O Sons of the Buddha!
By being thus associated with these various dharmas of the pure stages, the bodhisattva is said to dwell securely in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Stage of Extreme Joy, they give rise to such great vows, great resolute courage, and great renunciations as to universally make offerings to all Tathāgatas with every kind of offering implement and every category of service, leaving nothing remaining.

Having accomplished all aspects of conduct in their most excellent and sublime form, with the highest resolve, throughout the pure and vast realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), to the limits of space and for all future time, without ceasing through the succession of all kalpas and the appearance of all Buddhas, they first give rise to the great vow for the sake of performing great offerings.

Desiring to uphold the Dharma-eye taught by all Tathāgatas, desiring to embrace the Bodhi of all Buddhas, and desiring to protect the teachings of all Samyaksaṃbuddhas throughout the vast Dharma-realm, to the limit of the nature of space and to the end of the future, without ceasing for the duration of all kalpas, he makes the second great vow to embrace the Sublime Dharma.

For the sake of all Buddhas appearing in the world, throughout all worlds without exception—beginning with their dwelling in the Tuṣita heaven palaces, followed by their descent, entry into the womb, abiding in the womb, birth, growth, renunciation, attainment of enlightenment, acceptance of the Brahma King’s invitation, turning of the Great Wheel of Dharma, and demonstration of Great Nirvāṇa—I shall first go to them all to make offerings, receive the teachings, and apply myself to practice; and for the sake of all these events occurring simultaneously in every place, throughout the vast Dharma-realm, as far as the nature of space extends, until the end of the future, through all kalpas and all instances of a Buddha’s appearance without cessation, I shall go to them all and thus make my third great vow.

In order to bring forth the bodhisattva practices—which are vast, immeasurable, and embraced by the non-conceptual *pāramitās*—and to purify the general characteristics, specific characteristics, common characteristics, distinct characteristics, characteristics of formation, and characteristics of disintegration of the various stages; to manifest the path of the bodhisattva’s ground of wisdom as it truly is and without error; to adorn all the *pāramitās*; to bestow instructions and admonitions that support and assist the arousal of the mind of enlightenment; and to do so throughout the vast dharma-realm, to the limits of space, until the end of the future, without ceasing for even a single kalpa or a single moment of correct practice—for this purpose, he brings forth the fourth great vow.

Desiring to bring to fulfillment the entire realm of sentient beings without exception—those with form and those without form, those with perception and those without perception, those with neither perception nor non-perception; those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those bound to the three realms and entering the six destinies; those connected to all places of birth and comprised within name-and-form—in order to cause them to enter the Buddha-dharma, to cause them to forever sever the cycle of all destinies, and to establish them in the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), throughout the vast dharma-realm, as far as the nature of space extends, until the end of the future, without ceasing for the duration of all kalpas or the number of all sentient beings—they resolve to bring the realm of sentient beings to maturity; this is the fifth great vow.

Desiring to enter all the various distinct characteristics throughout the ten directions—encompassing all worlds, vast and immeasurable, whether coarse or subtle, disordered, inverted, or upright, and differentiated like Indra’s net—and to manifest the knowledge and vision of them all through successive practice, extending across the vast Dharma-realm, exhausting the nature of space, and reaching the end of the future, without ceasing throughout all kalpas and world-systems, he makes the sixth great vow to proceed toward that goal.

In order to cause all Buddha-fields to mutually enter one another so that all Buddha-fields are universally purified; to adorn them with the light and ornaments of immeasurable Buddha-fields; to leave behind all afflictions and accomplish the path of purity; to be filled with sentient beings whose nature is immeasurable wisdom; to universally enter the vast realm of all Buddhas; to manifest according to the inclinations of sentient beings and cause them all to rejoice; and to extend throughout the entire great Dharma-realm, the nature of space, and to the end of the future—without ceasing for the duration of all kalpas or the number of all Buddha-fields—I make this seventh great vow to adorn all Buddha-fields.
To share the same intention and application as all bodhisattvas; to accumulate roots of virtue without enmity;
to attain equality with all bodhisattvas through a single object of focus; to constantly encounter all buddhas and bodhisattvas without ever being parted;
to manifest the appearance of a Buddha in the world according to one's own wish; and to act in accordance with the mind...
Reflecting upon the Buddha’s majestic power, in order to attain the supernatural power of constant non-retrogression throughout all births until perfection is reached;
in order to travel extensively through all worlds; in order to manifest reflections within all assemblies;
in order to act in accordance with others in every place of rebirth; and in order to perpetually accomplish the...
Contemplating the principles of the Mahāyāna in order to practice the correct conduct of a bodhisattva— extending throughout the vast dharma-realm,
to the limits of space, and to the end of the future, with all kalpas and instances of correct conduct continuing without rest—
he made the eighth great vow for the sake of great wisdom and supernormal powers.

I make this ninth great vow so that my practice may serve as a vehicle for the bodhisattva conduct of the non-retrogressive wheel; so that my actions of body, speech, and mind shall not be in vain; so that those who see me even briefly may attain certainty regarding the *dharmatā* of all Buddhas, and those who hear my voice even briefly may realize it through wisdom; so that by the mere arising of pure faith, one may forever sever the afflictions; so that my body may become like the Great King of Medicines; so that my body and mind may become like a wish-fulfilling jewel; and so that I may practice the conduct of a Great Bodhisattva throughout the vast *dharmadhātu*, as far as the nature of space extends and until the end of the future, with no rest across all eons and all cycles of correct practice.
In order that, throughout all worlds, they may realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment without distinction; and so that, within a single hair-pore,
they may manifest throughout all hair-pores their birth, renunciation, the site of enlightenment, perfect awakening,
the turning of the great wheel of Dharma, and their return to great nirvana— will this be manifested?
Realizing the power and wisdom of the Buddha’s vast sphere, he manifests the appearance of a Buddha in accordance with the inclinations of all sentient beings,
causing those to be transformed to awaken to and cultivate tranquility moment by moment; for the sake of a single instant,
he universally pervades the nature of the cessation of all phenomena through a single perfect enlightenment, and expounds the Dharma with a single voice.
Essentially, it is to cause the minds of all sentient beings to be joyful; to demonstrate the power of practice that never ceases in order to reveal Great Nirvāṇa;
to establish all dharmas by demonstrating the ground of Great Wisdom;
and, through the supernatural transformations and miraculous powers of the wisdom of Dharma, to be able to pervade all worlds throughout the vast Dharma-realm, exhausting the nature of empty space.
Throughout the future limit, with all its kalpas and all its Buddhas never ceasing,
he formulates the tenth great vow to inspire bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
A Bodhisattva on the first stage (bhūmi) gives rise to such great vows, great resolute courage, and great renunciations."

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Supreme Joy, ten great doors of aspiration serve as the foremost, eliciting and bringing to perfection hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeyas of other correct aspirations; these great aspirations are, in turn, elicited by ten phrases of totality.

What are these ten? They are: the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings; the exhaustion of the realm of worlds; the exhaustion of the realm of space; the exhaustion of the realm of phenomena; the exhaustion of the realm of nirvana; the exhaustion of the realm of the appearance of Buddhas; the exhaustion of the realm of entry into the wisdom of the Tathāgata; the exhaustion of the realm of the objects of the mind; the exhaustion of the realm of the entry of wisdom into the sphere of the Buddha’s practice; and the exhaustion of the realm of the turning of the wheel of Dharma through the wisdom that turns the world.
If the realm of sentient beings were to have an end or exhaustion, then this great vow would also have an end or exhaustion;
even if the realm of the transformation of wisdom were to have an end or exhaustion, then this great vow would also have an end or exhaustion.

Yet the realm of sentient beings never comes to an end; may these roots of goodness likewise never come to an end. Even until the realm of the transformation of wisdom reaches its ultimate end, these roots of goodness shall never come to an end.
The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Translated at Longxing Monastery in Beiting, this is the continuation of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
the Stage of Utmost Joy. "Furthermore, having thus made these great vows, the bodhisattva attains a capable mind, a supple mind, and a well-disciplined mind, and achieves pure faith."

They are able to believe in the original practices entered by all Buddhas, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones; they believe in their cultivation and realization of the perfections, their cultivation and realization of the various sublime stages, their accomplishment of the powers, and their fulfillment of the fearlessnesses.

Because the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) cannot be eclipsed, and because they are brought forth by the inconceivable nature of all Buddha-dharmas, one enters into the profound realm of the Tathāgata—which is neither middle nor extreme—and achieves the fruit of faith that accords with the immeasurable conduct of the Tathāgatas.
To state the essentials: one is able to believe in all the correct practices of the bodhisattvas, up to and including the explanations and empowerments of the Buddha-ground.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva reflects thus: "The Dharma of the Buddhas is thus profound, thus tranquil, and thus quiescent."
Thus it is empty of intrinsic nature, thus signless, thus wishless,
thus boundless, thus vast, thus immeasurable, and thus difficult to realize; yet those foolish ordinary beings,
due to the continuity of their minds falling into wrong views and being entangled by the darkness of ignorance, [fail to perceive this].
Consciousness, by means of the high-raised banner of arrogance and its conceptualizations; by means of the attention of longing through the net of craving;
by means of the disposition that pursues the dense forest of flattery and deception; by means of the application toward rebirth in various realms associated with stinginess and envy;
by means of the accumulation of various karmas through greed, hatred, and delusion; and by means of the blazing flames of the mind through anger and resentment.
Driven by the activity induced through association with perversions, and with the mind, mentation,
and consciousness bound by the outflows of sensual desire and ignorance, the seeds give rise to the sprout of future existence within the three realms;
that is to say:
Name-and-form arise together and are inseparable; as name-and-form increase, they form the collection of the six sense bases.

Once the six sense bases are established, sensation arises through the causal condition of mutual contact. For one who takes delight in sensation, craving and grasping increase; from their increase, becoming is formed. Because this is accomplished, there arise birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the mass of suffering for sentient beings.
Thus they arise, devoid of self and what belongs to self, unreal and deceptive, empty and without function, motionless and dull, appearing like grass, trees, or shadows;
yet those sentient beings do not perceive nor understand this.

Seeing those sentient beings unable to attain liberation from the great mass of suffering, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion in order to uproot their suffering; and desiring to cause them to abide in the ultimate peace and bliss of nirvāṇa, he arouses great loving-kindness.
"Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva thus dwells in the first stage by means of this superior intentionality that accords with great loving-kindness and great compassion, their mind has no attachment to any worldly affairs. With wisdom, they long for the sublime knowledge of all Buddhas and practice great relinquishment (*mahātyāga*), giving away everything that can be given, namely:
wealth, grain, granaries, and so forth; or else gold, silver, *maṇi* gems, pearls,"
...or by giving lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, musaragalva, agate, money, and other goods;
or by giving precious jewels, ornaments, and necklaces;
or by giving excellent elephants, horses, chariots, and palanquins; or by giving pleasing monasteries and dwellings.
He may give away gardens, groves, towers, pavilions, flowing springs, and bathing pools;
or he may give away male and female slaves, servants, and attendants; or he may give away kingdoms, villages, towns, and royal capitals;
or he may give away wives, concubines, sons, and daughters; or he may give away everything that is dear to him.
He is able to relinquish all such things, giving away even his head, eyes, hands, feet, and all other parts of his body;
in all such acts of giving, his mind is free from attachment or regret. Seeking the sublime wisdom of all Buddhas through his insight, he is able to relinquish everything.
In this way, the Bodhisattva dwelling in the First Stage is able to achieve perfection.
Great Equanimity.

"Furthermore, once the bodhisattva has attained such mental dispositions of great loving-kindness, great compassion, and great equanimity, they seek out further all worldly and world-transcending matters of benefit in order to rescue and deliver all sentient beings;
while seeking them, their mind is free from weariness, whereby they attain this very nature of indefatigability."
Because one who is free from weariness does not become timid regarding any treatise, this bodhisattva achieves mastery of wisdom concerning all treatises.

By means of such wisdom that skillfully deliberates upon what should and should not be done in accordance with these various treatises, they practice correct conduct toward inferior, middling, and superior sentient beings as is appropriate and suitable for them; thus, they achieve mastery of worldly knowledge.
Having attained worldly knowledge, one should act in accordance with the proper time, the proper occasion, and the proper measure;

by adorning the continuity of the mind with shame and dread of blame, one diligently cultivates the applications for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, whereby the bodhisattva’s shame and dread of blame are perfected.

Within such correct application, one is able to transcend all [obstacles] and attain a state sustained by the power of being free from despondency and free from wavering; thus, the bodhisattva’s nature of being firmly sustained by strength arises.
Having attained this firm power of sustenance, the bodhisattva is then able to diligently make offerings to, serve, and properly practice within the teachings of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.

In this way, a bodhisattva accomplishes ten dharmas that purify the stages, namely: pure faith, loving-kindness, compassion, wisdom, equanimity, freedom from weariness, skill in all treatises, proficiency in worldly affairs, the adornment of shame and dread of blame, firmness and endurance, and making offerings to the Buddhas.

"When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), through vast vision and the power of aspiration, they directly perceive many Buddhas—many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas.

Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the bodhisattva, with a vast and superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), reveres, honors, serves, and makes offerings to them, presenting them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and all manner of life-sustaining necessities."
He offers various exquisite articles of pleasure to the assembly of the Sangha and pays them respect, dedicating all these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed enlightenment.

By means of this worship of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, they give rise to the skillful means for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings; they accomplish sentient beings through generosity and pleasant speech.
Regarding the latter two of the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they have not yet fully mastered them, but practice them solely by the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Regarding these ten perfections (*pāramitā*), one attains preeminence in the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), while the remaining perfections are practiced according to one’s strength and capacity; it is not that they are not practiced at all.

This bodhisattva makes offerings to all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as they truly are; cultivates and accomplishes the applications for maturing sentient beings; and upholds and practices the dharmas of the pure stages.
In this way, in this manner, these roots of goodness that have been dedicated toward omniscience become increasingly bright and pure, becoming fit for use according to one's will.
O Sons of the Buddha!

Just as a skilled goldsmith places gold of mineral origin into the fire, so that the more it is smelted and refined, the more it becomes increasingly bright, pure, and fit for use according to one's will.
O Sons of the Buddha!

You should know that it is likewise for the bodhisattva: just as they make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cultivate and bring to fruition the welfare of sentient beings, and apply themselves to upholding and practicing the dharmas of the pure stages, so too do these roots of goodness—which have been dedicated toward omniscience—become increasingly bright, pure, and fit for use according to their will.
"Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they should seek out and inquire from the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) regarding the characteristics of the first stage and the resulting attainments (*niṣyanda*). They should do so without weariness to fulfill the factors of this stage. The same applies to the characteristics and resulting attainments of the second through the tenth stages."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva should cultivate skillfulness regarding the remedies for the factors to be abandoned within each stage; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the dissolution and formation of the stages; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the cultivation for the attainment of the stages; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the purification of the branches of the stages; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the progression from stage to stage; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the stabilization in each stage; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the distinctions between the stages; he should cultivate skillfulness regarding the non-retrogression once each stage has been attained; and having purified all the bodhisattva stages, he should cultivate skillfulness until he enters the stage of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas have thus attained skill in the modes of practice that induce the various stages, they proceed from the first Bodhisattva stage upward without interval or rest, until they enter the tenth stage of knowledge. By means of the non-resting wisdom of the stages, they realize the light of the Buddha’s wisdom through the light of the wisdom of the stages.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is just as when a wise and skillful caravan leader, wishing to lead a great company of merchants toward a great city, first, before setting out, seeks out and inquires about the benefits along the way and the faults of turning back on the way; the specific benefits at various points along the route and the faults of turning back at those points; and he prepares the necessary provisions for the journey.
Although he has not yet set foot upon the path from its starting point, he understands it thoroughly; in this way, he is able to reach that great city.

This great caravan leader, having skillfully deliberated with such wisdom and being fully equipped with great provisions, crossed the perilous wilderness together with his great caravan; both he and his companions were entirely spared from distress and calamity, until they reached that great city in safety.

O Sons of the Buddha! It is just so with the Bodhisattva, the skillful and wise caravan leader. When he dwells in the first stage (*bhūmi*), he attains mastery in the remedies for what is to be remedied throughout all the stages; he attains mastery in the characteristics of the stages and their concordant flows; he attains mastery in the cultivation of the stages; he attains mastery in the purification of the factors of the stages; he attains mastery in the progression from stage to stage; he attains mastery in the stabilization within each stage; he attains mastery in the excellence of each stage; he attains mastery in the non-retrogression achieved at each stage; and having purified all the Bodhisattva stages, he attains mastery even unto entry into the stage of Tathāgata-knowledge.
At that time, the Bodhisattva has well acquired the vast and sublime provisions for the noble path of merit, as well as the provisions of wisdom through skillful discernment.

Intending to lead a great caravan of immeasurable sentient beings toward the great city of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), he must, prior to setting out, seek out and inquire from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) regarding the meritorious qualities of the noble paths of the various Bodhisattva stages, the faults of retrogression from those paths, the distinctions of excellence between the intervals of the paths, and the faults of retrogression during those intervals. He must perform what is required regarding the vast provisions of the noble path of merit and wisdom;
for even if one has not yet advanced from the first stage, by thus thoroughly understanding these matters, one will be able to reach the great city of omniscience.

By weighing matters with such wisdom, and possessing the provisions for the noble path of great merit and insight, he leads the great caravan of immeasurable sentient beings through the perilous wilderness of birth and death; both himself and his fellow travelers are entirely freed from suffering and affliction, until they reach the great city of omniscience in safety and peace.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
For this reason, Bodhisattvas should practice the distinct adornments of the stages without weariness.
O Sons of the Buddha!"
This is a brief explanation of the gateway for entering the first stage of the Bodhisattva, the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā*).
One who dwells herein is mostly born as a king of Jambudvīpa, attains great sovereignty, constantly protects the True Dharma,
is able to gather sentient beings through great giving, and is skillfully able to lead other sentient beings.
Far removed from the stain of stinginess, they constantly practice great giving without end.
Whatever deeds they perform— whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—
all of these are never apart from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha, nor apart from bodhicitta.
The mental engagement with the bodhisattva, the mental engagement with the bodhisattva’s practice, the mental engagement with the perfections, the mental engagement with the stages,

the mental engagement with the fearlessnesses, the mental engagement with the unique buddha-qualities, and so on, up to the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects that is in supreme and sublime correspondence and never separated from all modes of appearance.
He further made this aspiration:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; even unto the attainment of the knowledge of all modes."
Regarding the basis for this, if one joyfully exerts such diligence as to renounce all family, wealth, and status, and goes forth with pure faith into the Buddha’s holy teaching.
Once he has gone forth, in a single kṣaṇa, an instant, or a brief moment, he is able to realize one hundred bodhisattva samādhis and behold one hundred Tathāgatas.

He can fully comprehend the empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of those Buddhas; he can shake one hundred worlds, travel to one hundred buddha-fields, illuminate one hundred worlds, bring one hundred sentient beings to maturity, and maintain a lifespan for one hundred kalpas. He can enter one hundred kalpas each regarding the past and future limits, correctly discern one hundred Dharma-gates, manifest one hundred bodies, and from each body manifest a retinue of one hundred bodhisattvas surrounding him.

From this point forward, regarding the various displays of those bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration—whether through their superior vows, or their physical forms, or their radiance, or their supernormal powers, or their eyes, or their spheres of activity, or their voices, or their conduct, or their adornments, or their resolute understandings, or their empowerments, or their deeds—even for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons, these could not easily be enumerated.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there are those who have accumulated various virtues, Who fully cultivate pure and white dharmas;
Who make offerings to the Honored One of Gods and Humans, With pure intentions and great resolve."
Having achieved sublime and excellent resolve, and followed the path of compassion,
they have generated this unsurpassed mind in pursuit of the Buddha’s wisdom;
they do so to attain the ten powers of a Buddha, as well as the fearlessnesses.
To attain the unique qualities of a Buddha, to rescue and gather all classes of sentient beings,
to give rise to great compassion, to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields,
and to turn the Great Wheel of Dharma— for these purposes, they resolve upon this most supreme mind.
In a single thought-moment, one knows the three periods of time, yet without any discrimination;
though times are diverse and different, this is shown to the world.
Briefly stated, this is the seeking of all Buddhas and their every supreme merit.
One gives rise to the vast mind, equal in measure to the realm of empty space.
With compassion preceding wisdom as the primary guide, it is embraced by the wisdom of skillful means;
sustained by pure intention, the powers of the Tathāgata are immeasurable.
Unimpeded wisdom manifests before them, conforming to spontaneous gnosis;
receiving the instructions of the Buddha-dharma, they give rise to this most supreme mind.
As soon as the Son of the Buddha first generates such a wondrous jewel-mind, it is born.
Immediately transcending the stage of ordinary beings, one enters the bodhisattva’s state of right nature.
Born into the family of the Tathāgatas, one’s lineage is free from blemish;
inheriting the noble seed of all Buddhas, one is destined to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment.
As soon as such a mind arises, one immediately enters the first stage (*bhūmi*);
with an unshakable resolve and aspiration, one diligently cultivates the further applications (*prayoga*).
One experiences much joy and much delight, and likewise possesses much pure faith.
With a mind of supreme courage and a heart full of great joy,
one remains far removed from strife, harm, and malice; possessing a sense of shame and reverence,
being upright and sincere, and skillfully guarding all the sense faculties.
The peerless Savior of the World possesses all virtues and wisdom;
thinking, "I shall attain this state," one gives rise to supreme joy.
Having first entered the First Stage, one immediately transcends the five fears.
Non-sustenance, ill repute, death, The lower realms, and timidity in assemblies—
Because they do not cling to "I" And do not cling to "mine," Therefore,
the sons of the Buddhas Are far removed from all fears.
Always possessing faith and reverence, constantly practicing great compassion;
endowed with the virtues of shame and remorse, they increase wholesome dharmas day and night.
Delighting in roaming the garden of the True Dharma, they never tire of seeking extensive learning.
Contemplating the Dharma as it has been heard, one remains far removed from the practice of grasping and attachment.
Not coveting gain or offerings, one brings forth only a mind of equanimity;
with single-minded resolve seeking the Buddha’s wisdom, one takes the Ten Powers and other qualities as the object of contemplation.
Cultivating practice to reach the other shore, One remains far removed from flattery, vanity, and deception;
Practicing exactly as one speaks, One is always able to protect truthful speech.
Not defiling the family of the Tathāgata, One does not abandon the training of a bodhisattva.
The mind of omniscient wisdom is as immovable as the king of mountains;
Without abandoning worldly affairs, one enters the supramundane path;
With a mind of insatiable diligence, one cultivates the provisions for the factors of enlightenment.
Always maintaining constant and unwavering mindfulness, one seeks further the increasingly superior path;
being thus in accord with the Dharma is called "well-established in the first stage.
One brings forth great vows, great courage, and resolute great conduct.
May I be able to make offerings to and serve all the World-Honored Ones;
may I uphold the teachings of all Buddhas and embrace the path of the Great Sages;
may I constantly attend upon all Buddhas and practice the most supreme conduct.
Bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment, they proceed to all worlds;
purifying the Buddha-lands, they cause them to be filled with the wise.
Together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas, they practice with a single-minded equality.
Through the actions of body, speech, and mind, nothing that is done shall pass in vain.
Amidst all the realms of ordinary beings, may they simultaneously attain perfect enlightenment;
such great vows as these are immeasurable and boundless.
If the realm of sentient beings were to end, as would the realm of worlds,
the realm of space, the realm of phenomena, the realm of nirvana, the realm of the appearance of Buddhas in the world,
the realm of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, and the realm of the objects perceived by the mind—
Entering the realm of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the realm where worldly dharmas are transformed by wisdom—
if those realms were to ever come to an end, then my vow would likewise come to an end;
but as long as they have no end, my vow shall likewise never end.
Having thus made this great vow, with a mind supple and well-disciplined,
Able to believe in the Buddha’s merits, he observes all sentient beings.
Knowing that they arise from causes and conditions, he immediately gives rise to great compassion.
"Such suffering sentient beings—these I must now rescue and deliver.
For the sake of rescuing sentient beings, I shall practice various forms of giving:
my royal throne and precious jewels, as well as elephants, horses, and chariots."
Whether it be head, eyes, hands, or feet, Even unto the very flesh and blood of his body,
He is able to relinquish them all, His mind free from sorrow or regret.
In seeking various treatises and discourses, His heart never grows weary.
Skillfully understanding the meaning and intent of words, they are able to act in accordance with worldly ways.
Adorned by a sense of shame and remorse, their practice becomes increasingly firm;
they make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, honoring and respecting them with reverence.
Thus practicing constantly, without weariness day or night,
their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure, like gold repeatedly smelted and refined.
The Bodhisattva dwelling herein refines and purifies all the stages (bhūmis).
His actions are unimpeded, complete and uninterrupted.
Like a great caravan leader who leads a multitude of merchants,
he inquires about the dangers and ease of the path, reaching the great city in safety.
The Bodhisattva dwelling in the first stage should be known to be likewise;
with valor and without obstruction, they reach the tenth stage.
Abiding within this first stage, they act as a great king of merit.
Transforming sentient beings through the Dharma, with a compassionate heart free from harm;
ruling over Jambudvīpa, his transformative influence reached everywhere;
causing all to abide in great equanimity and achieve the wisdom of a Buddha.
Seeking the most supreme path, he renounced his royal throne;
Having gone forth within the Buddha’s teaching, he practiced with courageous diligence.
He attained one hundred samādhis and beheld one hundred Buddhas.
Shaking a hundred worlds, his wandering and illumination are likewise so.
He brings a hundred sentient beings to maturity, knows the events of a hundred eons,
enters a hundred Dharma-gates, and manifests a hundred transformation bodies.
And he manifests a hundred bodhisattvas as his retinue;
by the power of his sovereign vows, they exceed this number immeasurably.
Within the meaning of these stages, I have briefly described but a small portion thereof.
If one were to analyze it in detail, even ten billion eons would not suffice.
This is the supreme path of the Bodhisattvas, which brings benefit to all living beings;
thus have I now finished explaining the dharmas of the first stage.

2. The Bodhisattva Ground Free from Defilement, the Second. When the bodhisattvas heard this most supreme and subtle Dharma, their minds became entirely pure, and they all rejoiced with great delight.
They all rose from their seats and leaped into the midst of space;
scattering exquisite flowers everywhere, they simultaneously offered this praise: "Excellent!"
Vajragarbha! You of great wisdom and fearlessness have well expounded this stage, the dharma practiced by Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, knowing that the minds of the assembly were pure, [spoke].
Delighting to hear of all the characteristics of the practices belonging to the second bhūmi, they immediately entreated Vajragarbha:
“O Great Wisdom, we pray that you will expound upon the second bhūmi where these sons of the Buddha dwell; all of them long to hear it.”
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
If a bodhisattva who has well-polished the first stage (bhūmi) seeks the second bodhisattva stage of wisdom, they should give rise to ten kinds of mental dispositions."
What are the ten? They are:

the intention of rectitude, the intention of gentleness, the intention of capability, the intention of subduing, the intention of tranquility, the intention of nobility, the intention of non-mixture, the intention of non-attachment, the intention of excellence, and the intention of vastness.
Having generated these ten kinds of mental aspirations, one immediately attains abiding in the second bodhisattva stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*).
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stainless Stage, they naturally accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action. They distance themselves from taking life and renounce the sword and the staff; they harbor no malice or resentment, and are endowed with a sense of shame, dread of blame, benevolence, and forbearance. Toward all sentient beings who possess life, they constantly maintain a mind of compassion and the desire for their benefit and happiness.

This bodhisattva, even when conceptualizing a living being, does not cause them harm; how much less would they, while perceiving another sentient being as a sentient being, deliberately intend and carry out killing through coarse physical action?

He abstains from taking what is not given; he is always content with his own wealth and status, possesses compassion, and does not destroy the wealth and status of others. Regarding things belonging to another, he perceives them as another's property and never gives rise to the intent to steal;
he does not take even a blade of grass or a leaf if it is not given, much less any other articles of livelihood.

He abstains from sexual misconduct; he is always content with his own wife and does not seek the wives of others. He does not even give rise to a mind of lustful attachment toward women belonging to others, the wives or concubines of others, daughters of kinsmen, or women protected by legal marriage arrangements—let alone engaging in intercourse with those of both sexes or through improper orifices.

He abstains from false speech, always speaking words that are truthful, genuine, and timely; even in his dreams he is unable to utter false speech through the intention to deceive others by concealing what he has seen, heard, or known, let alone do so intentionally while awake.

He abstains from divisive speech; for the sake of never causing dissension among sentient beings and for the sake of freedom from affliction and harm, he practices right conduct. He does not repeat words heard here to those there in order to cause division, nor does he repeat words heard there to those here in order to cause division.
He causes those who are not divided not to be divided, and he prevents further increase in those already divided.
He takes no pleasure in divisiveness, finds no delight in divisiveness, and does not utter divisive speech, whether it be true or false.

He abstains from harsh speech; that is, he completely avoids all speech that stings, bites, is coarse, fierce, or piercing toward others; speech that causes others to feel resentment and turn away with a cruel expression; speech that is vulgar, base, and loathsome to hear; speech uttered out of anger that displeases the listener;

speech that burns the heart like fire and gives rise to enmity; speech that provokes mental affliction and is not to be cherished; speech that destroys the mental continuum of oneself and others—such speech as this he entirely leaves behind.

Instead, he constantly utters speech that is moistening, soft, and pleasing; deeply worth hearing, such that the listener feels joy; speech that enters well into the heart; speech that is elegant, refined, and beloved by many; speech that delights many and causes the heart to leap for joy; speech that brings gladness to the heart and can purify the mental continuum of both oneself and others.

He abstains from frivolous speech; he speaks with careful reflection, speaking at the proper time, speaking truthfully, speaking meaningfully, speaking in accordance with the Dharma, speaking in accordance with reason, speaking skillfully for the sake of discipline, speaking in measured portions, and speaking with due deliberation regarding the causal origins of things. Even in jest, he always speaks with careful reflection, let alone intentionally uttering distracted or idle words.

His mind is free from greed; regarding the desires and pleasures of others, their wealth and status, and their possessions, he does not give rise to craving, nor does he seek, wish for, or harbor a greedy mind toward them.

With a mind free from malice, they constantly give rise toward all sentient beings to a heart of loving-kindness, a heart of benefit, a heart of compassion, a heart of peace and happiness, a heart of moistening grace, and a heart that gathers and benefits the entire world; forever abandoning anger, resentment, envy, and hatred, they always contemplate acting in accordance with benevolence, kindness, and helpfulness, attaining right view and following the true path.

Having abandoned various forms of divination, the views of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, and heterodox observances, their vision is upright and true, free from flattery and deception, and they give rise to a resolute intention toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus maintains the ten paths of wholesome action without interruption or deficiency, they give rise to such an intention and aspiration: 'All the perilous, foul, and evil abysses into which sentient beings fall are entirely due to their engagement in the ten paths of unwholesome action;
therefore, I shall abide in right practice myself, and I shall also exhort others to abide in right practice.'"
Why is this? It is impossible for one who cannot practice right conduct oneself to cause others to practice it.
Furthermore, he reflects as follows:
"From the present experience of the ten unwholesome paths of action, there arise the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, from the present experience of the ten wholesome paths of action, there arise the distinctions of rebirth in the human realm up to the Peak of Existence."

From this point forward, through the cultivation of the aspects of wisdom, these very ten paths of wholesome action constitute the Śrāvaka Vehicle because the mind is narrow and inferior, because there is fear of the three realms, because great compassion is lacking, because understanding is attained by hearing sounds from others, and because one follows the conduct of the Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, by cultivating and purifying the ten paths of wholesome action beyond this point, one achieves the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha because of awakening through self-realization rather than being led by others, because of lacking the skillful means of great compassion, and because of realizing the profound nature of dependent origination.

Furthermore, by cultivating and purifying the ten paths of wholesome action beyond this point—due to the vastness and immeasurability of the mind, the presence of compassion, being embraced by skillful means, the arousal of great vows, not abandoning any sentient beings, and the direct realization of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable wisdom—one is able to accomplish the pure, ultimate, and vast right practice that purifies the various stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.
