Furthermore, because these progressively superior paths of the ten virtuous actions are purified in every respect, they can even bring about the realization and cultivation of the ten powers of the Buddhas and all other Buddha-dharmas; therefore, I shall now apply myself with diligence toward the purification of all aspects of renunciation, which is common to all.
"O Sons of the Buddha! A bodhisattva should train even further in this manner.
Furthermore, the ten unwholesome paths of action, when accumulated to a superior degree through frequent performance, serve as the cause for rebirth in the hells."
Through its medium degree, it becomes the cause for rebirth as an animal;
through its mild degree, it becomes the cause for the realm of hungry ghosts.
Killing leads one toward the hells, leads one toward the animal realm, and leads one toward the realm of hungry ghosts.
If one is again born among humans, it will lead to two kinds of results:
first, a short lifespan;
second, much illness.
Taking what is not given leads one to the hells, leads one to the animal realm, and leads one to the realm of hungry ghosts;
furthermore, if one is born among humans, it brings about two kinds of results:
first, a lack of material wealth.
Second, sharing one's wealth and resources leads to misconduct in sensual desires,
which leads to rebirth in the hells, leads to rebirth among animals, and leads to rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts;
furthermore, if one is born among humans, it brings about two kinds of results:
First, one's wife will not be chaste;
second, one's kinsmen and retinue will be unreliable.
False speech leads one to the hells, leads one to the animal realm, and leads one to the realm of hungry ghosts.
If one is again born among human beings, two kinds of results are drawn forth:
first, being frequently subjected to slander;
second, being deceived by others.
Divisive speech leads to rebirth in the hells, leads to rebirth among animals, and leads to rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts;
furthermore, if one is born among humans, it brings about two kinds of results:
first, estrangement from one's kin and followers.
Second, one will frequently be reviled.
Harsh speech leads one to the hells, leads one to the animal realm, and leads one to the realm of hungry ghosts;
furthermore, if one is reborn among humans, it brings about two kinds of results:
First, hearing what is disagreeable;
second, speech that leads to much contention and litigation.
Idle chatter leads to the hells, leads to the animal realm, and leads to the realm of hungry ghosts.
If one is born again among human beings, two kinds of results are drawn forth:
first, the claim that there is no one who experiences [karmic retribution];
second, a lack of clarity in one's speech and reasoning.
Greed leads to rebirth in the hells, leads to rebirth as an animal, and leads to the realm of hungry ghosts;
furthermore, if one is born among humans, it brings about two kinds of results:
first, a mind that knows no contentment.
Second, having many desires and no contentment.
Anger leads one to the hells, leads one to the animal realm, and leads one to the realm of hungry ghosts;
furthermore, if one is born among humans, it draws forth two kinds of results:
First, they are constantly sought out by others for their faults;
second, they are perpetually afflicted and harmed by others.
Wrong views lead them to the hells, lead them to the animal realm, and lead them to the realm of hungry ghosts.
If one is born again among humans, it will lead to two kinds of results:
first, falling into wrong views;
second, a mind full of flattery and deception.
In this way, these ten unwholesome paths of action can give rise to such immeasurable and boundless aggregates of great suffering;

therefore, I now forever distance myself from these ten unwholesome paths of action and enjoy the bliss of the Dharma within the inner garden of the Dharma. Thus, while the Bodhisattva himself dwells securely in the ten wholesome paths of action, he also exhorts others to abide therein.

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva further gives rise toward sentient beings to a mind of benefit, a mind of happiness, a mind of compassion, a mind of pity, a mind of gathering, a mind of protection, a mind of self, a mind of a preceptor, and a mind of a teacher."
He formed this thought: "Alas!
Sentient beings have fallen into wrong views; they follow erroneous reflections, conform to perverse inclinations, and wander upon the bypaths within the dense forest."
I shall cause them to return to the path of right conduct and right view, and lead them to abide securely within the Dharma as it truly is.
These sentient beings are constantly and incessantly estranged from one another, contending and bullying, with their fury and resentment burning fiercely;
I shall cause them to dwell in unsurpassed great compassion.
These sentient beings have no sense of contentment in their minds; they crave the wealth of others and sustain themselves through wrong livelihood.
I shall cause them to abide in the Dharma of right livelihood, consisting of pure actions of body, speech, and mind.

These sentient beings revolve according to the causes and conditions of greed, hatred, and delusion; they are constantly scorched by the flames of various afflictions and no longer seek out the skillful means for the essential path of liberation.
I shall cause them to extinguish all the blazing fires of affliction and abide in the disaster-free, cool tranquility of nirvana.

These sentient beings are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, clouded by the cataracts of delusion; they have entered the vast, dense forest of gloom, are far removed from the light of wisdom, have fallen into great obscurity, and have entered upon the perilous path of dogmatic views.
I shall cause them to obtain the unobstructed, pure eye of wisdom, so that they may know the true nature of all phenomena as it is, without following the teachings of others.

These sentient beings gallop through the vast wilderness and perilous paths of birth and death; they are on the verge of falling into the deep pits of the evil destinies of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; they are cast into the snares of false and evil views, shrouded by the thicket of ignorance, and travel upon deviant paths. Having lost the eye of wisdom and lacking a great guide, they wander within the realm of Pāpīyān with the notion that it is not a place of departure. Captured by bandits and far removed from the skillful guides of Great Compassion, they enter the dense forest of the Māras' inclinations and have become exceedingly distant from the inclinations of the Buddhas.
"I shall rescue and deliver these sentient beings from such a perilous wilderness of birth and death, causing them to dwell securely in the fearless great city of omniscience."

These sentient beings have sunk into a great torrent; they are submerged by waves and plunged into the realms of desire, existence, and views. Driven along the swift current of birth and death by the flood of ignorance, they are tossed about upon the river of craving, rushing and surging so violently that they have no leisure for observation. They are overwhelmed by thoughts of desire, malice, and harm, and are seized by the rākṣasa of the view of a self-identity. They enter into the eddies and whirlpools of the habitual tendencies of desire, sinking within them as they are cast about by the great waves of the mud of worldly delight. On the sandbanks of pride, they have no refuge and cannot transcend the village of the six sense bases, being far removed from those skilled in means who can deliver them.

By the power of the roots of goodness of my great compassion, I shall rescue them and establish them on the island of omniscience—a place free from calamity, tranquil and detached from dust, devoid of all terrors.

These sentient beings are confined within that state of manifold suffering, grief, and affliction; they are bound by the continuous fetters of aversion and attachment toward what is disagreeable and agreeable; they constantly revolve in association with lamentation and sorrow; they are shackled by the manacles and chains of craving; and they are obscured and imprisoned within the dark thicket of ignorance in the fortress of the three realms.
I shall cause them to forever leave the three realms behind and abide in unobstructed, ultimate *nirvāṇa*.

These sentient beings are attached to a self; unable to progress beyond their clinging to the aggregates, they act in accordance with the four inversions, dwell in the desolate villages of the six sense bases, are pursued by the venomous snakes of the four great elements, and are tormented by the enemy thieves of the five aggregates, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
I shall cause them to abide in the most supreme state of non-reliance and non-attachment—namely, the nirvana without remainder that is free from all obstructions.

These sentient beings possess inferior, timid, and narrow resolute conviction; upon hearing of the unsurpassed mind of omniscience, even if they seek liberation, they give rise only to the intentions of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles.
I shall cause them to contemplate the subtle and wondrous Buddha-dharma, so that they may abide in the vast and unsurpassed bodhicitta.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Thus, sustained by the power of conforming to pure ethical discipline, the bodhisattva skillfully brings forth all their activities."

When dwelling on the Bodhisattva stage *Vimalā* (The Stainless), through vast vision and the power of aspiration, he beholds many Buddhas—many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas, many koṭis, many hundreds of koṭis, many thousands of koṭis, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas. Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the Bodhisattva, with a vast and superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), honors, respects, serves, and makes offerings to them; he presents them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicines for the treatment of illness, and all necessities of life, offers various exquisite articles of pleasure for Bodhisattvas, and pays homage to the Saṅgha community.

Dedicating these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they further receive instruction on the ten paths of wholesome action from the Tathāgatas, the perfectly awakened ones, with a heart of deep respect; and according to what they have received, they shall never forget them until they reach final enlightenment.

Thus, throughout immeasurable eons, immeasurable hundreds of eons, immeasurable thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, immeasurable koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of koṭis of eons, immeasurable thousands of koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of eons, because this bodhisattva has remained far removed from the stains of stinginess and the violation of precepts, their generosity and pure ethical discipline become purified and perfected.
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is just as when genuine gold is placed in alum stone and, having been refined according to the proper method, becomes free from all impurities and becomes even more brilliant and pure;

so too it is for a Bodhisattva dwelling in this Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), for by remaining far removed from the stains of stinginess and immoral conduct throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, their generosity and pure ethical discipline become perfectly purified and fulfilled.

Nevertheless, among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva’s loving speech (*priyavāditā*) is predominant; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is preeminent; as for the remaining perfections, he practices them according to his strength and capacity, though not without doing so.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the second stage of the bodhisattva, the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are mostly reborn as a universal monarch (*cakravartin-rāja*), attaining mastery over the Dharma and being endowed with the seven treasures. Possessing sovereign power, they are able to remove the defilement of transgressing the precepts in sentient beings, skillfully establishing those beings in the path of the ten virtuous actions."

Whatever deeds they perform—whether through generosity, or through kind speech, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation—all of these are never apart from the mental engagement with the Buddha, the mental engagement with the Dharma, the mental engagement with the Saṅgha, the mental engagement with bodhisattvas, the mental engagement with the bodhisattva practices, the mental engagement with the perfections (pāramitās), the mental engagement with the stages (bhūmis), the mental engagement with the fearlessnesses, the mental engagement with the unique qualities of a buddha, and even until they are not apart from the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) that is perfectly associated with all supreme and wondrous characteristics.
He further made this aspiration:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; even unto the attainment of the state that serves as the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."
If one delights in initiating such diligence, abandoning all family, wealth, and status, and goes forth into the holy teaching of the Buddha with pure faith;

having gone forth, in a single kṣaṇa, a muhūrta, or a brief moment, one can realize a thousand bodhisattva samādhis, see a thousand Buddhas, and fully comprehend the empowerments bestowed by those Buddhas.

One can shake a thousand worlds, travel to a thousand buddha-fields, illuminate a thousand worlds, bring a thousand sentient beings to maturity, maintain a lifespan for a thousand kalpas, penetrate a thousand kalpas of the past and future, correctly discern a thousand dharma-gates, manifest a thousand bodies, and each body can appear surrounded by a retinue of a thousand bodhisattvas.

From this point forward, regarding these bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration, by virtue of their superior vows, all their playful manifestations—whether of body, light, supernormal powers, eyes, spheres of activity, sounds, conduct, adornments, resolute understandings, or deeds—could not easily be enumerated even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Uprightness, flexibility, and capability; Subduing, tranquility, and virtuous goodness;
Freedom from distraction, lack of attachment, and supreme vastness— By means of these ten aspirations, one enters the second stage.”
Abiding here, one accomplishes the merit of ethical discipline: Far removed from taking life, free from malice and harm;
Abstaining from taking what is not given and from sexual misconduct; Free from deceit, slander, and frivolous speech;
Without craving for wealth or status, always compassionate; Possessing right view and a straightforward mind, free from flattery and hypocrisy.
Free from danger, luxury, and pride, supremely disciplined and gentle, Acting according to the teachings without negligence.

The various sufferings endured in the hells and as animals, And the blazing, fierce flames of the hungry ghosts— All these arise solely from the consequences of transgressions; I shall leave them behind and dwell in the Garden of Dharma.
One may take birth at will among human beings, And even attain all the joys and pleasures up to the Peak of Existence;
The paths of the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas— All are accomplished by means of the ten wholesome actions.
Reflecting thus with heedfulness, he maintains pure precepts himself and teaches others to protect theirs;
seeing again the multitude of sentient beings undergoing various sufferings, his great compassion increases all the more.
Ordinary fools, with their perverse wisdom and incorrect understanding, constantly harbor resentment and engage in much contention;
they greedily pursue sensory objects without end—may I cause them to eliminate the three poisons.
Enveloped and shrouded by the great darkness of ignorance, They have entered the treacherous paths and the net of false views;
Bound by enemies in the wilderness of birth and death, I shall cause them to crush the demonic maras.
Distracted by the four floods, the mind is submerged; bound within the three realms, one undergoes manifold sufferings.
Calculating the aggregates as a house and the self as dwelling within it, I diligently practice the Path in order to deliver them.
If, while seeking liberation, their resolve becomes inferior and they abandon the supreme wisdom of the Buddha,
I desire to establish them in the Mahāyāna, inciting them to diligent effort without weariness.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here accumulates merit, Beholding immeasurable Buddhas and making offerings to them all;
Cultivating goodness for billions of eons, it becomes even more radiant, Like refining pure gold with alum.
The Buddha’s heirs dwelling here act as wheel-turning kings, Universally transforming sentient beings through the practice of the ten virtues;
Cultivating all wholesome dharmas, They achieve the Ten Powers to save the world.
Desiring to renounce royal sovereignty and wealth, he immediately abandoned the household life to rely upon the Buddha’s teaching;
through a single moment of courageous diligence, he attained a thousand samādhis and beheld a thousand Buddhas.
All the various supernormal powers, the bodhisattvas on this stage can manifest;
yet what is accomplished through the power of their vows exceeds even this, as they liberate all beings with immeasurable mastery.
The supreme conduct of Bodhisattvas practiced by those who benefit all the worlds—
such are the virtues of the second stage, which have been expounded for the sake of the sons of the Buddhas.
The Second Bhūmi, the Stainless (*vimalā*), of the Bodhisattva is completed. The *Buddhabhāṣita-daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll Two.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Translated at Longxing Monastery in Beiting.
The Third Bodhisattva Bhūmi: The Radiant (*Prabhākārī*) Having heard of the practice of this stage, O Son of the Buddha, The realm of the bodhisattvas is inconceivable;
There is none who does not rejoice with a respectful heart, Scattering flowers into the air as an offering.
He praised him, saying: "Excellent!
O Great Sage Lord!"
With a compassionate mind, one takes pity upon all sentient beings;
skillfully explaining the laws of discipline for the wise—this is the characteristic of practice in the second bhūmi.
These are the subtle and wondrous practices of all bodhisattvas, which are truly without variation or distinction.
For the sake of benefiting all living beings, you have thus proclaimed this most pure teaching.
O you who are honored by all devas and humans, we pray that you will expound upon the third bhūmi;
may you fully elucidate the activities of wisdom that accord with the Dharma, according to their respective spheres.
The giving and pure ethical discipline of the Great Sage, As well as patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
And the path of skillful means, compassion, and loving-kindness— I pray that you will explain this pure path of the Buddha.
Then Vimukticandra again requested, saying:
“O Great Master Vajragarbha, free from fear!
We pray that you will speak of the entry into the third stage and the virtues of those with gentle minds.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, having thoroughly purified their superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) in the second stage, desires to enter the third bodhisattva stage, they should enter it by means of ten kinds of mental intentions."

What are these ten? They are: the mental application of the intention of a pure mind; the mental application of the intention of a settled mind; the mental application of the intention of renunciation; the mental application of the intention of detachment from desire; the mental application of the intention of non-retrogression; the mental application of the intention of firmness; the mental application of the intention of ardor; the mental application of the intention of valor; the mental application of the intention of excellence; and the mental application of the intention of vastness. By means of these ten mental applications of intention, the bodhisattva enters the third stage.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this third stage, they observe all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and see them as entirely impermanent, suffering, impure, and unreliable; they see that they ultimately perish and cannot endure for long, arising and ceasing in every moment, not coming from the past, not going to the future, and not abiding in the present.

When the bodhisattva thus observes all conditioned phenomena without error, he further perceives that the body has no savior and no one to rely upon; it is associated with sorrow, lamentation, and distress; bound by love and hatred, it abounds in suffering and affliction, without any stability or accumulation.

Having seen that the fierce fires of greed, hatred, and delusion are ablaze and that all manner of illnesses increase together, one should cause the mind to advance beyond all conditioned formations and proceed toward the seal of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

This bodhisattva beholds the Tathāgata’s wisdom as inconceivable, unequaled, immeasurable, difficult to attain, unmixed, free from calamity, and free from affliction; having reached the city of fearlessness, they never again regress, and are able to rescue sentient beings from immeasurable suffering.

When a bodhisattva thus perceives the immeasurable benefits of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and perceives the immeasurable afflictions of all conditioned activities, they further give rise to ten kinds of mental dispositions toward sentient beings.

What are these ten? They are: the mental disposition of being solitary and without refuge; the mental disposition of perpetual poverty; the mental disposition of a mind ablaze with the fierce fires of greed, hatred, and delusion; the mental disposition of being imprisoned within the jail of existence (*bhava*); the mental disposition of a mind perpetually and uninterruptedly shrouded by the dense forest of afflictions (*kleśa*); the mental disposition of an inability to observe [the truth]; the mental disposition of a lack of desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*); the mental disposition of having lost one's way in the Buddha-dharma; the mental disposition of following the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); and the mental disposition of having lost the path to liberation. These are the ten kinds of mental dispositions that are generated.
Having thus perceived the manifold calamities and afflictions within the realm of sentient beings, the bodhisattva arouses great diligence and reflects:

"I must rescue these sentient beings; I must bring them to liberation; I must purify them; I must extract them [from suffering]; I must cause them to enter [the path]; I must cause them to abide [in it]; I must cause them to rejoice; I must cause them to find delight; I must cause them to be disciplined; and I must cause them to attain quiescence."

Thus, the Bodhisattva develops a profound sense of weary detachment toward those conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and gives rise to a heart of compassionate affection for all sentient beings. Perceiving the great benefit in the sublime wisdom of the Buddha, they take the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their foundation;
to rescue sentient beings, they diligently cultivate preparatory practices, reflecting thus:
"These sentient beings have fallen into the defilements of manifold sufferings and afflictions. By what path can I deliver them and cause them to abide in ultimate, eternal bliss and *nirvāṇa*?"
Then this bodhisattva reflects: "All these do not depart from the sphere of liberation through unobstructed wisdom;
and this liberation through unobstructed wisdom does not depart from the realization of all phenomena as they truly are."
To awaken to all these phenomena as they truly are is not to be separate from the wisdom of non-action and the practice of non-arising;
this light of wisdom is not separate from the sublime discernment of skillful meditative concentration and the observation of sublime wisdom;
furthermore, this skillful discernment of meditative concentration and the observation of sublime wisdom are all inseparable from the skillfulness of extensive learning.

With this wisdom of skillful observation, the Bodhisattva acts solely for the purpose of seeking the True Dharma; day and night he yearns for the Dharma and hears it without weariness. He contemplates the Dharma, delights in the Dharma, relies upon the Dharma, is devoted to the Dharma, abides in the Dharma, requires the Dharma, takes refuge in the Dharma, returns to the Dharma, follows the Dharma, and practices the Dharma.

When a bodhisattva thus cultivates correct practice in pursuit of the Buddha-dharma, there is not the slightest thing—whether articles of livelihood, wealth, grain, or storehouses—that they cannot relinquish; they never entertain the thought that this is difficult to do, but rather conceive the thought that a person who teaches the Dharma is difficult to encounter.

For the sake of the Buddha-dharma, there is not the slightest external object they will not relinquish, nor the slightest internal thing they will not relinquish; there is no teacher whom they do not vow to serve, setting aside pride and arrogance, humbling their mind to receive and practice [the teachings], and there is no physical hardship they do not vow to endure.
If one hears even a single four-line verse of the Buddha's Dharma and leaps with joy, this is superior to obtaining a great heap of precious jewels that fills the entire trichiliocosm.
If one hears a single verse of well-spoken, sublime Dharma, the joy is superior to obtaining the rank of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

Hearing the Dharma never heard before—which was spoken by the Buddha, which can lead to perfect enlightenment, and which can purify the bodhisattva practice—one leaps with joy; this is superior to obtaining all the positions of Śakra, Brahmā, and other kings, remaining in those most noble stations for hundreds of thousands of eons.
Suppose someone were to say:

"I have a single verse of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which can lead to perfect enlightenment and purify the bodhisattva conduct; if you can now cast yourself into a pit of fiercely blazing flames and endure extreme suffering, I shall speak it for you."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"For the sake of even a single phrase of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which can lead to equal and perfect enlightenment and purify the conduct of a Bodhisattva, I would cast myself even from the Brahma Heaven into a fire-pit as vast as the Trichiliocosm filled with blazing flames, let alone a small fire-pit."

Furthermore, for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, we should be willing to remain for a long time in the great hells and various perilous evil realms to undergo immense suffering; how much more so should we endure the various minor sufferings among human beings?
Having thus initiated such diligence to seek the True Dharma, the Bodhisattva is able to inwardly examine it according to principle as he has heard it.
Having heard the True Dharma, he dwells alone in a quiet place and, with his own mind, resolves and reflects thus:

"Only by practicing the Dharma correctly through practice in accordance with the Dharma can one be said to be in conformity with the Buddha's teachings; it is not attained through purity by means of verbal expression alone."

When the Bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Stage (Prabhākārī-bhūmi), desiring to practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, he becomes detached from desires and detached from all evil and unwholesome states; possessing applied thought and sustained thought, born of detachment and filled with joy and happiness, he enters and fully abides in the first dhyāna.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought and possesses the joy and bliss born of concentration.

With the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body"; thus he enters and dwells fully established in the third dhyāna.
With the fading away of joy and sorrow, and with the prior cessation of pleasure and pain, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva, by transcending all perceptions of form, by the disappearance of all perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, perceives infinite space and enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space in every respect, knowing infinite consciousness, he enters and fully dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness in every respect, knowing there is nothing whatsoever, he enters and fully dwells in the sphere of nothingness.
Having transcended the sphere of nothingness in every respect, perceiving neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and fully dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is solely for the sake of practicing in accordance with the Dharma and following the Dharma; it is not out of attachment to that state of abiding.

"Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates a mind associated with loving-kindness—vast, non-dual, immeasurable, free from resentment, free from enmity, unobstructed, and devoid of malice—which extends everywhere throughout all worlds, reaching as far as the realm of phenomena and the limits of space, universally covering all worlds with loving-kindness and dwelling therein in full stability."
The cultivation of the mind associated with compassion and the cultivation of the mind associated with sympathetic joy are likewise so.

He cultivates the mind associated with equanimity—vast, non-dual, immeasurable, free from resentment, free from enmity, unobstructed, and free from affliction or harm—pervading all things, reaching to the limit of the dharma-realm and the full extent of space; within all worlds, he dwells fully established, universally covering all the world-realms with equanimity.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva experiences immeasurable miraculous transformations that shake the great earth: he makes one body into many bodies and many bodies into one; he appears and disappears with unimpeded swiftness, passing through walls, barriers, and mountain crags as if walking through space; he travels cross-legged through the air like a bird; he emerges from and sinks into the earth as if it were water; he treads upon water as if it were solid ground; his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire, while from his body flows water like a great cloud; and even these sun and moon, which possess such great divine merit and majestic power, he touches with his hand, exercising mastery over his physical form even as far as the Brahma world.

With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, they hear all sounds of both humans and devas, whether near or far, even down to the voices of mosquitoes, gnats, dung beetles, and the like.

With the knowledge of others' minds, he knows the minds of other sentient beings as they truly are: he knows a mind with greed as a mind with greed; he knows a mind free from greed as a mind free from greed; [he knows] a mind with hatred and one free from hatred; a mind with delusion and one free from delusion; a defiled mind and one free from defilement; a narrow mind, a vast mind, an immeasurable mind, a concentrated mind, a scattered mind; a mind in meditative absorption and one emerged from absorption; a liberated mind and one not yet liberated; a slack mind and one that is alert; and a coarse mind and a subtle mind—all he knows as they truly are.
In this way, by means of the knowledge of others' minds, the bodhisattva personally and directly knows the thoughts and mental activities of other sentient beings and other individuals.

By means of the knowledge of past lives, one recollects immeasurable past existences; that is, one is able to recollect one's own and others' single birth, two, three, four, five, up to ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and even a hundred births, many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of births, as well as eons of formation, eons of destruction, and eons of both formation and destruction, even up to recollecting immeasurable eons of formation and destruction. One recollects a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, a *koṭi* of eons, a hundred *koṭis*, a thousand *koṭis*, a hundred thousand *koṭis*, and even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *nayutas* of eons—all of which one is able to recollect.

That is to say, one can recollect various past lives in detail or in brief: "In a former life, I was in such a place, with such a name, such a clan, such a lineage, such a physical appearance, such food and drink, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure; passing away from that place, I was reborn here; and passing away from this place, I was reborn there, with such a physical appearance and such speech. Thus, one is able to recollect all such matters of past abodes.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees sentient beings as they die and are reborn—whether beautiful or ugly, in happy or miserable realms, inferior or superior—and he knows all such classes of sentient beings exactly as they are, according to their karma.

It refers to those sentient beings who have accomplished misconduct of body, speech, and mind; who revile the noble ones; and who are possessed of wrong views. Due to the causal conditions of their present experience resulting from karma of wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the perilous evil destinies and are born in hell.

Furthermore, those sentient beings who have accomplished virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind, who praise the noble ones, and who possess right view—by virtue of the causes and conditions of their present experience resulting from karma of right view—upon the dissolution of the body after death, they shall ascend to the happy realms and be born among the devas to enjoy various pleasures.

In this way, with the divine eye-element purified beyond that of humans, by means of common physical forms and common speech, the Bodhisattva perceives sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, in happy or miserable realms, inferior or superior—and knows all such classes of sentient beings exactly as they are, according to their karmic conduct.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva enters and emerges from those meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*) at will; yet, they do not take birth through the power of those states. Rather, if they perceive that in a particular place the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) can be swiftly perfected, they take birth therein by the power of their vow (*praṇidhāna*).

"When a bodhisattva dwells in this Radiant Stage (prabhākari-bhūmi), through vast vision and by the power of their vows, they directly behold many Buddhas—many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas."

Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the bodhisattva, with a vast and superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), reveres, honors, serves, and makes offerings to them, presenting robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and various articles of life; he offers the exquisite articles of pleasure belonging to bodhisattvas and shows reverence to the Saṅgha community, dedicating these roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

With earnest devotion, he serves the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and in their presence reverently listens to the Dharma; having heard it, he receives and maintains it, practicing according to his capacity.
"Furthermore, the bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as being without transition or transformation, nor subject to destruction, yet existing through causes and conditions;
and for this bodhisattva, all bonds of desire become increasingly attenuated;
all bonds of form, all bonds of existence, and all bonds of ignorance likewise become increasingly attenuated."
All fetters of views have already been severed.

While dwelling in this Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), for immeasurable eons—immeasurable hundreds of eons, immeasurable thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of eons, immeasurable koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of koṭis of eons, immeasurable thousands of koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of eons—because they do not accumulate [unwholesome states], their false greed is severed; because they do not accumulate them, their false hatred is severed; because they do not accumulate them, their false delusion is severed; and all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is just as when a skilled goldsmith personally refines genuine gold; once it is free from all impurities, its weight does not diminish.

So too it is for a Bodhisattva dwelling in this Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*): throughout immeasurable hundreds of eons, even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *koṭi-nayuta* eons, because they do not accumulate false greed and have eliminated it, because they do not accumulate false anger and have eliminated it, and because they do not accumulate false delusion and have eliminated it, all their roots of goodness become increasingly bright and pure.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva becomes even more patient, and his gentle disposition attains purity.

Moreover, his delightful disposition, his non-angry disposition, his unshakable disposition, his unclouded disposition, his disposition free from high and low, his disposition that does not seek to bring sentient beings down, his disposition that expects no recompense, his disposition free from flattery and deception, and his disposition free from the thicket of afflictions—all these become increasingly pure.

Among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva’s practice of beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) is predominant; among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is especially enhanced, while he practices the remaining perfections according to his strength and capacity, though not without doing so.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the Bodhisattvas' third stage, the Luminous (*Prabhākari*).

When Bodhisattvas dwell securely in this stage, they for the most part take birth as Śakra, Lord of the Devas; possessing sovereign power, they skillfully transform sentient beings, causing them to leave behind desire and greed, and they skillfully rescue and protect those submerged in the mire of desire."

Whatever actions they perform—whether through generosity, or kind speech, or beneficial conduct, or cooperation—all of these are never apart from the mental engagement with the Buddha, the mental engagement with the Dharma, the mental engagement with the Saṅgha, the mental engagement with Bodhisattvas, the mental engagement with the Bodhisattva practices, the mental engagement with the perfections (pāramitās), the mental engagement with the stages (bhūmis), the mental engagement with the powers of a Buddha, the mental engagement with the fearlessnesses, and the mental engagement with the unique qualities of a Buddha; indeed, they are never apart from the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) that is perfectly associated with all supreme and sublime characteristics.
He further made this vow:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most subtle, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; even unto attaining the state that is the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."

"If one delights in initiating such diligence, abandoning all family, wealth, and status to take refuge in the Holy Teaching and go forth with pure faith, then in a single kṣaṇa, a muhūrta, or a brief moment, one can realize hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
see hundreds of thousands of Buddha-Tathāgatas and fully comprehend the empowerments bestowed by those Buddhas;

shake hundreds of thousands of worlds; travel to hundreds of thousands of buddha-fields; illuminate hundreds of thousands of worlds; bring hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to maturity; abide for hundreds of thousands of kalpas; and penetrate hundreds of thousands of kalpas regarding the past and future limits."

They are able to correctly discern and select among hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates; they manifest hundreds of thousands of bodies, and each body can manifest itself surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.

From this point upward, for those bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration, by virtue of their superior vows, all their playful manifestations—whether of body, light, supernormal powers, eyes, spheres of activity, voice, conduct, adornments, resolute understandings, or deeds—cannot easily be counted even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Purified and dwelling securely in the mind of renunciation, Free from desire, non-regressive, and steadfast;
Blazing, courageous, supreme, wondrous, and vast— By means of these ten minds, one enters the third stage."
When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they contemplate that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and impure;
they are without refuge, subject to decay, and do not endure for long; they are subject to change, lack stability, and are without coming or going.
Contemplating the body as having no rescue and no refuge, possessing sorrow and affliction, continuing with love and hatred,
abounding in suffering without rest, or like a blazing fire, it is ever accompanied by disease without respite.
Disgusted with the three realms of existence, they seek the Buddha-wisdom;

They behold that wondrous wisdom, inconceivable, Unequaled, immeasurable, and difficult to realize. Untainted, free from calamity, and without affliction, They take refuge in great nirvāṇa without regression, Able to rescue sentient beings from immeasurable suffering.
Having perceived the Buddha’s wisdom, he takes pity on sentient beings who are solitary, without refuge, and without protection;
who are constantly exhausted by the blazing fires of the three poisons; who dwell in the prison of existence and perpetually suffer;
who are shrouded by the habit-energies of afflictions and lack the eye of wisdom; and whose aspirations are base and inferior, causing them to lose the treasure of the Dharma.
Following along with birth and death, they fear nirvāṇa; I should rescue them through diligent effort.
Seeking wisdom to benefit sentient beings, I contemplate what skillful means will bring about their liberation.
The Buddha’s unimpeded wisdom does not depart from its locus; this arises from awakening to the reality of phenomena as they truly are.
Awakening comes through the wisdom of non-action and non-arising, and that wisdom is produced from meditative concentration, which in turn arises from hearing the Dharma.
Reflecting thus, he exhorted himself to listen to and study the honored Dharma day and night;
out of reverence for hearing the True Dharma, he was able to relinquish everything— kingdoms, cities, provisions,
and various treasures, as well as wife, children, kinsmen, and royal rank.

The head, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and teeth; hands, feet, marrow, heart-blood, and flesh—giving all these away is not difficult, provided one does not conceive a sense of difficulty toward the Dharma Master.
If someone were to say to a bodhisattva, "Who can cast their body into a great pit of fire?
I shall give you the treasure of the Buddha-dharma," upon hearing this, they would cast themselves into it without fear or dread.

Even if fire were to fill the three thousandfold world system, and one were to cast one’s body from the Brahma-world into it, this would not be considered difficult for the sake of seeking the Dharma; how much less so the various minor sufferings of the human realm?

From the first resolution until the attainment of Bodhi, even if there were the sufferings of the Avīci hell in between, one would endure them all for the sake of hearing the Dharma; how much more so the various sufferings of the human realm?

Having heard this, they reflect correctly and according to the principle, attaining the four dhyānas, the four meditative attainments, the four immeasurable minds, and the five supernormal powers; yet they do not take birth under the influence of their power.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here beholds many Buddhas; Making offerings and hearing the Dharma, their mind becomes resolute.
Severing all false delusions, they become ever more pure and luminous, Like refined gold whose essence never diminishes.
Abiding here, one frequently becomes Śakra, Lord of the Devas, To transform and guide immeasurable sentient beings;
Causing them to abandon greed and dwell in the wholesome paths, So that all may single-mindedly seek the merits of the Buddha.
Abiding in this moment of diligence, one can realize hundreds of thousands of samādhis;
one beholds hundreds of thousands of Buddhas with bodies adorned by the marks, and if endowed with the power of aspiration, it exceeds even this.
Bringing universal benefit, profit, and happiness to all sentient beings—this is the supreme practice of those Bodhisattvas.
Thus, I have explained the meaning of this Third Ground according to its significance.

Thus ends the third stage, the Radiant Ground (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*), of the Bodhisattva. The Fourth Stage: The Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*) When the Sons of the Buddha hear of this vast practice—this delightful, profound, subtle, and supreme Dharma—their hearts are filled with courage, joy, and great rapture;
they scatter myriad flowers everywhere as an offering to the Buddha.
When this sublime Dharma was being expounded, the great earth and the waters of the ocean all trembled;
all the celestial maidens were filled with joy, and they all uttered wondrous sounds in unison to offer praise.
The Sovereign Lord of Devas was greatly filled with joy, raining down mani-jewels as an offering to the Buddha;
he praised him, saying:
"The Buddha has appeared for my sake, expounding the foremost conduct of merit."
Such meanings of the stages for the wise are extremely difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of eons.
Now, all of a sudden, I have heard this sublime Dharma sound of the Bodhisattva’s supreme conduct;
O Wise One, pray further expound upon the definitive stages that leave no path remaining.
"To benefit all the great assemblies, these sons of the Buddhas all delight in hearing this.
The courageous and great-minded Vimukticandra addressed Vajragarbha, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
"From this, one enters the fourth stage; please explain all its characteristics.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, having already clarified and purified the third stage, wishes to enter the fourth bodhisattva stage of knowledge, they should do so by means of ten kinds of illumination of the Dharma.

What are these ten? They are: the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of sentient beings; the clear entry through contemplation of all worlds; the clear entry through contemplation of the true dharma-realm; the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of space; the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of consciousness; the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of desire; the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of form; the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of formlessness; the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of sublime intention and resolute conviction; and the clear entry through contemplation of the realm of vast intention and resolute conviction. By means of these ten clear entries, the bodhisattva ascends to the fourth stage.
O Sons of the Buddha!
As soon as a bodhisattva has attained the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, they grow within the family of the Tathāgatas and attain its essential nature through ten ways in which their wisdom matures.

What are these ten? They are: because of non-retrogression in one's intention, there is indestructible pure faith in the Triple Gem; because of reaching the ultimate, there is the observation of the nature of arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); because of observing that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is non-arising; because of observing the formation and destruction of the world; because of observing that karma has birth and death; because of observing saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; because of observing sentient beings, lands, and karma; because of observing the past limit and the future limit; and because of observing the absence of intrinsic nature and inexhaustibility.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas accomplish these ten methods for maturing wisdom, they grow within the family of the Tathāgatas and attain that essential nature.
Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha!"

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom, they dwell contemplating the body within the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly covetousness and grief;
they dwell contemplating the body within the external body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly covetousness and grief;
and they dwell contemplating the body within both the internal and external bodies, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly covetousness and grief.
It is likewise with regard to internal feelings, external feelings, and both internal and external feelings;
it is likewise with regard to the internal mind, the external mind, and both internal and external minds.
He dwells observing phenomena in relation to internal phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
Abiding in the contemplation of phenomena with respect to external phenomena, he dwells ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow;
abiding in the contemplation of phenomena with respect to both internal and external phenomena, he dwells ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
Furthermore, regarding unarisen evil and unwholesome states, the bodhisattva generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies diligence, and sustains the mind so that they do not arise;
regarding arisen evil and unwholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies diligence, and sustains the mind so that they are permanently abandoned;
regarding unarisen wholesome states, he generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies diligence, and sustains the mind so that they may arise.

In order to cause already arisen wholesome states to remain stable, not to be forgotten, and to increase, expand, and reach fulfillment through repeated cultivation, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses diligence, rouses the mind, and sustains the mind.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates the basis for psychic power consisting of concentration of desire and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment;

he cultivates the basis for psychic power consisting of concentration of effort and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment;

he cultivates the basis for psychic power consisting of concentration of mind and the accomplishment of the formative forces of abandonment, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment.

He cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through the cultivation of contemplation, which is accomplished by the exertions of abandonment; he relies on detachment, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and is directed toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates the faculty of faith, relying on detachment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and directing it toward relinquishment;
he cultivates the faculty of energy, relying on detachment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and directing it toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the faculty of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
one cultivates the faculty of concentration, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
one cultivates the faculty of wisdom, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment.
"Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates the power of faith, relying on detachment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;
he cultivates the power of energy, relying on detachment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment;
he cultivates the power of mindfulness, relying on detachment, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and dedicating it toward relinquishment."
One cultivates the power of concentration, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
one cultivates the power of wisdom, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
he cultivates the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
he cultivates the awakening factor of energy, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment.
One cultivates the factor of enlightenment of joy, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
one cultivates the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
one cultivates the factor of enlightenment of concentration, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment.
He cultivates the enlightenment factor of equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva cultivates right view, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment;
he cultivates right mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and inclining toward relinquishment.
He cultivates right thought, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment;
he cultivates right speech, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment;
he cultivates right action, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
He cultivates right effort, depending on seclusion, depending on dispassion,
depending on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment; he cultivates right concentration,
depending on seclusion, depending on dispassion, depending on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment.
He cultivates the wisdom of discernment, which relies on detachment, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and is dedicated toward relinquishment.

When a bodhisattva practices these factors of enlightenment, it is because he possesses compassionate affection for the entire realm of sentient beings; because he is sustained by the inspiration of his original vows; because he is preceded by great compassion; because he has perfected great loving-kindness; because he takes as his object of focus the wisdom of omniscience; because he brings forth the various adornments of the Buddha-fields; because he brings forth the powers, fearlessnesses, unique qualities of a Buddha, and the physical marks and vocal tones of a Tathāgata; because he yearns for ever more sublime dharmas; because he accords with the profound liberation and the teachings of the Buddha as he has heard them; and because he contemplates vast skillful means.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), all subtle afflictions such as the view of a self-body—including [the notions of] a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, a person, or a transmigrating being; attachment to the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; and all agitated thoughts, investigations, protections, graspings, accumulations, and points of clinging—all such things are entirely abandoned."
All actions that ought not to be performed—those censured by all Buddhas and induced by defilements—all such things he completely abandons.
All actions that ought to be performed, which accord with the bodhisattva’s provisions for right practice and are praised by all Tathāgatas, he fully undertakes and practices.

Furthermore, for the sake of successively bringing the bodhisattva path to full completion, through the power of skillful means and wisdom as they are realized, one cultivates the various branches of the path in such and such a manner, thereby attaining a mind of moistening, a pliant patience, a capable mind, a mind that draws forth benefit and happiness, an undefiled mind, a mind that seeks ever-higher and more excellent dharmas, a mind that yearns for supreme knowledge, a mind capable of rescuing all the world, a mind that respects and complies with all teachers and elders, and a mind that practices according to the Dharma as it has been heard.

Furthermore, he is well-acquainted with gratitude and well-acquainted with repaying kindness; his mind is harmonious, and he dwells in peace and happiness with others. He is upright and gentle, free from the conduct of dense thicket-like afflictions, without deceit or pride. Being one whose speech is well-accordant, he receives instruction and admonition with respect. In this way, the bodhisattva achieves patience, achieves self-mastery, and achieves tranquility.

When one thus achieves the practice of contemplation through patience, discipline, and tranquility, and is able to purify the various karmas of the higher stages, one attains great diligence that is unceasing, untainted diligence, non-retrogressive diligence, vast diligence, boundless diligence, blazing diligence, incomparable diligence, unassailable diligence, diligence that matures all sentient beings, and diligence that skillfully discriminates between the path and what is not the path.

Furthermore, this Bodhisattva’s realm of virtuous intention becomes increasingly pure; the realm of superior intention is not lost; the roots of virtue are purified through sharp and clear resolve; they are freed from worldly defilements and sever all doubts; the nature of being free from doubt manifests fully, and they realize joy and pliancy; through the empowerment of the Tathāgatas, it manifests before them, and their immeasurable mental intentions are all completely accomplished.

"When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), through vast vision and the power of their vows, they directly perceive many Buddhas—many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas."

Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the bodhisattva, with a vast and superior intention, honors, respects, serves, and makes offerings to them. He presents them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and all other articles of life; he offers the various exquisite articles of pleasure belonging to bodhisattvas; and he shows reverence to the Saṅgha community. With these roots of virtue, he dedicates them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, serving the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, with earnest devotion, and listening to the Dharma with reverence in their presence.

Having heard this, they receive and uphold it; they practice it extensively according to their capacity, and with pure faith in the holy teachings of those Buddhas, they go forth into homelessness. Furthermore, their aspiration, superior aspiration, and resolute conviction regarding all these bodhisattva qualities become increasingly purified in their state of equanimity.

“Once the Bodhisattva has dwelled in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), for further immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, they dwell with an intention and resolve that are equal and pure; all their roots of goodness become even more intensely blazing and increasingly bright and clear.”
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is like a skilled goldsmith who, having refined gold, fashions it into ornaments; these cannot be outshone by other gold that has not yet been fashioned into ornaments.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is likewise for a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī): all their roots of goodness cannot be eclipsed by the roots of goodness of other bodhisattvas dwelling in lower stages.
Furthermore, O Sons of the Buddha!

Just as the radiance emitted by the pure halo of light from a maṇi jewel cannot be eclipsed by any other precious gems, and the light it emits cannot be extinguished by any wind, water, or rain in the entire world; so too is it with the Bodhisattvas.
O Sons of the Buddha!

It is likewise when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arcismatī-bhūmi*): they cannot be eclipsed by other Bodhisattvas dwelling in lower stages, and their light of wisdom cannot be extinguished by the manifestation of any maras, adversaries, or afflictions (*kleśa*).

Among the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), this bodhisattva predominantly practices "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*); among the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*) becomes preeminent; as for the remaining perfections, he practices them according to his capacity and his lot, though not without cultivation.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the fourth bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arcismatī-bhūmi*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this fourth stage, they are mostly reborn as the King of the Suyāma Heaven. Possessing sovereign power, they skillfully transform sentient beings, causing them to eliminate the false view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and enabling them to abide in right view."

Whatever deeds they perform—whether through generosity, or through kind speech, or through beneficial conduct, or through cooperation—all of these are never apart from the mental engagement with the Buddha, the mental engagement with the Dharma, the mental engagement with the Saṅgha, the mental engagement with bodhisattvas, the mental engagement with the bodhisattva practices, the mental engagement with the perfections, the mental engagement with the stages, the mental engagement with the powers of a Buddha, the mental engagement with the fearlessnesses, and the mental engagement with the unique qualities of a Buddha; indeed, they are never apart from the mental engagement with all-aspect supreme and wondrously corresponding omniscient wisdom.
Furthermore, he made this aspiration:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall become the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; even unto the attainment of the state that serves as the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."
If one delights in initiating such diligence, through this diligence, in a single kṣaṇa, muhūrta, or moment, one can realize ten million samādhis and behold ten million Buddhas.

They are able to comprehend all the empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of those Buddhas; they can shake ten million worlds (*koṭi-loka-dhātu*), travel to ten million Buddha-fields, illuminate ten million worlds, bring ten million sentient beings to maturity, remain for ten million eons (*kalpa*), enter into ten million eons of the past and future, correctly discern ten million Dharma-gates, manifest ten million bodies, and each of these bodies can manifest being surrounded by a retinue of ten million bodhisattvas.

From this point upward, for those bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration, by virtue of their superior vows, all their playful manifestations—whether of body, radiance, supernormal powers, eyes, spheres of activity, voice, conduct, adornments, resolute understandings, or deeds—could not easily be numbered even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva, having already purified the third stage, Next contemplates the world of sentient beings and the realms of phenomena:
The realms of emptiness, consciousness, desire, form, and formlessness; With a superior and great resolve, they are able to enter therein."
As soon as the Bodhisattva ascends the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), they enter the family of the Tathāgata and never again regress;
their faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha remains indestructible. They contemplate that while phenomena arise and perish, there is no true origination;
they contemplate that while the world is formed and destroyed, karma gives rise to existence; and they contemplate the equality of saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, and the buddha-fields.
Contemplating that the past and future limits are devoid of intrinsic nature and ultimately exhausted, one thus practices and grows within the Buddha-family.
Having attained this Dharma, one increases compassion and further exerts oneself in the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness;
by contemplating the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena both internally and externally, all worldly craving and attachment are dispelled.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the four right efforts, Eliminating unwholesome dharmas and increasing the wholesome;
He skillfully practices the bases of psychic power, as well as the faculties and powers, And the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path.
To deliver sentient beings, they cultivate the factors of enlightenment; their original vows support them, with compassion as their foremost guide.

Seeking all-knowledge, they adorn the Buddha-lands, and likewise take as their object the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the extraordinary marks and signs, and the profound, beautiful voice.
They also seek the sublime path and the state of liberation, seeking great skillful means to cultivate the factors of enlightenment.
The sixty-two views, headed by the view of a self-body, as well as the infinite varieties of "I" and "mine," and all attachments to the aggregates,
elements, and sense-bases— these are all completely abandoned in the fourth stage.
The Tathāgata has condemned the defilements of affliction; abandon all such meaningless karma.
As for the pure karma praised by the Buddhas, there is nothing that is not performed for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
By diligently practicing without indolence, the Bodhisattva shall attain the ten mental states in their full perfection.
Dedicatedly seeking the Buddha-way without weariness, Hoping to receive empowerment to deliver sentient beings;
Respectfully honoring the virtuous and practicing the Dharma, Grateful, easily repentant, and free from resentment or violence.
Abandoning pride and leaving behind deceit, their minds become supple and gentle; they apply themselves with even greater diligence, never turning back.
Furthermore, the realm of their intention is pure, and their superior intention is never lost.
Supreme resolve increases the roots of goodness; the defilements of the net of doubt are forever abandoned.
With no doubt present before them, they attain joy and peace, sustained by the Buddha’s empowerment with immeasurable intent.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), they make offerings to nayutas of immeasurable Buddhas;
hearing the True Dharma and likewise leaving the household life, they cannot be outshone, like gold ornaments.
The Bodhisattva dwelling here, endowed with all virtues, practices the Path through wisdom and skillful means;
his mind does not retreat before any demons, for he is like a wondrous jewel that nothing can destroy.
He frequently becomes a king among the Yāma devas, Master of the Dharma and honored by the multitude;
Universally transforming sentient beings to eliminate evil views, He single-mindedly seeks Buddha-wisdom and cultivates wholesome deeds.
Through the power of diligent and vigorous effort, the Bodhisattva attains tens of millions of samādhis;
yet when acting through the power of the wisdom of aspiration, these exceed all such numbers beyond calculation.
Thus have I, for the sake of the Buddha’s sons, proclaimed this fourth stage of the Bodhisattva—
the subtle path of practice through diligence, which is perfectly conjoined with merit, meaning, and wisdom.
The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three;
The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Translated at Longxing Monastery in Beiting.

The Fifth Bodhisattva Bhūmi: The Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*) When the bodhisattvas heard of this supreme stage, they attained realization regarding the Dharma and their hearts were filled with joy;
flowers rained from the sky as they offered these words of praise:
"Excellent, Great Being Vajragarbha!
The Sovereign King of Devas and his celestial host, having heard the Dharma, leap for joy as they abide in the void."
Universally emitting clouds of various wondrous lights, they made offerings to the Tathāgata, filling all with joy.
The celestial maidens played heavenly music and also praised the Buddha with their voices;
through the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattvas, these words were uttered from within those sounds:
"The Buddha's vow, long in duration, is now fulfilled; the Buddha-way, long in duration, is now attained.
Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived at the celestial palace; the benefactor of devas and humans is seen after a long time."
The great ocean, after a long time, now begins to stir; The Buddha’s light, after a long time, now finally radiates.
Sentient beings, after a long time, now find peace and joy; The voice of Great Compassion is heard only after a long time.
You have reached the further shore of all merit and virtue; The darkness of pride has been entirely extinguished.
Supremely pure like space, unstained by worldly dharmas like a lotus;
the Great Muni has appeared in the world, like Mount Sumeru emerging from the vast ocean.
Making offerings can exhaust all suffering; making offerings will surely yield the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This object of worship is worthy of peerless offerings; therefore, with a joyful heart, one should make offerings to the Buddha.
Thus, after these immeasurable goddesses had uttered these words of praise,
they all remained gazing up at the Tathāgata in silent reverence, their hearts filled with joy.
At that time, the Great Being Vimukticandra again entreated Vajragarbha, who is fearless:
"I pray that you will now expound for the sake of the Buddha’s sons the characteristics of practice in the fifth stage."
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, having fully perfected the path of the fourth stage, wishes to enter the fifth bodhisattva stage, they should enter it by means of ten kinds of pure mental dispositions characterized by equanimity."

What are these ten? They are: the pure intention of equality regarding the Buddha-dharmas of the past; the pure intention of equality regarding the Buddha-dharmas of the future; the pure intention of equality regarding the Buddha-dharmas of the present; the pure intention of equality regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*); the pure intention of equality regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the pure intention of equality regarding the removal of views and doubts; the pure intention of equality regarding the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path; the pure intention of equality regarding the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*); the pure intention of equality regarding the successive examination of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); and the pure intention of equality regarding the maturation of all sentient beings. By means of these ten kinds of pure intentions of equality, the bodhisattva enters the fifth stage.
O Sons of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva has reached this fifth stage, having well-polished the factors of enlightenment and the branches of the path,
and having well-purified the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), while seeking the further, superior path for future lives, they act in this manner:
Because their activities accord with correct practice; because they are sustained by the power of their vows;
because they do not abandon any sentient beings due to their great compassion; because they accumulate the two provisions of merit and wisdom without ceasing;
because they bring forth skillful and excellent means; because they contemplate the radiance of each successive stage; and because they constantly and diligently seek [the higher].
Through the empowerment of the Buddha, and sustained by the power of mindfulness, wisdom, and the inclination toward awakening, having attained non-retrogressive right attention,

one understands as it truly is this noble truth of suffering, "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering," knowing all the noble truths of right practice exactly as they are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva attains skillfulness regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); skillfulness regarding the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), the truth of differentiation (*prabheda-satya*), the truth of establishment (*vyavasthāna-satya*), the truth of phenomena (*vastu-satya*), and the truth of arising (*utpāda-satya*); skillfulness regarding the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*), and the truth of the knowledge of entering the path (*mārga-praveśa-jñāna-satya*); and because they have already accomplished the successive continuity of all the bodhisattva stages (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*), they attain skillfulness even within the truth of the accumulation of the Tathāgata’s wisdom (*tathāgata-jñāna-samudaya-satya*).

"Furthermore, because this bodhisattva causes other sentient beings to all rejoice according to their inclinations, he knows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through his ability to enter into all modes of reasoning; he knows the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) by awakening to the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; he skillfully knows the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*) by realizing the meaning of the distinctions and establishments of phenomena; he knows the truth of distinctions (*viśeṣa-satya*) by understanding the establishment of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; he knows the truth of establishment (*vyavasthāna-satya*) by comprehending the afflictions of body and mind; he is said to know the truth of things (*vastu-satya*) because he penetrates the continuity of births in the various realms of existence; he is able to know the truth of birth (*janma-satya*) because all burning afflictions are ultimately extinguished; it is called the truth of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna-satya*) because it brings forth non-duality; and he knows the truth of the knowledge of entering the path (*mārgapraveśa-jñāna-satya*) because he awakens to everything through all aspects of practice."
Having achieved the successive continuity of all the bodhisattva stages, they are able to know even the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding the truth of the origin of suffering.
Furthermore, this is known solely through the power of the wisdom of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*), and not by means of ultimate wisdom (*niṣṭhā-jñāna*).
