In this way, through the correct wisdom induced by skill in the truths (*satya-kauśalya*), the bodhisattva understands all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as they truly are: as false, deceptive, and delusive toward the foolish. Thereupon, as that bodhisattva turns further toward all sentient beings, great compassion manifests and the radiance of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) arises.

Sustained by such power of wisdom, the Bodhisattva feels a sense of concern for the realm of sentient beings and aspires to the Buddha-wisdom. He observes all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*): how those born from the thirst of ignorance (*avidyā-tṛṣṇā*) drift along the current of birth and death from the past to the future; how those who do not advance beyond the attachment to the storehouse of the aggregates (*skandha-ālaya*) increase their mass of suffering; and how they are without self (*ātman*), without a life-principle (*jīva*), without a nourisher (*poṣa*), and without a person (*pudgala*). He knows as it truly is that they are devoid of "I" and "mine. Furthermore, he knows as it truly is their future state: the ultimate cessation of the limits of existence through the abandonment of delusion and craving regarding non-existence, or likewise, the state of non-existence itself.
Then this bodhisattva reflects thus:
"These classes of deluded ordinary beings are truly to be pitied; countless bodies have already perished, will perish, and are now perishing.
Though they are thus utterly destroyed, they are unable to generate [disenchantment] toward the body."
Disenchantment further increases the machinery of manifold suffering;

one follows the stream of birth and death without being able to return, unable to relinquish the grasping at the aggregates, unable to feel revulsion toward the poisonous snakes of the great elements, unable to extract the barb of views and conceit, and unable to extinguish the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion. Not...
They are able to drift upon the dark gloom of ignorance, yet they cannot dry up the vast ocean of craving;
failing to seek the Great Holy Guide endowed with the Ten Powers, they wander according to the dense forest of Māra’s inclinations,
incessantly tossed about amidst the turbulent waves and sea-monsters of various discursive thoughts within the boundless, deep abyss of saṃsāra.

Now, for the sake of those sentient beings who are oppressed by such immeasurable sufferings—those who are solitary, without rescue, without refuge, without shelter, without an island, without a path, blind and sightless, and enveloped by the thick membrane of the eggshell of ignorance and shrouded in darkness—I alone, without companion, shall cultivate and accumulate immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom. By means of these provisions, I shall cause all those sentient beings to realize ultimate purity, even unto the attainment of the Tathāgata’s ten powers and unimpeded Buddha-wisdom.

In this way, the Bodhisattva, through the wisdom induced by such skillful observation and the roots of virtue thus cultivated, practices and accumulates them all for the sake of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings; for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings; for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings; out of compassion for all sentient beings; so that sentient beings may be free from calamities and afflictions; for the sake of liberating all sentient beings; for the sake of uplifting all sentient beings; so that sentient beings may give rise to pure faith; for the sake of subduing all sentient beings; and for the sake of leading all sentient beings to final nirvana.
When a bodhisattva dwells securely in this fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), they are called one endowed with mindfulness, because they do not forget the true Dharma;
they are called one endowed with wisdom, because their intelligence is skillfully decisive;
they are called one endowed with penetration, because they awaken to the profound intent of the sūtras and the secret teachings.
They are called "possessing shame and dread" because they protect themselves and others;
they are called "firmly persistent" because they do not abandon their vows (*saṃvara*) or ethical conduct (*śīla*);
they are called "awakened" because they have attained skillfulness through contemplating what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
They are called "those who act in accordance with wisdom" because they are not led by others;
they are called "those who act in accordance with insight" because they have attained skillfulness regarding both meaningful and meaningless statements;
they are called "those who manifest supernormal powers" because they have attained skillfulness in the cultivation of their manifestation.
They are called those skilled in means because they conform to the ways of the world;
they are called those who are insatiable because they skillfully accumulate the provisions of merit;
they are called those whose diligence knows no rest because they seek out the provisions of wisdom.
They are called those with the intention of indefatigability because they gather the provisions for great compassion;
they are called those who apply themselves to all sentient beings because they are able to lead all sentient beings to final liberation;
they are called those who seek application without pride because they seek the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of a Tathāgata.
They are called practitioners who skillfully induce mental attention because they induce the various adornments of the Buddha-fields;
they are called practitioners who perform various kinds of wholesome karma because they accumulate the primary and secondary marks;
they are called practitioners of constant and perpetual virtuous application because they seek the adornments of the Buddha’s body, speech, and mind.
They are called "greatly venerable ones who are capable of service" because they practice according to the instructions of all Bodhisattvas and Dharma teachers;
they are called "those whose minds are unimpeded" because they continuously enter the world through great skillful means;
and they are called "those who day and night are free from other thoughts" because they practice solely for the sake of maturing all sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva practices with such diligence, they bring sentient beings to maturity through generosity, as well as through kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation; furthermore, by manifesting a majestic physical form, by teaching the Dharma, by revealing the various practices of bodhisattvas, by demonstrating the Great Self of the Tathāgata, by pointing out the faults of saṃsāra, and by praising the excellence of the Buddha’s wisdom; thus, by eliciting the play of great supernormal powers and applying various skillful means and activities, they bring sentient beings to maturity.

Thus, this bodhisattva diligently matures sentient beings, their mental continuum constantly tending toward the wisdom of the Buddha. Because they seek the supreme Dharma, their roots of goodness and applications never regress;

and because they desire to benefit all sentient beings, they diligently train in all the various worldly scripts and treatises, seals and insignia, calculations, and treatises on metallurgy and the like, as well as medical treatises—namely those for treating consumption, epilepsy, demonic possession, and the neutralization of malevolent poisons and vengeful spirits—and in the arts of incantations, composition, praise, song, dance, music, jesting, conversation, and all places of pleasure.

Nations, cities, villages, towns, palaces, residences, gardens, groves, springs, streams, ponds, and lakes; the arrangement of flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and forests; the manifestation of the natures of gold, silver, *maṇi* jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, and so forth; entry into the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, as well as earthquakes; the cries of various birds and beasts and the auspicious or inauspicious signs of dreams; the marks received throughout the body and its limbs; ethical discipline, ascetic practices, meditative concentration, and supernormal powers;

the four immeasurable minds, the formless absorptions, and all other matters free from affliction and harm that can lead to the benefit, happiness, and blameless activities of all sentient beings—all such things he is able to manifest because of his compassion for sentient beings, gradually causing them to dwell securely in the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in this Difficult to Conquer stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*), through vast vision and the power of their vows, they directly perceive many Buddhas, many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas."

Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the bodhisattva—with vast and superior resolve—reveres, honors, serves, and makes offerings to them; he presents them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and all articles of life; he offers the various exquisite implements of pleasure belonging to bodhisattvas; and he shows reverence toward the Saṅgha. He dedicates these roots of virtue to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. He serves the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, with earnest devotion, and listens to the true Dharma with reverence, honor, and a sense of its rarity. Having heard it, he upholds it and practices it extensively according to his capacity.
Having developed pure faith in the holy teachings of those Buddhas, they leave the household life; once ordained, they are able to become Dharma-preachers who retain what they have heard.
Furthermore, for the most part, by means of the mode of hearing and practicing, they attain *dhāraṇī* and act as Dharma-preachers.

For a Bodhisattva dwelling in this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*), these roots of goodness become increasingly intense and blazing, attaining clarity and purity over immeasurable eons.

Over immeasurable hundreds of eons, immeasurable thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of eons, immeasurable koṭis of eons, and even up to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of eons, these roots of goodness become increasingly intense and blazing, attaining clarity and purity.
O Sons of the Buddha!
It is just as when a goldsmith takes refined gold and fashions it into an ornament; by polishing it with musaragalva, it becomes increasingly radiant and ever more bright and pure.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*sudurjayā bhūmi*), these roots of goodness are likewise transformed: through the contemplative observation of skillful means and wisdom, they become even more intensely blazing and increasingly pure. Drawn forth by the merit of the application of knowledge, this contemplative observation cannot be eclipsed by anything else.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha!
For example, all the light emanating from the sun, the moon, the stars, and their palaces cannot be eclipsed by any wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), nor is it shared with the winds.
O Sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in the Ground of Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), it is likewise with these roots of goodness; because they are contemplated and examined through the wisdom of skillful means according to their practice, they cannot be eclipsed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor are they shared with other worldly roots of goodness.

Among these ten perfections (pāramitā) of the bodhisattva, the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā) is predominant; yet he does not fail to practice the remaining perfections according to his strength and capacity.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the fifth bodhisattva stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are mostly reborn as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven (*Santuṣita*), where they are able to exercise sovereign power to skillfully transform sentient beings, causing them to abandon all heterodox and false teachings, and enabling them to abide within the true reality (*satya*)."

Whatever deeds they perform—whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—all of these are never apart from the mental attention directed toward the Buddha, the mental attention directed toward the Dharma, the mental attention directed toward the Saṅgha, the mental attention directed toward the bodhisattvas, the mental attention directed toward the bodhisattva practices, the mental attention directed toward the perfections, the mental attention directed toward the stages, the mental attention directed toward the powers of a buddha, the mental attention directed toward the fearlessnesses, and the mental attention directed toward the unique qualities of a buddha; even unto the mental attention directed toward the omniscient wisdom that is perfectly associated with all supreme and sublime aspects of practice.
He constantly makes this aspiration, saying:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; even unto attaining the state that serves as the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."

If one delights in initiating such diligence, through this diligence, in a single kṣaṇa, a muhūrta, or an instant, one realizes a hundred koṭis of samādhis; one is able to see a hundred koṭis of Buddhas and can fully comprehend their empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*); one can shake a hundred koṭis of worlds, travel to a hundred koṭis of Buddha-fields, illuminate a hundred koṭis of worlds, and bring to maturity a hundred koṭis of sentient beings to be converted; one can maintain a lifespan for a hundred koṭis of kalpas and enter into a hundred koṭis of kalpas each regarding both the past and future limits; one can correctly discern a hundred koṭis of Dharma-gates and manifest a hundred koṭis of bodies, with each body surrounded by a retinue of a hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas.

From this point upward, for those bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration, by virtue of their superior vows, all their playful manifestations—whether of body, light, supernormal powers, eyes, spheres of activity, voice, conduct, adornments, resolute understandings, or deeds—cannot easily be numbered even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The fourth stage of the Bodhisattva, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, Has its correct practice already purified;
One then awakens to the equality of the Buddhas of the three times, Realizing that this is through precepts and concentration, which eliminate views and doubt."
Regarding the path, the non-path, and correct practice, He observes the wisdom of the successive factors of enlightenment;
Because he brings sentient beings to maturity with equanimity, He penetrates this and enters the fifth stage.
The foundations of mindfulness are the bow, the faculties are the sharp arrows; the right efforts are the horses, the bases of power are the chariot;
the five powers are the sturdy armor that destroys the enemy—through such valor, one enters the fifth stage.
Shame and remorse are their garments; the factors of enlightenment are their wreaths; pure precepts are their fragrant scent; meditative concentration is their unguent;
skillful means provide their exquisite adornment as they roam through the groves of dhāraṇīs and the gardens of samādhi.
The bases of psychic power are his feet, right mindfulness his neck; compassion and loving-kindness are his eyes, wisdom his tusks.
This lion among men roars the "I am not" cry, utterly destroying the beasts of delusion as he enters the fifth stage.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this fifth stage, they further cultivate the supreme and pure path;
with a resolve to seek the Buddha-dharma that never regresses, they contemplate compassion without weariness.
Having accumulated the supreme merit of merit and wisdom, they diligently apply skillful means to contemplate the higher stages;
empowered by the Buddha’s strength and endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, they understand the Four Truths exactly as they are.
They skillfully know the conventional truth and the ultimate truth, The truth of characteristics, the truth of distinctions, and the truth of establishment;
The truth of phenomena, the truths of arising and cessation as well as the path, And even the truth of the unimpeded wisdom of a Buddha.
Although such contemplation of the truths is subtle and refined, one has not yet attained unimpeded, supreme liberation;
because it can generate great merit, it thus surpasses worldly wisdom.
Having contemplated the truths and realized that conditioned phenomena are illusory in nature and lack any solid substance,
they receive a portion of the Buddha’s compassionate light and seek the wisdom of a Buddha for the benefit of sentient beings.
Contemplating the past and future limits of all conditioned phenomena, Obscured by the darkness of ignorance and bound by the fetters of craving;
Wandering and circling within the realms of suffering, Therein exists no self, no sentient being, and no life-principle.
With craving and grasping as causes, one undergoes future suffering; though one seeks its limit, it cannot be found.
Drifting in delusion with no time for return—these are pitiable ones whom I should deliver.
The aggregates are a burning house, the elements are serpents, and the various views are arrows; the fire of desire blazes fiercely, and ignorance is darkness.
Drifting on the river of craving, one lacks the means for contemplation; sinking in the ocean of suffering, one is bereft of a guiding light.
Having known this, one applies diligent effort; all that is done is for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Such a person is called one endowed with mindfulness and wisdom, and even one who possesses the skillful means of awakening and understanding.
Practicing merit and wisdom without weariness, Revering the learned without fatigue;
Adorning buddha-fields and manifesting the marks and signs— All such deeds are for the sake of sentient beings.
Desiring to transform and guide all the worlds, he was well-versed in writing, treatises, mathematics, and seals;
he was also adept at understanding various medicines and formulas, curing all manner of ailments until they were entirely healed.

Their literary compositions, songs, and dances are all exquisite; they arrange palaces, residences, gardens, and ponds, displaying every kind of precious substance to people for the sake of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
The sun, moon, and constellations, as well as earthquakes, And even the physical marks of the body, they observe;
Dhyānas, samāpattis, and supernatural powers— They manifest all these for the benefit of the world.
When the wise abide on this Ground Difficult to Conquer (Durjayā), they make offerings to all Buddhas and listen to the Dharma;
just as when mother-of-pearl polishes true gold, their roots of goodness become increasingly pure in the same way.
Just as the light of the palaces of the stars is not eclipsed by the wind-circle,
and as a lotus remains unstained though it dwells in the mud, so too is the conduct of the Bodhisattva in the world.
May I frequently become the Heavenly King Tuṣita, Able to subdue the heterodox paths and all false views;
May all the virtues I cultivate lead to Buddha-wisdom, And may I attain the Ten Powers to deliver all living beings.
If one arouses great diligence here, one sees a hundred koṭis of Buddhas in a single kṣaṇa;
even when attaining meditative concentration, the manifestations of the present body are likewise so, yet what is accomplished through the power of vows exceeds this.
Thus concludes the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer, the true path of the Honored One, the World-Honored among Men;
by means of various powers of skillful expedients, I have finished proclaiming it for the sake of all the sons of the Buddha.

Thus ends the fifth stage of the Bodhisattva, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*). **The Sixth Stage of the Bodhisattva: The Manifest (*Abhimukhī*)** Part One of the Sixth Stage of the Bodhisattva: The Manifest. Having heard these supreme practices, the Bodhisattva’s heart rejoices and rains down exquisite flowers;
emitting pure light and scattering precious jewels, they make offerings to the Tathāgata and praise his excellent teaching.
Hundreds of thousands of devas all rejoiced, together raining down various jewels from mid-air;
with flower garlands, necklaces, banners, and streamers, as well as precious parasols and scented ointments, they all made offerings to the Buddha.
The Sovereign King of Heaven and his retinue, their hearts filled with joy, stood in the air;
scattering jewels that formed clouds as offerings, they praised him, saying: "O Son of the Buddha, please proclaim this eloquently!"
Immeasurable celestial maidens dwell in the air, together praising the Buddha with the sounds of music;
within those sounds they all speak these words:
"The Buddha’s words can eliminate the disease of afflictions; the nature of phenomena is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of all marks."
Just as space is free from conceptual discrimination, transcending all grasping and attachment, and beyond the path of words—truly equal in nature and eternally pure;
if one can penetrate the nature of all phenomena, the mind remains unmoved by existence or non-existence;
practicing diligently out of a desire to save the world, such a person is a true son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s own mouth.
Practicing giving without grasping at any signs, fundamentally severing all evils while firmly upholding the precepts;
understanding that phenomena are unborn and always remaining patient, knowing that the nature of phenomena is detached and possessing diligence;
with afflictions already exhausted, entering meditative concentration, and skillfully penetrating the emptiness of nature to discern all phenomena.
"Endowed with the power of wisdom, you are able to bring extensive salvation; by extinguishing all evils, you are called a Great Being.
Having offered such millions of kinds of sublime sounds in praise, they fell silent and gazed up at the Buddha.
Then Vimukticandra said:
"Vajragarbha! By what mode of practice does one enter the subsequent stage?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, having fully perfected the path cultivated in the fifth stage, wishes to enter the sixth stage of a bodhisattva, they should do so by means of the ten kinds of equality of phenomena."

What are these ten? They are: the equality of all phenomena through their signlessness; the equality of all phenomena through the absence of self-characteristics; the equality of all phenomena through their lack of arising; the equality of all phenomena through their lack of birth; the equality of all phenomena through their quiescent purity; the equality of all phenomena through their primordial purity; the equality of all phenomena through the absence of conceptual proliferation; the equality of all phenomena through neither grasping nor rejecting; the equality of all phenomena through being like a magical illusion, a dream, a shadow, an echo, the moon reflected in water, an image in a mirror, a mirage, and a transformation; and the equality of all phenomena through the non-duality of existence and non-existence. By means of these ten kinds of equality of phenomena, one enters the sixth stage.

When a bodhisattva thus contemplates and polishes [the mind], because they accord with and do not oppose the equality of all phenomena, they penetrate the sixth stage, the Stage of Manifest Wisdom (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
One must realize this through a mind of fierce and sharp resolve, yet one has not yet attained the gate of the non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in the present.

When a bodhisattva practices in accordance with the self-nature of all phenomena in this way, because they take great compassion as their precursor, because they take great compassion as their sovereign, and because they desire to fulfill great compassion, they contemplate the assembly and dispersal, the arising and ceasing, of all worlds.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the arising and ceasing of this world, they reflect:
"All conventional designations for birth in the world arise from the grasping at a self; if one is free from the grasping at a self, there are no conventional designations for birth in the world."

Again, he reflects: "These ordinary beings are foolish and ignorant, clinging to a self; they are shrouded by the cataracts of ignorance, seeking existence and non-existence in accordance with what is irrational. Their minds are distracted and scattered, rushing down deviant paths and following what is erroneous. They accumulate formations of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable; yet the seeds of the mind—contaminated and grasping, planted by those formations of theirs—continue into future births, old age, and death, being stored away within the field of karma consisting of the intermediate state and subsequent existence."

Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, moistened by the water of craving, irrigated by the sprinkling of self-conceit, and flourishing within the net of views, the seed-sprout of name-and-form arises;
having arisen, it grows; once name-and-form has grown, the five sense-faculties evolve;
once the faculties have evolved, there is contact through their mutual encounter with consciousness; and from this encounter of contact, various sensations arise.
Birth; following birth, the delighting in sensation is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*); as craving increases, grasping (*upādāna*) arises; from grasping, becoming (*bhava*) is produced;
due to becoming, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise; once the five aggregates have arisen, they gradually decay within the five destinies;
having decayed, they perish; because of this decay and perishing, there is feverish affliction (*paridāha*), and by reason of this feverish affliction...
Therefore, all lamentation, sorrow, suffering, grief, and affliction—all these sufferings gather together;
yet there is no one who gathers them, and they cease spontaneously without anyone causing their cessation.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva observes dependent origination by means of such conforming modes of practice.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
'In terms of the ultimate characteristic, the lack of knowledge regarding the truths is called ignorance; that which is produced as the fruit of action by ignorance is [suffering]."

Formations (*saṃskāra*) are so named; consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the initial mind that serves as the basis for formations. The remaining four aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) arising simultaneously with consciousness are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The further development of name-and-form is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The conjunction of the three factors—the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness—is called tainted contact (*sāsravaspṛśana*).
That which arises simultaneously [with contact] is called feeling (*vedanā*). The attachment to the flavor of feeling is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—the intensification of that craving—is called grasping (*upādāna*). From grasping arises contaminated karma, which is called becoming (*bhava*).

The arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) as the outflow of that karma is called birth (*jāti*). The maturation of the aggregates is aging (*jarā*), and the disintegration of the aggregates is death (*maraṇa*).
For one who is deluded and about to perish at the point of death, there is a fever of the mind due to attachment, which is called sorrow (*śoka*). From this sorrow...
The uttering of cries, wailing, and sighs; the dissatisfaction associated with the five sense-faculties is called suffering (*duḥkha*);

the dissatisfaction associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called grief (*daurmanasya*); and the groaning and moaning produced by grief and suffering is called despair (*upāyāsa*).
Thus, this great mass of suffering arises and increases; within it, there is ultimately no agent and no experiencer.
Again, he thought: "It is by grasping at an agent that there is activity;
since there is no agent, from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), activity also does not exist."
Then this Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"That which is called the triple world is nothing but mind; it is upon this that the Tathāgata has analytically expounded the twelve links of existence, all of which are established based upon the single mind."

Why is this? If, regarding an object, there is a mind associated with craving, that which arises is consciousness; the object itself is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Delusion regarding these formations is ignorance (*avidyā*). Volitional formations, ignorance, and the mind arising together are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The growth of name-and-form is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The differentiation of the six sense bases is called contact (*sparśa*). That which arises together with contact is sensation (*vedanā*). Being insatiable when experiencing sensation is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The compulsive grasping and refusal to let go driven by craving is clinging (*upādāna*). The arising of those factors of existence is becoming (*bhava*). What is produced from becoming is birth (*jāti*). The maturation of birth is aging (*jarā*). The decay of aging is death (*maraṇa*).
In this context, ignorance has two functions:
first, it deludes sentient beings by way of its object;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) also have two functions:
first, they can produce future maturation (*vipāka*);
second, they serve as the cause for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness also has two functions:
first, it is able to continue existence;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of name-and-form.
Name-and-form also has two functions:
first, they mutually support one another;
second, they serve as the cause for the arising of the six sense bases.
The six sense bases also have two functions:
first, they can manifest the distinctions among their respective objects;
second, they serve as the cause for the arising of contact.
Contact also has two functions:
first, it can contact the object;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of sensation.
Feeling also has two functions:
first, it is able to experience objects that are pleasant, unpleasant, or neither;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of craving.
Craving also has two functions:
first, it causes attachment to objects that provoke passion;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of grasping.
Appropriation also has two functions:
first, it can continue the process of affliction;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of existence.
Existence (*bhava*) also has two functions:
first, it causes rebirth in other realms of existence to manifest;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of birth (*jāti*).
Birth also has two functions:
first, it can give rise to the aggregates;
second, it serves as the cause for the arising of old age.
Old age also has two functions:
first, it causes the faculties to undergo decay and transformation;
second, it brings about conjunction with death and gives rise to its cause.
Death also has two functions:
first, it can destroy all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra);
second, it is not abandoned through thorough knowledge (parijñā).
"Furthermore, regarding 'ignorance conditions volitional formations,' the nature of ignorance as a condition means that volitional formations are not severed and are further assisted.
Regarding 'volitional formations condition consciousness,' the nature of volitional formations as a condition means that consciousness is not severed and is further assisted."
Regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form": the nature of consciousness as a condition means that name-and-form is not interrupted and is further assisted.
Regarding "name-and-form conditions the six sense bases": the nature of name-and-form as a condition means that the six sense bases are not interrupted and are further assisted.
Regarding "contact conditioned by the six sense bases," this refers to the nature of the six sense bases as conditions, meaning that contact is uninterrupted and further assisted.
Regarding "feeling conditioned by contact," this refers to the nature of contact as a condition, meaning that feeling is uninterrupted and further assisted.
Regarding "feeling as the condition for craving": within the nature of feeling as a condition, it means that craving is not severed and furthermore receives support.
Regarding "craving as the condition for clinging": within the nature of craving as a condition, it means that clinging is not severed and furthermore receives support.
Regarding "clinging conditions existence": within the nature of clinging as a condition, it means that existence is uninterrupted and further assisted.
Regarding "existence conditions birth": within the nature of existence as a condition, it means that birth is uninterrupted and further assisted.
Regarding "birth as the condition for aging and death": with respect to the nature of birth as a condition, it means that aging and death are not severed and are further assisted.

Regarding "because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease": because the nature of ignorance as a condition is absent, all volitional formations are severed and extinguished, no longer receiving any assistance.
"Because formations cease, consciousness ceases": because the causal condition of formations is absent, consciousness is also severed and extinguished, lacking further support.
"Because consciousness ceases, name-and-form ceases": because the causal condition of consciousness is absent, name-and-form is severed and extinguished, lacking further support.
"Because name-and-form ceases, the six sense bases cease": because the causal nature of name-and-form is absent, the six sense bases are severed and extinguished, no longer receiving any support.
"Because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases": because the causal nature of the six sense bases is absent, contact is also severed and extinguished, no longer receiving any support.
"Because contact ceases, feeling ceases": because the condition of contact is absent, feeling is also severed and extinguished, with nothing further to sustain it.
"Because feeling ceases, craving ceases": because the condition of feeling is absent, craving is also severed and extinguished, with nothing further to sustain it.
"Because craving ceases, grasping ceases": because the condition of craving is absent, grasping is also severed and extinguished, no longer receiving any support.
"Because grasping ceases, existence ceases": because the condition of grasping is absent, existence is also severed and extinguished, no longer receiving any support.
"Because existence ceases, birth ceases": because the nature of the condition of existence is absent, birth is also extinguished and no longer receives support.
"Because birth ceases, old age and death cease": because the nature of the condition of birth is absent, old age and death are extinguished and no longer receive support.
"Furthermore, therein, ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the uninterrupted flow of afflictions;
formations and existence constitute the uninterrupted flow of karma;
and the remaining links constitute the uninterrupted flow of suffering."

Because of their differentiation, the past and future limits are extinguished; thus these three flows are severed. All these three flows are without self, free from "I" and "mine," and their arising and ceasing by intrinsic nature are like a bundle of reeds.
"Furthermore, that which was stated—'ignorance conditions volitional formations'—refers to the dependence of the previous life;
'consciousness up to feeling' refers to the dependence of the present life;
and 'craving up to existence' refers to the dependence of the future life, by means of which there is the subsequent continuous flow and wandering."
The cessation of formations due to the cessation of ignorance refers to the severance of dependent observation.
Furthermore, by means of these twelve links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), there are three types of suffering:
herein, from formations up to the six sense bases, these constitute the nature of the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*)—these two are of the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
the remaining members of existence are of the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Through the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*) cease; this is the ultimate eradication of these three types of suffering.
That "conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise" reveals that the nature of volitional formations is produced from causes and conditions; the same applies to the others.
That "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" demonstrates that volitional formations lack intrinsic nature; the same applies to the others.
That "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" refers to the bond of arising; the others are likewise.
That "because of the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" refers to the bond of cessation; the others are likewise.
"Conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise" refers to the contemplation of conformity to existence; the others are likewise so.
"With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" refers to the contemplation of conformity to exhaustion and cessation; the others are likewise so.
In this way, the bodhisattva contemplates the phenomena of dependent origination through ten aspects, both in direct and reverse order:

namely, because of the continuity of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*); because of their entry into a single mind; because of the differentiation of one's own karma; because of their mutual inseparability; because of the uninterrupted flow of the three streams; because of the principle of mutual dependence between the past and future lives; because of the accumulation of the three types of suffering; because of being produced by causes and conditions; because of the continuous binding of arising and ceasing; and because of contemplating the exhaustion of existence.

By means of these ten modes of observation, the bodhisattva contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Because they observe dependent origination as being devoid of a self, a life-span, or a person (*pudgala*), and as being by nature empty and quiescent—freed from an agent and a recipient—the door of liberation that is emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before them. Furthermore, because the intrinsic nature of those links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) has ceased for this bodhisattva, and because they dwell in the realization of ultimate liberation, not even the slightest mark of a phenomenon arises thereafter; thus, the door of liberation that is signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) manifests before them.

Furthermore, once this bodhisattva has thus entered into emptiness and signlessness, they have no further aspirations or desires except for great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which serves as their precursor. For the sake of maturing sentient beings, the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) consequently manifests before them.

When a bodhisattva thus cultivates these three gates of liberation, they are free from the notions of self and other, they distance themselves from the notions of an agent and a recipient, and they are free from the notions of existence and non-existence. With great compassion as their foremost priority, in order to cultivate and realize those factors of enlightenment not yet cultivated or realized, they further engage in practice, reflecting as follows:
"Conditioned phenomena proceed by virtue of association; through dissociation, they cannot flow on.
Conditioned phenomena flow on by virtue of conjunction; if there is no conjunction, they do not flow on."
I have understood that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) thus proceed, defiled by many faults; therefore, I shall now sever their association and their conjunction.
"However, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity, one should not permanently extinguish all conditioned phenomena.
O Sons of the Buddha!

In this way, the Bodhisattva contemplates that although all conditioned phenomena are full of faults and defilements, they ultimately lack intrinsic nature; their fundamental nature is such that they are ultimately neither born nor extinguished."

Because one observes at this time with the arousal of great compassion and does not abandon the assembly of all sentient beings, it is called the dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) wherein non-attached knowledge is manifest; it is brought before one through the manifestation of its imputation.

Once the bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, they abide in the illumination of the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitā), which brings forth and induces the various conditions for the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma); yet, they do not abide in any abiding.
Observing that conditioned phenomena are by nature quiescent and non-abiding, yet the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) therein are not yet perfected,
the bodhisattva dwelling in this Stage of Presence (Abhimukhī-bhūmi) is said to have the samādhi of entering emptiness manifest before them.

The samādhi of the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the samādhi of the emptiness of the ultimate, the samādhi of supreme emptiness, the samādhi of great emptiness, the samādhi of corresponding emptiness, the samādhi of engendering emptiness, the samādhi of non-conceptual emptiness according to reality, the samādhi of emptiness with attachment, and the samādhi of emptiness that is neither separated nor not separated—all these became manifest before him.

This bodhisattva, thus taking emptiness as the foremost gateway, brings one million samādhis before him; likewise, one million samādhis appear before him through the gateway of signlessness, and one million samādhis appear before him through the gateway of wishlessness.
The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four;
The Scripture on the Ten Stages Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Translated at Longxing Monastery in Beiting, as a continuation of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "O Sons of the Buddha!
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this *Abhimukhī* Stage, their unshakable intention (*āśaya*) becomes even more perfectly fulfilled."

They attain the perfection of the resolute intention, the noble intention, the profound intention, the non-regressive intention, the unceasing intention, the stainless intention, the boundless intention, the intention seeking wisdom, and the intention associated with skillful means and insight.

Thereupon, with these various intentions, the Bodhisattva accords with the Buddha’s enlightenment and confronts all heterodox arguments; with unflagging diligence, they enter the ground of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*).

Having abandoned the grounds of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, they proceed resolutely and exclusively toward the wisdom of the Buddha. Because they cannot be eclipsed by the manifestation of Māras, enemies, or afflictions (*kleśa*), they dwell securely within the light of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom. They skillfully cultivate the practice of the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), remaining constantly associated with the insight of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*) while intermittently eliciting the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Presence (*abhimukhī*), their dwelling in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) becomes preeminent, and they realize the third kind of intense conformative patience (*tīkṣṇānulomikī kṣānti*), because they accord with all phenomena in accordance with reality and do not oppose them.

"When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), by means of vast vision and the power of their vows, they directly perceive many Buddhas, many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas."

Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the Bodhisattva, with a vast and superior resolve, honors, respects, serves, and makes offerings to them. He presents them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and various articles of daily life; he offers the exquisite implements of pleasure belonging to Bodhisattvas and shows reverence to the Saṅgha. He dedicates these roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. He serves the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, with earnest devotion, and listens to the True Dharma with reverence and respect, regarding it as something rare. Having heard it, he upholds it, and through the light of non-erroneous meditative concentration and wisdom, he practices firm right conduct, maintaining it without forgetfulness, thereby further gaining entry into the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.

Thus, for a bodhisattva dwelling in this sixth stage, the Manifest (Abhimukhī), these roots of goodness become increasingly blazing and increasingly bright and pure over immeasurable eons—over immeasurable hundreds of eons, immeasurable thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of eons, immeasurable koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of koṭis of eons, immeasurable thousands of koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of eons; these roots of goodness become increasingly blazing and increasingly bright and pure.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
It is just as when a goldsmith fashions ornaments from refined gold and inlays them with lapis lazuli gems; they become increasingly radiant and ever more brilliant and pure."
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), these roots of goodness are likewise: through skillful means and wisdom, as they are reflected upon and examined, they become increasingly radiant, increasingly clear and pure, and progressively tranquil, such that nothing can eclipse them.
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha!
It is like the light of the moon, which can bring joy and satisfaction to the bodies of sentient beings; it cannot be interrupted or destroyed by the movement of the four winds.
Thus it is, O sons of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Presence (Abhimukhī), these roots of goodness likewise function in such a way that they can extinguish the flames of affliction of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, and cannot be severed or destroyed by the paths of the four māras.
He attains preeminence in the perfection of wisdom among the ten perfections; as for the remaining perfections, he practices them according to his power and capacity, though not exclusively.
"O Sons of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the sixth stage of the Bodhisattva, the Stage of Manifest Wisdom (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are mostly reborn as the King of the Gods of Transformation (*nirmāṇarati-deva-rāja*), capable of exercising sovereign power to skillfully transform sentient beings and causing their arrogance to cease forever."
He is always such that no questioning or challenge from any śrāvakas can overshadow him, and he is able to lead sentient beings to realize and enter into dependent origination.

Whatever deeds he performs—whether through generosity, kind words, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—all of these are never apart from the mental attention directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the bodhisattva, the bodhisattva practices, the perfections (pāramitās), the stages (bhūmis), the powers of a buddha, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a buddha, and even until they are not apart from the mental attention directed toward the omniscient wisdom that is perfectly conjoined with all aspects of practice.
He constantly makes this aspiration:

"Among all sentient beings, may I be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; and may I even attain the state that serves as the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."

If one delights in initiating such diligence, through this diligence, in a single kṣaṇa, muhūrta, or moment, one realizes and enters hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodhisattva samādhis; one is able to see hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas and fully understands the empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of those Buddhas;

one can shake hundreds of thousands of koṭis of worlds, travel to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddha-fields, illuminate hundreds of thousands of koṭis of worlds, and bring to maturity hundreds of thousands of koṭis of sentient beings; one dwells for a lifespan of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of great kalpas, and is able to enter hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas regarding both the past and future limits; one contemplates and selects hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Dharma-gates, and is able to manifest hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodies, each body surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodhisattvas.

From this point upward, for those bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration, by virtue of their superior vows, all their playful manifestations—whether of body, light, supernormal powers, eyes, spheres of activity, sounds, conduct, adornments, resolute understandings, or deeds—cannot be easily numbered even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The Bodhisattva has already purified the fifth stage; He contemplates phenomena as signless and lacking intrinsic nature, Unarisen, unborn, and eternally quiescent, Their nature fundamentally pure and free from conceptual proliferation."
There is neither grasping nor rejecting, like illusions and the like; existence and non-existence are non-dual, free from conceptual discrimination.
Contemplating in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in this way, one enters the sixth stage by means of this wisdom.
Endowed with the wisdom of fierce and compliant patience, he contemplates the marks of arising and ceasing in all worlds;
knowing that the world arises from the grasping at a self, he sees that once self-grasping is removed, the world no longer exists.
Thoroughly penetrating dependent origination as empty according to reality, Without destroying the conventional use of designations for the composite;
There is no agent, no experiencer, and no life-principle— All conditioned phenomena arise everywhere like clouds.
Ignorance regarding the truths is called ignorance; the karma produced by delusion is called formations;
the initial moment of consciousness at birth is called consciousness; the remaining aggregates arising simultaneously with it are called name-and-form;
their further development is called the six sense bases; the meeting of the three is contact, and that which arises simultaneously with it is feeling.
The pleasant feeling is called craving; when craving increases, it becomes grasping. With grasping as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, the aggregates arise, which is birth.
The maturation of the aggregates is called aging; the disintegration of the aggregates is death. Thus does this entire great mass of suffering come to be.
Thoroughly realizing that the three realms are nothing but mind, The twelve links of existence depend upon the mind;
Birth and death are all produced by the mind, And when the mind ceases, birth and death are exhausted.
The functions of ignorance are twofold: through delusion regarding conditions, it serves as the cause for volitional formations;
thus it continues until old age and death, from which this suffering arises without end.
Ignorance is the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); they continue without interruption and are further assisted by it.
Because this [ignorance] is absent, the formative forces are severed; since there is no longer any support, the rest likewise cease.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping are the stream of afflictions; volitional formations and existence are karma, while all the rest are suffering.
Ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past; consciousness through feeling belong to the present;
craving, grasping, and existence give rise to future suffering. By contemplating their cessation, one reaches the end of suffering.
The six sense bases constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*); contact and feeling constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*);
and the remaining links of existence constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). If one perceives non-self, these three sufferings are extinguished.
Arising from the activity of causes and conditions, their nature is empty because they are severed when conditions depart;
ignorance is the condition for the bondage of birth, and once one is freed from that condition, bondage is eliminated.
Following along with ignorance, the various states of existence arise; If one does not follow along, those existences are severed.
Because of this, the non-existence of those existences is likewise so; Through these ten kinds of reflection, the mind becomes free from attachment.
The continuity of the links of existence is subsumed within a single mind; it does not depart from its own karma and consists of the three flows.
Arising through the causes and conditions of the three periods and the three types of suffering, it arises and ceases in a continuous bond, following on without end.
Thus universally observing the activity of dependent origination— It is without agent, without recipient, and without intrinsic nature;
Like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection of light, And like a fool chasing a mirage.
Contemplating this, one enters the gate of liberation of emptiness; knowing that the nature of conditions is detached, one enters the signless;
understanding their falsity, one has no wish for anything, except for compassionately rescuing sentient beings.
The Great Master practices the gates of liberation, Increasing his great compassion as he seeks the Buddha-dharma;
Knowing that conditioned things arise from combination, He is resolute in his aspiration and diligent in his vigor.
He realizes a hundred thousand samādhis of emptiness; the same is true for signlessness and wishlessness.
His patience in accordance with prajñā is supreme, and his liberating wisdom reaches full perfection.
Furthermore, with a pure intention, they made offerings to many Buddhas and cultivated the Path within the Buddha’s teachings;
having attained the treasury of the Buddha-dharma and increased their roots of goodness, they were adorned like gold and lapis lazuli.
Just as the cool moonlight pervades all things, And the four winds cannot destroy it upon contact;
so too this Sage can transcend the path of the four Māras, and thus extinguish the fever of worldly delusion.
Dwelling here, they mostly become kings who transform through virtue, guiding sentient beings to eliminate their pride;
all that they do seeks omniscience, having already far surpassed the path of the śrāvakas.
In this stage, through diligent effort, one attains hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodhisattva samādhis;
one also beholds various immeasurable Buddhas, like the sun in the sky during the height of summer.
Profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive or know, It cannot be understood by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
Thus have I, for the sake of the Buddha’s sons, Expounded this sixth stage of the Bodhisattva.

The Sixth Stage, the Bodhisattva Ground of Manifestation, is concluded. 7. The Bodhisattva Ground of Far-Reaching Practice (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi), the Seventh: At that time, the great assembly was filled with joy; they scattered jewels that formed clouds abiding in the sky.
Universally emitting various wondrous sounds, they addressed the Most Victorious and Pure One:
“You have mastered the wisdom of ultimate truth and attained mastery; you have accomplished hundreds of thousands of millions of meritorious virtues.”
A lotus among men, free from all attachment, you proclaim profound practice for the benefit of all beings.
The Sovereign Lord of Devas, abiding in the sky, emits great radiance that illuminates the Buddha’s body;
he also scatters clouds of the most sublime and wondrous incense, universally making offerings to the One who has removed sorrow and affliction.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with joy, and they all raised their voices in unison to offer praise:
"Having heard these merits of the earth, we have already attained a most excellent benefit."
At that time, the goddesses were filled with joy in their hearts, and they vied with one another to play thousands of kinds of musical sounds.
By the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, these sounds together uttered these words:
"Your majestic deportment is tranquil and most peerless; you are the one who can tame those difficult to tame, the Worthy One of the World."
Having transcended all worlds, they traverse the world to reveal the wondrous Way.
Though they manifest various infinite bodies, they know that each body is devoid of inherent existence.
Skillfully using words and phrases to expound all dharmas, they do not grasp at the marks of letters or sounds.
They travel to hundreds of thousands of lands, making supreme offerings to the Buddhas;
with wisdom that is sovereign and unattached, they do not give rise to the notion of "my Buddha-field."
Though they diligently teach and transform all sentient beings, they harbor no thoughts of "self" or "other";
though they have already cultivated and perfected vast goodness, they do not give rise to attachment toward those wholesome dharmas.
Seeing that all worlds are constantly ablaze with the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion,
he completely detaches from all conceptual notions and gives rise to the power of great compassion and diligence.
All the devas and devīs, having offered various kinds of worship and praise,
remained silent together for a time, gazing up at the Honored One among Men, wishing to hear the Dharma.
Then Vimukticandra again requested, saying:
"The minds of this great assembly are pure; regarding the characteristics of the practices within the seventh stage, we pray that the Son of the Buddha will proclaim them for us."
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, having fully perfected the stages of the path cultivated in the sixth stage, wishes to enter the seventh bodhisattva stage, they should enter by means of ten kinds of superior practices for advancing on the path, which are induced by sublime skillful means and wisdom and are unique [to the bodhisattvas]."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
skillfully cultivating the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, while accumulating a vast store of merit;
They realize the selflessness of all phenomena, the absence of a life-principle, and the absence of a person, yet they do not abandon the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds;
they initiate vast merit and the practice of the Dharma through the supreme conduct of the perfections, yet they have no attachment whatsoever to any phenomena;
having already attained detachment from all three realms, they are nevertheless able to manifest the adornments of the three realms.

Having attained ultimate tranquility and cessation, and being far removed from the flames of all afflictions, they are able to initiate in all sentient beings the practice of extinguishing the flames of greed, hatred, and delusion;

knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, shadows, echoes, the moon in water, and reflections in a mirror—being non-dual in their intrinsic nature—they are able to initiate the infinite variety of karmic activities and intentions;
and relying on the well-cultivated path of the buddha-fields which is equal to space, they are able to initiate the practice of purifying and adorning the buddha-fields.
They understand that the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is by nature like space, yet they are able to manifest a body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence;
furthermore, they know that the intrinsic nature of the Buddhas' voices is quiescent and ineffable, yet they are able to manifest the adornment of all diverse vocal modulations;

they understand that all Buddhas realize the three periods of time instantaneously in a single moment, yet they are able to enter into and manifest various signs, eons, and so forth, in accordance with their observation of the mental dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings.

In this way, by means of these ten kinds of extraordinary practices for progressing on the path, which are induced by skillful means and wisdom, the bodhisattva enters the seventh stage from the sixth stage.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

Because these ten kinds of extraordinary practices for advancing on the path, induced by sublime skillful means and wisdom, have become manifest, the Bodhisattva is said to have entered the seventh stage."
When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, they enter into the infinite realms of sentient beings;
they enter into the infinite Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who have accomplished the work of taming and transforming sentient beings;
and they enter into the infinite networks of worlds.
They enter the purity of the buddha-fields of immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones;
they enter the nature of the infinite distinctions of the Dharma;
and they enter the perfectly awakened wisdom of immeasurable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones.
They enter into the distinctions of immeasurable eons;
they enter into the immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who awaken to the three periods of time;
and they enter into the characteristics of the distinctions in the inclinations of immeasurable sentient beings.
They enter into the infinite Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifesting various names and physical forms;
they enter into the infinite distinctions among the inclinations and faculties of sentient beings;
and they enter into the infinite Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, whose vocal sounds bring joy to other sentient beings.
They enter into the distinctions among the various mental activities of immeasurable sentient beings;
they enter into the vast conduct of wisdom of immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;

they enter into the paths of travel, inclinations, and resolute convictions of immeasurable followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle, as well as the immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, expounding the entry into the Way.
They enter into the immeasurable attainments of the realization and practice of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
they enter into the immeasurable profound gateways of wisdom taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones;
and they enter into the immeasurable preparatory practices cultivated through the bodhisattva deeds.
He enters into the immeasurable Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who proclaim the collection for entering the Mahāyāna.
Then this Bodhisattva reflects: "The realm of the Buddhas is thus immeasurable;

it cannot be calculated even in hundreds of koṭis of kalpas, nor in thousands of koṭis, nor in hundreds of thousands of koṭis, nor even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of kalpas. I should give rise to this realm of the Buddhas and, through effortlessness (*anābhoga*), non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*), and the absence of diverse conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), cause it to be perfected."

Thus, through this manifold wisdom of skillful observation and supernormal powers, the bodhisattva practices with unceasing and flawless diligence; because it is immovable, it is called "already abiding in the superior practice of the path of uncommon cultivation through the wisdom of skillful means."

Furthermore, this bodhisattva is able to induce the path in a single kṣaṇa without arising from meditative absorption. While walking, he induces such right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), training with diligent application; even while standing, sitting, lying down, or even during sleep and dreams, he remains free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Amidst all modes of deportment, without needing to apply deliberate effort, he correctly directs his attention and, within a single moment of one-pointed concentration, fully accomplishes the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

Why is this? Because all thoughts and mental activities arising from this bodhisattva are, in every moment of mind, preceded by great compassion; they are dedicated toward the cultivation and realization of all Buddha-dharmas, proceeding toward the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Regarding all the roots of virtue possessed by this bodhisattva, giving them to sentient beings for the sake of seeking the Buddha-wisdom is their perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*);
having compassion as the foremost priority and not causing harm to any sentient beings is their perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
and progressing without weariness toward each successive stage of wholesome dharmas is their perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
The constant presence of the path of omniscience without ever becoming distracted is the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*);
the patience that manifests regarding phenomena that are by nature neither arising nor ceasing is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*);
and the eliciting of immeasurable knowledge is the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-pāramitā*).
To induce successive stages of wisdom is the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā);
that no heterodox arguments or hosts of Māras can destroy one’s path is the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā);
to establish all phenomena as they truly are is called the perfection of knowledge (jñāna-pāramitā).
O Sons of the Buddha!

When Bodhisattvas dwell in this Far-Reaching Stage (*dūramgamā bhūmiḥ*), these ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are, in every instant, fully endowed with the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and, in brief, all factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are entirely perfected in every single moment.
When he had spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O Sons of the Buddha!
Does the Bodhisattva merely attain the perfection of all factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) in the seventh stage, or does he also fulfill them throughout all the Bodhisattva stages?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Within all the ten stages of a bodhisattva, all factors of enlightenment are fully perfected; however, they are most preeminent in the seventh stage of the bodhisattva."
Why is this so? O Son of the Buddha!
In this bodhisattva stage, the practice of application has now reached fulfillment, and one is further able to enter into the superknowledges of wisdom and spiritual power.

However, O Son of the Buddha! In the first stage (*bhūmi*), all great vows serve as the objects of focus for the perfection of the factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*). In the second stage, it is because the defilements of the mind are dispelled; in the third stage, it is because right aspirations increase and the light of the Dharma is attained; in the fourth stage, it is because one enters the path; in the fifth stage, it is because one accords with all worldly activities; and in the sixth stage, it is because one enters the profound gateways of all phenomena (*dharmamukha*).
Now, in this seventh stage, because this bodhisattva fully initiates all the qualities of a Buddha, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are perfected. Why is this?
Because it consists of the portion of wisdom-application (*jñāna-prayoga-bhāga*) that has been induced by the bodhisattva from the first stage up through the seventh stage.
From the eighth stage of wisdom of a bodhisattva, these are all accomplished through effortlessness.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like there being two worlds: one is defiled and pure, and the other is purely pure;
The space between these two realms is difficult to traverse, except for those who possess the power of great supernormal abilities.
Son of the Buddha!

It is the same with the bodhisattva’s gate of mixed and pure practices: it is difficult to transcend, except for those who possess the power of great vows, skillful means, wisdom, and supernormal powers.
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said: "O Sons of the Buddha!
Could it be that the correct practice of a bodhisattva within the first seven bodhisattva stages is defiled by the conduct of afflictions?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!

Because of the practices of the bodhisattvas from the first stage onward, it should be said that they are far removed from the karma of all afflictions; this is due to the superior power of dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment. Nevertheless, because they are equal to the paths according to their respective types, one cannot yet say within the seventh stage that they have transcended the practice of afflictions."
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a wheel-turning sage king who, riding upon the precious celestial elephant, traverses the four great continents among humans; he fully perceives all poverty, suffering, and defilements, yet is not defiled by those various afflictions. Nevertheless, he is not yet said to have transcended the human state.

If he relinquishes his royal body and is born in the Brahma world, riding upon a Brahma palace to tour the thousand worlds and manifesting the radiance and majestic virtue of a Brahma god, only then is he said to have transcended the human state.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is likewise with the bodhisattva: from the very first ground, they mount the bodhisattva vehicle that leads to the further shore and travel throughout the world, perceiving the afflictions and faults of sentient beings; yet, because they ride upon the true path, they are not defiled by those various afflictions. Nevertheless, even at the seventh ground, it cannot yet be said that they have transcended the afflictions.

If one relinquishes all effortful application and enters the eighth stage from the seventh stage, one mounts and governs the pure vehicle of the bodhisattva to traverse the world; knowing the afflictions of defilement, one is not stained by them, for one has already transcended them.

When Bodhisattvas dwell securely in this seventh bodhisattva stage, they for the most part transcend all afflictions such as greed; when these Bodhisattvas cultivate this Stage of Far-Going, it should be said that they neither possess afflictions nor are free from them.
Why is this? Because all afflictions do not manifest, one should not say that they possess afflictions;
yet because they have not yet attained the Buddha-wisdom they seek, one should not say that they are free from afflictions.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, they accomplish the purification of superior intention and the actions of body, speech, and mind; they transcend all unwholesome paths of action censured by all Tathāgatas, and they constantly and perpetually uphold the ten wholesome paths of action praised by all Buddhas, as previously described.

Regarding all the worldly arts and crafts introduced in the fifth bhūmi, these are all performed spontaneously and effortlessly by the bodhisattvas of the seventh bhūmi; they are universally acknowledged as teachers throughout this trichiliocosm. With the exception of the Tathāgatas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and those great bodhisattvas already established in the eighth bhūmi and beyond, there is no one who can equal them in their intention and application.
All dhyānas, samādhis, samāpattis, abhijñās, and vimokṣas—all these become manifest before him.
This occurs because the signs of cultivation appear before him, and not because they are accomplished through karmic maturation.

Just as in the eighth stage, for this bodhisattva dwelling in the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), the power of cultivation through skillful means and sublime wisdom within all mental activities reaches fulfillment, and all factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are further perfected.

Furthermore, when this bodhisattva dwells in this seventh bodhisattva stage, they enter the bodhisattva samādhi named "Thoroughly Discerning," the samādhi named "Thoroughly Discerning Meanings," the samādhi named "Exalted Wisdom," the samādhi named "Discerning the Treasury of Meanings," the samādhi named "Discerning All Meanings," the samādhi named "Well-Abiding in Firm Roots," the samādhi named "Gateway to the Supernormal Knowledges of Wisdom," the samādhi named "Adorning the Dharma Realm," the samādhi named "Victory of the Tathāgata," and the samādhi named "Entering the Gate of the Various Treasuries of Meaning: Saṃsāra and Nirvāṇa."

With great wisdom and supernormal powers as his foremost attributes, the bodhisattva enters one million samādhis to purify this stage. Because he has cultivated these samādhis through such sublime skillful means and wisdom, and because he has attained great compassion, he transcends the stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, and the stage of the observation of wisdom manifests before him.

Thereupon, for a bodhisattva dwelling in this seventh bodhisattva stage, immeasurable physical actions proceed in accordance with the departure from signs; immeasurable verbal actions proceed in accordance with the departure from signs; and immeasurable mental actions proceed in accordance with the departure from signs—all manifested by the thoroughly pure forbearance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Does a Bodhisattva of the first stage not possess immeasurable actions of body, speech, and mind that transcend the practices of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
Although such practice exists, it arises solely through the superior power of the focal objects of the Buddha-dharma, and not through the observation of self-awakened wisdom."
In this seventh stage of the bodhisattva, because one observes the objective realm through the wisdom of self-awakening, nothing can eclipse or surpass it.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a prince born into a royal family, begotten by the principal queen and endowed with the marks of royalty; as soon as he is born, he is able to outshine the assembly of ministers.
It was solely due to the sovereign power of his father, the King, and not through what he had contemplated with his own wisdom.

However, once his body had grown and his arts and crafts were fully perfected, it was by virtue of being sustained by his own intellectual power that he surpassed all that his ministers could accomplish.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is likewise with the Bodhisattva: from the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), they outshine all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas solely by virtue of their vast and superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), and not through the observation of their own realized wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*).
Now, in this seventh stage (*bhūmi*), because the Bodhisattva establishes wisdom regarding their own sphere of activity, they transcend all the deeds performed by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
"O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, although they have attained the extremely profound, tranquil, and non-active bodily, vocal, and mental actions, they do not abandon them, but rather seek superior progress through courageous application."
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
To what stage must a bodhisattva reach in order to be able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation?"
Vajragarbha Bodhisattva said:
"O Son of the Buddha!
From the sixth stage onward, a bodhisattva is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation."

Now, while dwelling in the seventh bodhisattva stage, one is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation within each and every moment of mind; yet, it should not be said that one has realized cessation.

For this reason, it is said that this Bodhisattva has accomplished extremely difficult and marvelous deeds of body, speech, and mind; namely, while constantly dwelling within the abode of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), he is able not to realize cessation (*śānta*).
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a person who boards a great ship and enters the vast ocean; because they possess skill in navigation and thoroughly understand the characteristics of the water, they will never encounter the perils of the ocean waters.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is likewise for a bodhisattva dwelling in this seventh stage: riding upon the ship that reaches the other shore, they are always able to dwell securely within the abode of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), yet they do not personally realize cessation (*śānta*).
O Son of the Buddha!

Having attained this wisdom, the bodhisattva, through the sublime insight induced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), manifests the gateway of birth and death by means of the skillful power of great expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*); yet his underlying intention remains dwelling in *nirvāṇa*, surrounded by its retinue.
Always delighting in seclusion, he takes birth within the three realms through the power of his vows, yet remains untainted by the faults and afflictions of worldly phenomena.
