Although they are eternally quiescent, they manifest through skillful means as being ablaze, yet they are not burned;
they constantly accord with the Buddha’s wisdom, yet manifest entry into the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
having attained the treasury of the Buddha-realm, they manifest dwelling within the realm of Māra.
Having transcended the paths of the four māras, they manifest the practice of māra’s arts;
they demonstrate the performance of all the practices of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), yet their underlying intention never abandons the Buddha-dharma;
they manifest compliance with all worldly activities, yet they always delight in entering the supramundane path and all manner of sublime adornments.

They surpass all that is possessed by humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, ghosts, spirits, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, yet they do not abandon their mental attention directed toward the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom and dwells in this Bodhisattva Ground of Far-Going, through vast vision and the power of their vows, they directly behold many Buddhas—many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, many koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, many thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and many hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas.

Having seen these Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the bodhisattva, with a vast and superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), honors, respects, serves, and makes offerings to them. He presents them with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and various articles of life; he offers the bodhisattva’s own exquisite instruments of joy and shows reverence to the Saṅgha community. He dedicates these roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). He honors and serves the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and listens to the true Dharma with a sense of its rarity, honoring and respecting it. Having heard it, he upholds it and practices with the light of wisdom and concentration (*samādhi*) free from error, thereby accomplishing the holy teachings protected by all the Buddhas.

Regarding all the questions and challenges posed within their own direct realization by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they are incapable of being discouraged; thus, for the most part, they attain purity in the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) toward the Dharma that benefits sentient beings.

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*), these roots of goodness become increasingly intense, pure, and capable, and they grow ever more luminous and clear throughout immeasurable hundreds of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of koṭis of kalpas, immeasurable thousands of koṭis of kalpas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of kalpas; these roots of goodness become even more intense and even more luminously pure.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a goldsmith who fashions ornaments from refined gold and embellishes them by inlaying and setting various maṇi jewels; these become exceedingly radiant and supremely pure, such that no other ornaments can equal them.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this seventh stage, the Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), these roots of goodness are likewise thus: impelled by skillful means and wisdom, they become increasingly radiant and further purified, such that the roots of goodness of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot outshine them.
O Son of the Buddha!
Furthermore, just as the light of the sun cannot be eclipsed by all the stars or the moonlight, it largely dries up the foul, damp mud and marshes within Jambudvīpa.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of Far-Reaching (dūraṃgamā), these roots of goodness are likewise such that they cannot be eclipsed by the roots of goodness of any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; for the most part, they dry up the defilements and impurities of the afflictions of all sentient beings.

Regarding those ten perfections (*pāramitā*), he takes the perfection of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya-pāramitā*) as predominant; as for the remaining perfections, he practices them according to his strength and capacity, though not without practicing them at all.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This is called the brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā).

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, they are mostly reborn as the King of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), skillfully bestowing upon all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas the means for the realization of clear observation (abhisamaya).”

They are able to lead sentient beings into the correct nature of transcendence (*niyāma*). Whatever deeds they perform—whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—all of these are never apart from the mental engagement with the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the bodhisattva, the bodhisattva practices, the perfections (*pāramitā*), the stages (*bhūmi*), the powers of a buddha, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a buddha, and even until they are never apart from the mental engagement with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) that is associated with all supreme and wondrous characteristics.
One should constantly make this aspiration:

"Among all sentient beings, may I be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the guide, the leader, and the commander; and may I even attain the state that serves as the basis for the knowledge of all modes."
If one delights in initiating such diligence, by means of this diligence, in a single kṣaṇa, muhūrta, or moment, one realizes hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of samādhis;
one is able to see hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas, and one is able to fully comprehend the empowerments (adhiṣṭhāna) of those Buddhas; one is able to shake [a hundred...]
He can travel to a thousand koṭi-nayuta worlds, illuminate a hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta buddha-fields, bring to maturity a hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta sentient beings,
and remain for a lifespan of a hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta kalpas throughout the preceding and succeeding [eons].
In each moment, they are able to enter hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas;

they are skillfully able to discern hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of dharma-gates; they manifest hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodies, and each body is surrounded by hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattva retinues.

From this point upward, for all those Bodhisattvas who possess the power of aspiration, by virtue of that power of aspiration, their various forms of play—whether of body, or light, or supernormal powers, or eyes, or spheres of activity, or voices, or conduct, or adornments, or resolute understandings, or deeds—cannot easily be numbered even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of eons.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Having fully prepared the practices of the sixth stage, One then cultivates those sealed by skillful means and wisdom;
Through uncommon progress and sublime conduct on the path, One thereby enters the seventh stage.”
Abiding in the three gates of liberation, they accumulate merit; Penetrating non-self, they cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
Merit and the Dharma are ever-filling; They reach the other shore through practice, free from attachment.
Detached from the three realms yet adorned, Tranquil in cessation, free from worldly afflictions;
Knowing dharmas are like illusions yet performing deeds, Realizing lands are like space yet delighting in adorning the Buddha-fields.
Understanding that the body is signless yet gathers the marks and signs of excellence, Realizing that echoes are beyond words yet skillfully expounded;
Sudden awakening in a single instant reveals all manifold characteristics— By this, the wise ascend to the seventh stage.
Observing these dharmas with clear understanding, one brings benefit to the vast multitude of the deluded;
entering the boundless realm of sentient beings, the Buddha’s work of transformation is likewise immeasurable.
They are able to enter into the number of lands, dharmas, and kalpas, as well as the inclinations, aspirations, and mental activities [of beings];
they preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles without limit, thereby teaching and transforming all classes of sentient beings.
In each instant, one brings forth the path of union, constantly cultivating wisdom throughout the four modes of conduct;
dedicating each act toward the Buddha’s enlightenment, every thought-moment is endowed with the ten pāramitās.
Bestowing gifts upon sentient beings is generosity; extinguishing delusions is ethical discipline; non-harming is patience;
seeking the good without weariness is diligence; remaining unmoved in the Path is meditative concentration;
the realization of the non-arising of phenomena is wisdom; and giving rise to immeasurable knowledge is skillful means.
The aspiration that induces successive stages of wisdom is called "vow"; its invincibility is "power";
the establishment of phenomena as they truly are is "knowledge. In this way, every moment of thought is brought to full perfection.
On the first ground, the branch of enlightenment of superior aspiration is fulfilled; on the second, because of the removal of mental impurities;
on the third, because of the increase of vows and the light of Dharma; on the fourth ground, because of entering the path;
on the fifth, because of conforming to worldly activities; and on the sixth, because of entering the profound gateways of Dharma.
In the seventh stage, through its arousal, all factors of awakening and all Buddha-dharmas are fulfilled;
by this, one is able to make all activities in the eighth stage entirely pure.
This ground is difficult to traverse; only the wise can cross it, doing so through the wisdom of their great vows.
Just as one must rely on supernormal powers to pass between the realms of the impure and the pure, so too must one transcend this stage.
Furthermore, like a wheel-turning monarch who is free from defilement, yet is not yet called one who has transcended the human stage;
if one abides within the eighth ground of wisdom, only then does one transcend the realm of the mind.
Like being born in the Brahma world and thus transcending the human stage, one is like a lotus in water, free from defilement.
Although this stage transcends all hosts of afflictions, it is neither called "possessing afflictions" nor "free from afflictions," for while no afflictions manifest in practice,
the aspiration for Buddha-wisdom has not yet been attained.
All the various arts and crafts in the world, And the scriptures, rhetoric, and treatises— One understands them all thoroughly;
As for meditative absorption, concentration, and supernormal powers, These are swiftly accomplished through cultivation.
When Bodhisattvas cultivate these seven stages of the path, they transcend all practices of the two vehicles;
because of their vows in the first stage, this arises from wisdom, like a prince who is fully endowed with power.
Having accomplished the profound, they continue to advance on the path; though frequently entering the meditative absorption of cessation, they do not realize it as a finality.
They are like those who board a ship and enter the great ocean: though they are in the water, they are not drowned by it.
Endowed with the merit of skillful means and the practice of wisdom, they cannot be fully understood by anyone in all the worlds;
having made offerings to many Buddhas, their minds become increasingly luminous, like gold adorned with exquisite jewels.

The wisdom of the Bodhisattvas on this stage is most luminous; Like the sun spreading its light to dry the waters of craving, They further become sovereign lords among the gods, Transforming and guiding all living beings to cultivate right wisdom.

If one applies the power of courageous and diligent effort, one will attain many samādhis and behold many Buddhas—hundreds, thousands, koṭis, nayutas; through the mastery of the power of vows, it exceeds even this.
This is the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Far-Reaching Travel, The pure path of skillful means and wisdom;
All the worlds, including gods and humans, As well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, are unable to fathom it.
The Seventh Stage, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi, is completed. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll Five.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīladharma, a Śramaṇa from Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Translated at Longxing Monastery in Beiting.
The Bodhisattva’s Immovable Ground, the Eighth. At that time, the celestial kings and their hosts, Hearing of these supreme practices, were all filled with joy;
Desiring to make offerings to the Tathāgata, As well as to the immeasurable great bodhisattvas.
They rained down exquisite banners, flowers, and canopies, as well as fragrant garlands, necklaces, and precious robes;
in measureless, boundless, and myriad varieties, all were adorned with mani-jewels.
The heavenly maidens simultaneously played celestial music, universally producing all manner of wondrous sounds;
making offerings to the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, they spoke these words in praise:
"O All-Seeing One, Honored Among Two-Legged Beings, out of compassion for sentient beings, you manifest your spiritual power."
May these various celestial music of the gods Universally produce wondrous sounds so that all may hear them.
Upon a single hair-tip, within hundreds of thousands of billions Of *nayuta* lands, as numerous as atoms of dust—
Within such infinite Tathāgatas Sitting serenely therein, they preach the sublime Dharma.
Within a single pore are immeasurable lands, each with its four continents and great oceans;
Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains are likewise there, all seen within it without any crowding.
Upon the tip of a single hair there are the six realms of existence:
the three evil paths, as well as humans, devas, nāgas, hosts of spirits, and asuras, each receiving their retribution according to their own karma.
In all those buddha-fields, the Tathāgatas everywhere proclaim the wondrous Dharma;
in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings, they turn the most supreme and pure wheel of Dharma.
Within the lands are the various bodies of sentient beings, and within those bodies, there are again various lands;
the realms of humans, devas, and all other destinies are each distinct, yet the Buddha, having known them all, preaches the Dharma for them.
Great lands may be transformed into small at will, and small lands may be transformed into large at will;
such spiritual powers are immeasurable, beyond what can ever be fully described by the world.
Having universally emitted these wondrous sounds and praised the virtues of the Tathāgata,
the assembly remained silent with joy, gazing with single-minded devotion as they desired to hear the Dharma.
Then Vimukticandra again requested, saying:
"This assembly is now all tranquil; we pray that you will explain, in due order, the characteristics of the practices within the eighth stage."
At that time, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva has well cultivated discernment within the seventh stage, has well purified all paths through wisdom and skillful means, has well gathered the provisions, has well bound the great vows, has well received the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s sustaining power, and has attained a nature sustained by the power of their own roots of goodness; they then practice in accordance with the mental engagement of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-qualities."
They contemplate with a thoroughly pure and superior intention, arising through the power of merit and wisdom;
they do not abandon their application toward all sentient beings out of great compassion, proceeding according to the path of immeasurable knowledge;
they enter into the nature of all phenomena as being originally unborn, unarisen, signless, unformed, indestructible, inexhaustible, non-cyclic, and non-cessant.
In the initial, middle, and final stages, all are entirely equal; because there is no discrimination within True Suchness (tathatā), one enters into omniscience (sarvajñā).

This very Bodhisattva, having distanced himself from all conceptualizations and delusions of mind, intellect, and consciousness, and being without any attachment, clearly enters into the nature [of reality] which is equal to space; this is called "having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such non-arising dharmic patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and has just realized the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), they attain a profound dwelling that is difficult to comprehend. It is indistinguishable from [the ultimate], free from all signs, and brings to rest all conceptual attachments in their immeasurable and boundless extent. It is a state of tranquility that cannot be eclipsed by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, which now manifests before them.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a bhikṣu who, being fully endowed with supernormal powers and having attained mastery over the mind, gradually enters the ninth meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, wherein all agitation, discursive thought, and conceptualization are entirely stilled.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is likewise for a bodhisattva as soon as they attain the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*): they depart from all deliberate effort and spontaneously reach the state of effortless nature (*anābhoga-svabhāva*), remaining far removed from all activities of body, speech, and mind, and dwelling securely in the maturation (*vipāka*).
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a person who dreams that they have fallen into a great river; desiring to cross it, they exert great courage and diligence. Because of this exertion of great courage and diligence, they immediately awaken from their sleep.
Once awakened, all the courageous and urgent efforts they were engaged in come to a complete rest.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is the same for the bodhisattva: seeing the multitude of sentient beings fallen into the four great torrents of the afflictions (*kleśa*), he gives rise to great courage and exerts great diligence in order to rescue them. Because he has initiated such great vigor, as soon as he reaches the Bodhisattva’s Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), all functional efforts cease;
and all instances of the two-fold grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) that this bodhisattva previously manifested—whether as appearances or as mental activities—no longer appear.
O Son of the Buddha!
It is like a celestial being born in the Brahma realm, for whom the afflictions of the desire realm never manifest again.
O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), it is likewise so: all activities of mind, mentation, and consciousness no longer manifest.

Furthermore, even the activities of the Buddhas, the activity of enlightenment (*bodhi*), the activity of a bodhisattva, and the activity of nirvāṇa do not yet manifest; how much less could worldly activities ever arise?
"Furthermore, Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva thus practices this eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), having become established through the sustaining power of their original vows, they are awakened and exhorted by all the Tathāgatas within the swift current of such Dharma-gates.
At that time, the Buddhas bestow and induce the sublime wisdom of a Tathāgata, speaking these words:"
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
This is the patience that accords with the ultimate meaning of all Buddha-dharmas.”
However, son of good family!

We Buddhas possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; you have not yet attained these masteries. To achieve mastery over the Buddha-dharma, you should arouse diligence and must never again abandon this gate of patience.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Although you have attained this liberation of quiescence, all those of the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have not yet attained tranquility, nor have they yet achieved cessation; they constantly follow the manifestation of various and diverse afflictions and are afflicted by manifold discursive thoughts and investigations.
You should take pity upon them.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should call to mind your original vow, namely: to cause all sentient beings to attain benefit and the gateway of inconceivable wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Such is the dharmatā of all phenomena: whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the dharma-realm remains eternally constant and undergoes no change. It is not only by means of this that all Buddhas manifest; all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas likewise realize this non-conceptual dharmatā.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Observe that our Buddha-bodies are immeasurable, our wisdom is immeasurable, our buddha-fields are immeasurable, our circles of light are immeasurable, that which is induced by our knowledge is immeasurable, and our pure vocal tones are likewise immeasurable; you too should now induce these matters.
Furthermore, son of good family!
At present, you have obtained only this one illumination of the Dharma, namely, the non-conceptual wisdom regarding all phenomena.
Yet, son of good family!

Such illumination of the Dharma—the infinite conduct, infinite activities, and infinite bonds of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas—one should give rise to the factors that induce it in order to realize them.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should observe the infinite lands, infinite sentient beings, and infinite phenomena of the ten directions in all their various distinctions; you should thoroughly penetrate them all in accordance with reality.
"O Son of the Buddha!

In this way, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, awaken and exhort the Bodhisattvas of this stage, bestowing upon them these immeasurable and boundless gateways of wisdom that give rise [to realization]. Because they are free from the distinctions of ignorance, they are able to accomplish such karmic activities of manifestation."
O Son of the Buddha!

I now tell you this for your understanding: if, at any time, the Buddhas did not bestow their instructions and guidance to lead these Bodhisattvas into such gates of manifestation, they would have entered ultimate nirvana at that very moment, ceasing all activities for the benefit of sentient beings.

Because all Buddhas have bestowed upon him such karma for the elicitation of immeasurable wisdom, the karma of wisdom elicited by this Bodhisattva in a single moment of thought surpasses all the practices cultivated from the first production of the thought of enlightenment up to the seventh stage by a factor of a hundred; it surpasses them by a factor of a thousand, a hundred-thousand, a koṭi, a hundred koṭis, a thousand koṭis, a hundred-thousand koṭis, and a hundred-thousand koṭi-nayutas; it even surpasses them by factors of calculation, analogy, and even up to an *upaniṣad*.
Why is this so? O Son of the Buddha!

Previously, the Bodhisattva initiated all practices with a single body; now, by mounting this stage, he cultivates the Bodhisattva practices through the differentiation of immeasurable manifested bodies. Because he can initiate immeasurable sounds, because he can initiate immeasurable wisdom, because he can initiate immeasurable births, because he can purify immeasurable Buddha-fields, because he can mature immeasurable sentient beings, because he serves all immeasurable Buddhas, because he awakens to the principles of immeasurable dharmas, because he gives rise to immeasurable powers of supernormal knowledge, because he relies upon the distinctions of immeasurable assemblies, and because—through the power of all the correct practices of Bodhisattvas consisting of immeasurable actions of body, speech, and mind—all these are brought to complete fulfillment, being unshakable.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a sea vessel that, before reaching the great ocean, must be towed and pulled with effort; yet once it has reached the ocean, it proceeds spontaneously without effort, drifting upon the wind-circles of the great sea. The distance it travels in a single day by this effortless means cannot be matched by the distance it could travel in a hundred years while previously requiring such effort. It would not reach even a fraction of that immeasurable distance.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is the same for the bodhisattva: having already well accumulated the provisions of roots of goodness and cultivated the realization of the Mahāyāna, they reach the great ocean of the bodhisattva’s correct practices. In a single moment, by means of effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), they enter into the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajña-jñāna*). Compared to this, the previous effortful activities—even if practiced for hundreds of thousands of kalpas—could not reach such immeasurable results.
"O Sons of the Buddha!

When a Bodhisattva has reached the eighth stage, through vast skillful means and the effortless practice induced by sublime wisdom, as they observe all-knowledge with right insight, they contemplate the formation of worlds and the destruction of worlds;
they fully comprehend how the world is formed and they fully comprehend how the world is destroyed."
He fully understands by what karma the formation of the world is accomplished;
he fully understands by what karma the destruction and dissolution of the world occurs;
and he fully understands for how long the world remains formed.
He is able to fully know for how long the world remains in the process of destruction;
he is able to fully know for how long the world remains after it has been formed;
and he is able to fully know for how long the world remains after it has been destroyed.
Furthermore, one knows the small, large, immeasurable, and differentiated characteristics of the earth element;
one thoroughly knows the small, large, immeasurable, and differentiated characteristics of the water element;
and one thoroughly knows the small, large, immeasurable, and differentiated characteristics of the fire element.
They thoroughly understand the small, large, and immeasurable dimensions of the wind element, as well as its various characteristics;
they also know the subtle, coarse, and immeasurable characteristics of atoms, along with their various distinctions;
and they are able to fully comprehend the accumulation of all the various atoms within any given world-system, as well as every distinction among those atoms.
They are able to fully know all the various atoms of the earth element within any world-system;
they are able to fully know all the various atoms of the water element;
and they are able to fully know all the various atoms of the fire element.
They are able to know all the atoms within the various wind-elements;
they are able to know all the atoms within the various realms of sentient beings;
and they are able to know all the atoms within the various assemblages of buddha-fields.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva knows the coarse characteristics, the subtle characteristics, and the distinct characteristics of the bodies of sentient beings;
he knows how many atoms depend upon the bodies of those in the hells,
and he knows how many atoms depend upon the bodies of animals.
He knows how many atoms depend upon the body in the realm of ghosts;
he knows how many atoms depend upon the body in the world of asuras;
he knows how many atoms depend upon the body in the world of devas.
He knows how many atoms there are in the bodies of beings in the human world.

Once the bodhisattva has thus entered the wisdom that discerns the differentiation of atoms, he knows the formation of the desire realm, the formation of the form realm, and the formation of the formless realm; he knows the destruction of the desire realm, the destruction of the form realm, and the destruction of the formless realm;
and he is able to know the small, the large, the immeasurable, and the specific characteristics of the desire realm.
He is able to know the small, the great, the immeasurable, and the distinct characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
he is able to know the small, the great, the immeasurable, and the distinct characteristics of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Having thoroughly understood the three realms and having further skillfully brought forth the light of wisdom within the wisdom that accords with the observation of the three realms, he attains mastery in the wisdom regarding the differences in the bodies of sentient beings and mastery in the wisdom regarding the differentiation of bodies. Thus, in manifesting birth and inducing wisdom, this bodhisattva—according to the differences in the births and the accomplishments of the bodies of various classes of sentient beings—manifests his own body as one of their own kind as appropriate, thereby maturing sentient beings.

"Furthermore, within a single trichiliocosm, a bodhisattva is able to manifest birth throughout its entirety, in accordance with the differences in the inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings' bodies, because they follow their course through the wisdom of reflected appearance (*pratibhāsa-jñāna*). Likewise, whether it be two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even hundreds, up to unspeakably many and immeasurable trichiliocosms, they are able to manifest birth throughout them all, in accordance with the differences in the inclinations of sentient beings' bodies as appropriate, because they follow their course through the wisdom of reflected appearance."

Once the Bodhisattva has accomplished such wisdom, without his body moving from a single Buddha-field, he manifests himself within the assemblies of unspeakably many Buddha-fields. Furthermore, according to the differences in the bodies, inclinations, and mental dispositions of sentient beings, he is able to manifest his body in this way or that way in various Buddha-lands, and in various locations within those various assemblies and places of enlightenment.

That is to say: among the assembly of śramaṇas, he manifests the form of a śramaṇa; among the assembly of brāhmaṇas, he manifests the form of a brāhmaṇa; among the assembly of kṣatriyas, he manifests the form of a kṣatriya; among the assembly of vaiśyas, he manifests the form of a vaiśya; among the assembly of elders, he manifests the form of an elder; among the assembly of householders, he manifests the form of a householder; among the assembly of the Four Great Kings, he manifests the form of the Four Great Kings; among the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, he manifests the form of a Trāyastriṃśa god; among the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and the assembly of Māra kings, he manifests forms according to each respective class; and among the assembly of Brahmās, he manifests the form and color of a Brahmā.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva manifests the form of a śrāvaka for those who are to be disciplined by the body of a śrāvaka;
manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha for those who are to be disciplined by the body of a pratyekabuddha;
and manifests the form of a bodhisattva for those who are to be disciplined by the body of a bodhisattva.
To those who are to be disciplined by the physical form of a Tathāgata, he manifests the physical form of a Tathāgata.
O Son of the Buddha!

In this way, according to the various inclinations of sentient beings within unspeakably many buddha-fields, the Bodhisattva manifests such and such differences in bodily forms in each respective place.

"Furthermore, this bodhisattva remains far removed from all conceptualization of bodily characteristics and attains the equality of the body. He knows the bodies of sentient beings, the bodies of buddha-fields, the bodies of karmic results, the bodies of śrāvakas, the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, the bodies of bodhisattvas, the bodies of tathāgatas, the bodies of wisdom, the bodies of dharma, and the bodies of space. This bodhisattva also knows how to evoke the mental inclinations of sentient beings."

If one wishes, one may transfer the bodies of sentient beings into one's own body; likewise, one may transfer the bodies of buddha-fields, the bodies of karmic fruition, the bodies of śrāvakas, the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, the bodies of bodhisattvas, the bodies of tathāgatas, the bodies of wisdom, the dharma-body, and the space-body into one's own body.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands the arousal of the mental dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings; if they so desire, he is able to place his own body within the bodies of all sentient beings.

He is likewise able to place his own body within the bodies of buddha-fields, the bodies of karmic results, the bodies of śrāvakas, the bodies of pratyekabuddhas, the bodies of bodhisattvas, the bodies of tathāgatas, the bodies of wisdom, the bodies of dharma, and the bodies of space.

Having already understood the mental dispositions and inclinations of all sentient beings, the bodhisattva can, according to their wishes, place this body within those various bodies. Within the bodies of sentient beings, the bodhisattva knows the karmic body, the ripening body, the afflictive body, the material body, and the immaterial body.

Within the bodies of those buddha-fields, they are able to fully know the small marks, the large marks, the immeasurable marks, the defiled marks, the pure marks, the disordered arrangements, the upward-facing arrangements, the downward-entering arrangements, and the distinctions of the square lattice-work.
Within the body of karmic fruition, they are able to know its distinctions and understand its conventional designation;
within the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, they are able to know their distinctions and understand their designations;

and within the bodies of Tathāgatas, they are able to fully know the body of perfect enlightenment, the body of aspiration, the transformation body, the body of empowerment, the subtle form-body adorned with the marks and signs, the body of light, the mind-made body, the body of merit, the dharma-body, and the wisdom-body.

Within the body of wisdom, one is able to fully know the characteristic of thorough investigation, the characteristic of observing according to reality, the characteristics comprised by the fruit and its preparatory application, the characteristics of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, the characteristics of the establishment of the three vehicles, the characteristics of the common and the uncommon, the characteristics of renunciation and non-renunciation, and the characteristics of those in training and those beyond training.

He is able to fully know the characteristic of the equality of the dharmakāya, the characteristic of its indestructibility, the characteristics established according to various states and conventional designations, the characteristics established for phenomena pertaining to sentient and insentient beings, and the characteristics established for the Buddha-dharma and the noble Saṅgha-dharma.

Within the body of space, one fully knows the characteristics of infinite faculties operating universally, the characteristic of being formless, the characteristic of being undifferentiated and boundless, and the characteristic of being made manifest by sustaining the aggregates of matter. All these are known.
Thus, this bodhisattva, having already been able to bring forth physical wisdom and attain mastery over lifespan by sustaining their life-span for unspeakably unspeakable eons;
having attained mastery over the mind through the wisdom of entering and observing immeasurable and innumerable samādhis;
and having attained mastery over requisites of life by being able to manifest all manner of infinite ornaments in every world through the power of their sustaining grace;
They attain mastery over karma, because they are able to manifest the empowerment of karmic results at the appropriate time;
they attain mastery over birth, because they manifest taking birth in all worlds;
and having attained mastery over resolute belief, they are able to manifest all worlds as filled with Buddhas.
They attain mastery over vows, because they manifest equal enlightenment in whatever Buddha-field and at whatever time they desire;
they attain mastery over supernormal powers, because they are able to manifest the play of supernormal powers within all Buddha-fields;
having attained mastery over the Dharma, they are able to manifest the illumination of boundless and centerless Dharma-gates.

They attain mastery over wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*), because they manifest the powers of a Buddha, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the minor signs (*anuvyañjana*), and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because Bodhisattvas attain these ten masteries, they are named possessors of inconceivable wisdom, possessors of vast wisdom, and possessors of wisdom that cannot be eclipsed.
Thus, the bodhisattva having reached such a state and being able to accomplish such wisdom, is ultimately free from fault;
his physical actions as they manifest proceed spontaneously and are ultimately free from fault;
his verbal actions as they manifest proceed spontaneously and are ultimately free from fault.

The mental karma that manifests operates spontaneously; for all actions, wisdom serves as the precursor, and they proceed in accordance with wisdom, with the perfection of insight (prajñāpāramitā) acting as the predominant influence.

With great compassion as its foremost quality, well-discriminated through skillful means, properly induced by aspiration, and well-protected by the empowerment of the Tathāgatas, it never ceases its application for the benefit of all sentient beings, proceeding according to the distinctions of infinite worlds.
O Son of the Buddha!
To state the essentials:
once a bodhisattva has reached the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*), all activities of body, speech, and mind that manifest are solely for the purpose of accumulating all the Buddha-dharmas.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva thus reaches the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), they attain firm abiding through the power of their intention (*āśaya*), because all manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) have been distanced;
they attain firm abiding through the power of their superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), because they do not depart from the Path;
and they attain firm abiding through the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because they do not abandon the task of benefiting sentient beings."
They dwell securely in the power of great compassion, because they are able to rescue all worlds;
they dwell securely in the power of dhāraṇī, because they possess the quality of non-forgetfulness;
they dwell securely in the power of eloquence, because they have attained skill in the discernment and analysis of all Buddha-dharmas.
They attain firm abiding in the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), because they have attained skill in traversing the various locations within boundless world-systems;
they attain firm abiding in the power of great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*), because they do not abandon any of the deeds performed by bodhisattvas;
they attain firm abiding in the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*), because they universally gather all the qualities of a Buddha.
Through the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment, they attain excellent stability, because all modes of appearance and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvajñajñāna) manifest before them.
Thus, this bodhisattva, being sustained by such power, is able to manifest all activities, yet remains free from any fault or transgression in all those activities.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This eighth bodhisattva stage of wisdom is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), because it cannot be eclipsed;
it is called the Non-retrogressive Stage, because wisdom does not regress.”
It is called the Stage Difficult to Attain, because no one in any world can fathom it;
it is called the Stage of Youthful Innocence, because it is free from faults;
it is called the Stage of Birth, because one exercises sovereign mastery according to one's aspirations.
It is called the Stage of Accomplishment because there is nothing further to be done;
it is called the Ultimate Stage because of its ability to skillfully exercise the discernment of wisdom;
it is called the Stage of Nirvana because of its skillful elicitation of the power of original vows.
It is called the stage of sustaining, because it cannot be destroyed by others;
it is called the stage of effortlessness, because it is drawn forth from the prior limit.
O Son of the Buddha!

Once the bodhisattva has brought forth such wisdom, they enter the lineage of the Buddhas. Illumined by the light of the Buddha’s merits, they accord with the majestic deportment and correct conduct of the Tathāgata. The realm of the Buddha manifests before them without interruption or deficiency; they are constantly sustained by the majestic power of the Tathāgata and welcomed by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World Protectors. Vajrapāṇi spirits always follow and guard them, and they never abandon the power of samādhi. They bring forth the various bodily activities of infinite emanations and, through corresponding power, achieve vast supernormal powers of maturation (*vipākābhijñā*), acting with sovereign mastery within boundless samādhis.
They are able to receive the immeasurable predictions of enlightenment (*bodhy-avyākaraṇa*) and manifest perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) in accordance with the maturation of sentient beings.

Thus, these Bodhisattvas penetrate and enter the assemblies of the Mahāyāna; they attain the great wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of skillful observation, and constantly emit the radiance of sublime insight. They enter the path of the unobstructed true *dharmadhātu*, know the paths of the distinctions between worlds, and manifest all great merits. They exercise mastery over the arising of their own minds, possess excellent knowledge of the past and future limits of time, and are well-versed in the wisdom that penetrates and subdues all demonic paths, thereby entering the sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas.
Because they are already able to accomplish non-retrogression, they are capable of practicing the bodhisattva conduct within infinite worlds;
this is what is called a bodhisattva who has reached the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi).
“O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi), they are constantly and uninterruptedly never separated from the direct perception of immeasurable Buddhas, because they are drawn forth by the power of samādhi.”

Nevertheless, they do not abandon the extensive vision of the Buddhas, attending upon and making offerings to them; for in each and every world, this bodhisattva sees immeasurable Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of Buddhas, immeasurable thousands of Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, immeasurable koṭis of Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of koṭis of Buddhas, immeasurable thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddhas, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas.

Having seen the Buddhas, they revere and honor them, manifesting offerings through all modes of conduct and presenting them all to those Tathāgatas, serving them in every way. From the presence of these Buddhas, they receive immeasurable clarifications of the Dharma, such as the distinctions between worlds; they further attain the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas and become invincible in answering questions regarding the distinctions of all worlds.

Throughout immeasurable eons, these roots of goodness become increasingly radiant, brilliant, and pure; throughout immeasurable hundreds of eons, immeasurable thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of eons, immeasurable koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of koṭis of eons, immeasurable thousands of koṭis of eons, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of eons, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas of eons, these roots of goodness become increasingly radiant, brilliant, and pure.
O Son of the Buddha!

It is like a skilled goldsmith who, having fashioned ornaments from refined gold, places them upon the crown of the head or around the neck of a Universal Monarch of Jambudvīpa; among all the subjects and ministers of Jambudvīpa, no other ornaments can equal them.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells within this Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), these roots of goodness are likewise such that no roots of goodness belonging to any śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or even bodhisattvas up to the seventh ground can equal them.

Because, by abiding in this stage, one uses the light of great wisdom to universally extinguish the darkness of afflictions for all sentient beings and is well able to open and reveal the gates of wisdom.
O Son of the Buddha!
For example, just as Mahābrahmā, the lord of a thousand worlds, universally exercises a mind of loving-kindness and radiates light that fills a thousand worlds,

so too does the Bodhisattva dwelling in this Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi) likewise use his light to shine universally and pervasively, even reaching as many worlds as there are atoms in a million Buddha-fields, gradually extinguishing the burning heat of the afflictions of sentient beings and causing their bodies to be joyful and at ease.

Regarding the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), one aspires to reach the further shore with them as the primary focus; as for the remaining perfections, one practices them according to one's strength and capacity, not failing to cultivate them.
“O Son of the Buddha!
This is called a brief explanation of the Bodhisattva’s eighth stage, the Stage of Immovable Wisdom.
Were it to be explained in detail, it could not be exhausted even in the course of immeasurable eons.”

Once the bodhisattva is firmly established in this stage, they take birth primarily as a Great Brahmā King, sovereign over a thousand worlds, possessing supreme majesty and glory that cannot be eclipsed by others.

Skillfully perceiving what is meaningful, he attains great mastery and skillfully expounds for all sentient beings the paths of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas that lead to the other shore. Within the questions and answers concerning the distinctions of worlds, there is no one who can defeat him. All his deeds—whether through generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, or cooperation—are entirely inseparable from the mental attention directed toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the bodhisattva, the bodhisattva practices, the perfections (pāramitās), the stages (bhūmis), the powers of a Buddha, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; indeed, they do not even depart from the mental attention directed toward the omniscient wisdom (sarvajñajñāna) associated with all supreme and sublime aspects of practice.
He constantly makes this aspiration:

"Among all sentient beings, I shall be the foremost, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the sublime, the most exquisite, the superior, the unsurpassed, the peerless, the equal to the unequaled, the guide, the leader, and the commander; even unto attaining the state that serves as the basis for the knowledge of all-knowledge."

If one delights in initiating such diligence, through this diligence, in a single kṣaṇa, muhūrta, or instant, one will realize as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems;

one will be able to see as many Buddhas as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, and will be able to fully comprehend the empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of those Buddhas.

He is able to shake as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; he is able to illuminate as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; he brings to maturity as many sentient beings as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; he dwells for as many eons as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; he enters into the past and future limits each for as many eons as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; he is skillfully able to discern as many Dharma-gates as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; he manifests as many bodies as there are atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems; and from each body, he can manifest a retinue of Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems surrounding him.

From this point upward, regarding the various manifestations of play—whether of body, light, supernormal power, eye, sphere of activity, voice, conduct, adornment, resolve, or deed—possessed by those bodhisattvas who have the power of aspiration through their superior vows, these cannot easily be numbered even in as many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Having already cultivated skillful means and wisdom in the seventh stage, He has well accumulated the provisions and made great vows;
Empowered by the Buddha and endowed with virtuous strength, He accords with the Buddha’s merits and purifies his resolve and mindfulness."
Having already transcended through merit and wisdom, you possess constant compassion; your wisdom is vast and equal to space.
To seek supreme knowledge, you have ascended to the eighth stage, realizing the patient endurance of the cessation of non-arising.
Knowing that phenomena are without birth and without the nature of arising, Without marks, without formation, and without destruction,
Without exhaustion, without transition, and without cessation, Their nature is the nature of no-nature, eternally equal.
Entering the Buddha’s wisdom through non-conceptualization, one transcends the conceptualizations of mind, intellect, and consciousness;
having realized this patience, one attains tranquil abiding—profoundly unmoving and eternally quiescent.
Nothing in all the worlds can fathom it; All mental characteristics of grasping and attachment are entirely abandoned.
Abiding in this stage, one is free from discrimination, Just like a bhikṣu who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation.
Just as one who has dreamed of crossing a river exerts great effort, yet upon waking finds all is calm and free from urgency;
so too do the Bodhisattvas’ functional efforts cease on this stage.
Just as one born in the Brahma-world is severed from lower desires, the removal of these two characteristics here is likewise.
Within the swift current of the Dharma, you have been graced by all the Buddhas, who awakened you and exhorted you toward the stages of patience, saying:
"Though you have already extinguished the fire of afflictions, the flames of delusion in the world still blaze fiercely."
One should keep in mind the original vow to deliver sentient beings, Causing them all to cultivate the causes for attaining liberation.
The nature of phenomena is eternally thus, free from conceptual construction;
It is not only by this that the World-Honored One is revealed, For even those of the two vehicles can attain it here; Therefore, one should bring forth all spiritual practices.
Thus, this Honored One, worthy of offerings by humans and devas, bestows this wisdom for the sake of contemplative observation;
all boundless Buddha-dharmas are thereby fully accomplished, surpassing all former practices in a single thought-moment.
When Bodhisattvas dwell in this stage of wondrous wisdom, They then attain vast and great supernormal powers;
In a single thought-moment, they manifest bodies throughout the ten directions, Like a ship entering the sea that reaches its destination by means of the wind.
With minds free from effort, they rely on the power of wisdom To fully know the formation, destruction, and abiding of all worlds.
The various elements, each distinct and diverse, whether small, large, or immeasurable, he is able to comprehend.
The four great elements within the three thousandfold world system, the individual bodies of sentient beings in the six realms of existence,
as well as the number of atoms in all manner of jewels— he observes them all with wisdom, leaving nothing out.
The Bodhisattva can know all bodies, assuming forms identical to theirs in order to transform sentient beings;
though buddha-fields are infinite and diverse, he manifests his form within them all without exception.
Just as the sun and moon abide in space, And their reflections appear in all waters;
So they abide unmoving within the dharma-realm, Yet appear differently according to the inclinations of beings' minds.
Manifesting bodies within all assemblies— whether as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas,
or the body of a Buddha— there is none that is not manifested.
These various manifestations of the wisdom-dharmakāya and the space-body are all equal in their essential characteristics.
He manifests his deeds for the sake of all living beings;
further, through compassion, he performs manifold activities. All the Buddha-dharmas he brings to fulfillment;
his pure precepts are as immovable as Mount Sumeru. Having accomplished the ten powers, he remains unshakable.
None among the hosts of Māras can turn it back;
Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi constantly attends and guards it. The merit of this ground is boundless and infinite;
even in billions of kalpas, one could not exhaustively describe it.
Furthermore, through offerings made to the Buddhas, his goodness becomes even more radiant, like the ornaments upon a king’s crown;
when a Bodhisattva dwells in this eighth stage, he often becomes a Brahmā King, lord of a thousand worlds, expounding the three vehicles without end.
With the light of compassion shining everywhere, he extinguishes the delusions of all beings, and in a single thought-moment, he attains mastery over a million worlds.
Samādhis as numerous as atoms, and all other deeds performed likewise;
the manifestations through the power of vows exceed even this.
I have already explained this briefly for you; were it to be analyzed in detail according to its sequence, [it would be infinite].
"Even after passing through hundreds of millions of kalpas, one could not exhaust [its qualities].
The Eighth Stage, the Immovable Bhūmi, of the Bodhisattva concludes. The Sixth Fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
The Seventh Fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty at Longxing Monastery in Beiting.
The Ninth Bodhisattva Ground: The Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī*). The eighth bodhisattva ground has already been explained; now, the Tathāgata manifests great supernormal powers.
He causes all the lands of the ten directions to tremble, In measureless billions, beyond the reach of thought.
The Unsurpassed Honored One, possessed of all-knowledge and vision, Causes his body to radiate great light everywhere;
It illuminates those immeasurable lands, Causing all sentient beings therein to obtain peace and happiness.
Countless hundreds of thousands of billions of bodhisattvas simultaneously leapt up and remained suspended in the air;
with sublime offerings surpassing those of all the heavens, they made offerings to the Most Victorious among speakers.
Maheśvara, the Sovereign Lord, together with all his retinue, rejoiced with immeasurable hearts;
each, with various kinds of manifold offerings, made worship to the ocean of profound merit.
Furthermore, there were ten trillion celestial maidens, their bodies and minds filled with pervasive joy;
each played countless varieties of music as an offering to the Great Teacher of humans and devas.
At that time, various musical instruments were played simultaneously, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions;
through the majestic spiritual power of the Sugata, they all produced wondrous sounds in praise:
"Tranquil, harmonious, stainless, and without harm, You have skillfully cultivated each stage as you entered it."
The mind is like space, pervading the ten directions; It extensively expounds the Buddha-way to awaken the deluded masses.
In all places, whether in heavens or among humans, It manifests peerless and wondrous adornments;
Born from the merits of the Tathāgata, It causes all who see it to delight in the Buddha’s wisdom.
Without leaving a single land, they universally manifest to illuminate the world;
their voices and mental activities are entirely extinguished, yet like an echo in a valley, there is nothing to which they do not respond.
If there are sentient beings whose minds are inferior, for them I expound the practice of the Śrāvakas;
if their minds are sharp and they delight in the Pratyekabuddhas, then for them I teach the path of the Middle Vehicle;
if they possess compassion and delight in benefiting others, for them I explain the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas.
If one possesses the mind of supreme wisdom, One immediately reveals the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Just as a magician performs various feats, Whose diverse forms and appearances are all unreal;
The magical illusion of a Bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise: Though manifesting all things, it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Thus, with millions of such beautiful sounds, they sang praises of the Buddha and then remained silent.
Vimukticandra said:
"The assembly is now pure; I pray that you will speak of the practice of the ninth stage."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha addressed the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

If a bodhisattva, by means of such immeasurable merit, wisdom, and investigative discernment, further exerts diligent aspiration toward the progressively higher states of cessation and liberation; and further contemplates the progressively higher ultimate wisdom, entering the secret gate of the Tathāgata; and correctly selects the inconceivable wisdom of the Great Self-nature (*mahātman*); and purifies and selects the various *dhāraṇī*s and *samādhi* gates; and is well able to bring forth the vast supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); and is well able to universally survey the distinctions of worlds; and polishes the unassailable nature of the Tathāgata’s powers, fearlessnesses, and unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); and enters the heroic nature in accordance with the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas; and does not abandon the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the great compassion already attained—such a one realizes the ninth stage of bodhisattva wisdom.

When a bodhisattva dwells securely in this stage, they know, as they truly are, the activities of all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; the activities of dharmas with outflows and without outflows; the activities of mundane and supramundane dharmas; the activities of dharmas that are conceivable and inconceivable; the activities of dharmas that are determinate and indeterminate; the activities of dharmas pertaining to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the activities of dharmas pertaining to bodhisattvas and the activities of dharmas pertaining to the stage of a Tathāgata; and the activities of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas—all these they know as they truly are.

By means of such wisdom that accords with knowledge, he understands, as they truly are, the dense forest-like movements of the minds of sentient beings; the dense forest-like movements of their afflictions; the dense forest-like movements of their karma; the dense forest-like movements of their faculties; the dense forest-like movements of their inclinations; the dense forest-like movements of their spiritual lineages; the dense forest-like movements of their intentions and latent tendencies; the dense forest-like movements of their rebirths; the dense forest-like continuities of their habitual tendencies; and the dense forest-like establishments of the three groups—all of which he knows as they truly are.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, as it truly is, understands the various natures of the minds of all sentient beings; that is to say: the nature of the mind’s diversity;

the nature of the mind’s rapid transformation, its decay and non-decay; the nature of the mind’s lack of substantiality; the nature of the mind’s boundlessness and its sufficiency in all places; the nature of the mind’s primordial purity; the nature of the mind’s being with or without defilement; the nature of the mind’s bondage and liberation; the nature of the mind’s illusory arising; the nature of the mind’s manifest abiding in accordance with the various realms of existence; and even the countless hundreds of thousands of such diverse distinctions of mind—he knows them all as they truly are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands, as they truly are, the nature of afflictions that follow at a distance, their boundless nature in application, their nature of being co-emergent and inseparable, the nature of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) dwelling in one place, their nature of being associated with or dissociated from the mind, their nature of persisting through the continuity of rebirth according to various destinies, their differentiated nature within the three realms, the nature of craving, ignorance, and the arrowheads of views as mental faults, and the nature of the uninterrupted causal conditions of the three types of action; in brief, he understands all the differences among the eighty-four thousand modes of affliction as they truly are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands, as they truly are, all the various distinctions of karma: its nature as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; its nature as manifest (*vijñapti*) or non-manifest (*avijñapti*); its nature of arising simultaneously with the mind and being inseparable from it; its nature of accumulating through the destruction of self-characteristics and causes without losing the continuity of its results; its nature of having retribution or being without retribution; the distinct natures of experiencing black karma, white karma, both black and white karma, and neither black nor white karma; the immeasurable nature of the field of karma; the distinct natures of the karma of noble and ordinary sentient beings; the nature of being experienced in the present life, upon rebirth, or in subsequent lives; the nature of being fixed or unfixed regarding the vehicles or non-vehicles; and even the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various other distinctions of karma. All these he knows exactly as they are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva thoroughly understands the nature of the faculties as being weak, middling, or superior; their nature of having distinctions or no distinctions between the past and future limits; their nature of being superior, middling, or inferior; their nature of arising simultaneously with afflictions and being inseparable from them; their nature of being fixed or unfixed regarding the vehicles or non-vehicles; their nature of being matured or immature; their nature of following the web of faculties, rapidly decaying, and grasping at signs; their nature of being incapable of being destroyed due to the predominance of the faculties; their nature of the distinctions between faculties that regress and those that do not; and their nature of evolving differently over long periods of time.
In brief, he knows all such differences among immeasurable hundreds of thousands of faculties exactly as they are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva thoroughly understands the nature of weak, middling, and superior inclinations (*adhimukti*); their nature of having distinctions or no distinctions between the past and the future; their nature of being superior, middling, or inferior; their nature of arising simultaneously with and never being separated from the afflictions (*kleśa*); their nature of being fixed or unfixed regarding the vehicles (*yāna*) or non-vehicles; their nature of being matured or immature; their nature of following the web of faculties (*indriya-jāla*), quickly decaying, and grasping at signs; their nature of being indestructible due to the predominance of inclination; their nature of the distinction between inclinations that regress and those that do not;

and their nature of being diverse as they have followed along for a long time. To state it briefly, he knows all such distinctions of inclinations—up to hundreds of thousands of immeasurable varieties—as they truly are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva thoroughly understands the inferior, middling, and superior natures of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); its nature of having distinctions or no distinctions between the past and future limits; its superior, middling, and inferior natures; its nature of arising simultaneously with and being inseparable from the afflictions (*kleśa*); its nature of being fixed or unfixed regarding the vehicles (*yāna*) or non-vehicles; its nature of being matured or immature; its nature of following along with the web of faculties (*indriya-jāla*), being quickly destroyed, and grasping at signs; its indestructible nature due to the predominance of the spiritual lineage; the distinction between lineages that regress and those that do not;

and the distinct natures of long-term habitual tendencies and co-arising factors. To state it briefly, he knows all such immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various distinctions of spiritual lineage exactly as they are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva thoroughly understands the inferior, middling, and superior natures of their intentions; their differentiated and undifferentiated natures regarding the past and future; their superior, middling, and inferior natures; their nature of arising simultaneously with and never being separate from afflictions; their determined or undetermined natures regarding the vehicles and non-vehicles; their matured and immature natures; their nature of following the web of faculties, quickly decaying, and grasping at signs; their indestructible nature due to the predominance of their intention; the distinction between their regressive and non-regressive intentions;
and their diverse natures that have co-arisen through long-term practice. In brief, they know all such distinctions of infinite hundreds of thousands of various intentions as they truly are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands, exactly as it is, that these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arise together with the mental intention and arise together with the mind; that they are associated with the mind and yet dissociated from it without being separated from it; that they have followed along for a long duration; that they have never been vomited out since beginningless time; that they are difficult to subdue by means of the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); that they are capable of binding the continuity of rebirth within the three realms; that they manifest as the bondage of the mind from beginningless time; that they are the nature of discernment gathered at the sense-gates; that they possess the reality of having acquired their respective antidotes; that they are associated or dissociated with other factors; and that they can only be vomited out by the Noble Path alone. All such things he knows as they truly are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands, exactly as it is, the various distinct natures of taking birth according to karma; the nature of being established in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, humans, and devas; the nature of taking birth in the form realm and the formless realm; the nature of taking birth with perception and without perception; the nature by which karma acts as the field, craving acts as the moisture, ignorance acts as the darkness that covers, and consciousness acts as the seed to produce the sprout of future existence; the nature of name-and-form arising together and being inseparable; the nature by which delusion regarding existence and the thirsting desire for it lead to the continuation of birth; the nature of the desire for existence and the delight of sentient beings in birth, which is without beginning or end; and the nature of grasping at the three realms and being mutually drawn out from them. All these he knows as they truly are.

Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands, exactly as they are, the nature of habitual tendencies regarding whether actions are performed or not; the nature of perfuming according to the continuity of rebirth states; the nature of perfuming according to the conduct of sentient beings; the nature of habitual perfuming by karma and afflictions; the nature of habitual perfuming by wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas; the nature of perfuming according to subsequent existence; the nature of sequential perfuming; the nature of perfuming by the persistence of delusions that are neither severed nor extinguished; the nature of perfuming by substantial entities; and the nature of perfuming through seeing, hearing, and associating with śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas. All these he knows in accordance with reality.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva understands, as they truly are, the assemblies of sentient beings who possess the nature of being fixed in the right, fixed in the wrong, or neither (indeterminate).

Those who fall into the state of being fixed in the right due to right view, those who fall into the state of being fixed in the wrong due to wrong view, and those who fall into the indeterminate state by being devoid of both;

those who fall into the state of being fixed in the wrong because they have committed any one of the five deeds of immediate retribution, and those who fall into the state of being fixed in the right through the cultivation of the five faculties—those who fall into the indeterminate state by being devoid of both these two [sets of causes].

By practicing the eightfold wrong path, one falls into the fixed nature of the wrong; by cultivating the eightfold right path, one falls into the fixed nature of the right. When neither of these two is practiced, one falls into the indeterminate nature.

By the incessant manifestation of stinginess, envy, and lack of compassion, one falls into the fixed nature of the wrong; by instructing others in the cultivation of the unsurpassed noble path, one falls into the fixed nature of the right. When neither of these two is practiced, one falls into the indeterminate nature. All such things are known as they truly are.
“O Son of the Buddha!
When a bodhisattva has conformed to such wisdom, they are said to dwell in the Bodhisattva stage of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*).

While dwelling in this Bodhisattva stage of Good Intelligence, they thus understand the distinctions among the various conducts of all sentient beings and bestow upon them the appropriate means for liberation. They are well able to understand the maturation of sentient beings and their discipline; they are well able to expound the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle; and they understand how to expound the Dharma of the Tathāgata stage.”

Having realized this, this bodhisattva expounds the sublime Dharma so that sentient beings may attain the nature of suchness. He teaches the Dharma by following the various inclinations, latent tendencies, faculties, and resolutions of sentient beings; by following their spheres of activity and the wisdom that accords with all modes of conduct through various habitual practices; by following the conduct within the dense forest of dispositions; by following the permanent cessation of the latencies of afflictions, karma, and rebirth; by following the establishment of the assemblies; and by following the liberation attained through the resolution for each vehicle. Thus he preaches the Dharma.
O Son of the Buddha!

When a bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), they act as a great Dharma-preacher and is constantly able to protect the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma. Thus, the bodhisattva possesses the conduct of a Dharma-preacher; through skillful application following immeasurable wisdom, they expound the Dharma using the sounds and words inspired by the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) of all bodhisattvas.
In this regard, the Bodhisattva’s four unhindered analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are perfected and remain constantly active.
What are these four?
They are as follows:

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
By means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena, one thoroughly understands the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning, one thoroughly understands the distinctions (*viśeṣa*) among all phenomena.
Through the analytical knowledge of unimpeded expression, one is skillfully able to expound all phenomena without confusion;
through the analytical knowledge of unimpeded eloquence, one is able to know the sequential continuity and uninterrupted nature of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one is able to know the essence of all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one understands, in accordance with reality, the arising and ceasing of all phenomena;

and by means of the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one is able to follow the provisional designations of all phenomena and can expound the True Dharma without interruption."

By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), they do not disrupt the phenomena as they have been established, yet they are able to expound the essential points of infinite teachings.
Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), they thoroughly understand the distinctions among all present phenomena;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), they accordingly understand the distinctions among all past and future phenomena.
By means of the analytical knowledge of language, one teaches the Dharma without confusion regarding the past, future, and present;
by means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence, one is able to teach the Dharma with boundless illumination of the teachings within each and every age.
"Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among phenomena;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions among meanings;
and by means of the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one expounds the True Dharma in accordance with all languages and sounds."
By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one expounds the essentials of the Dharma according to the inclinations and wisdom of others.

Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one relies on the knowledge of the present dharma (*dṛṣṭadharma-jñāna*) to understand the skillful distinction between them without confusion;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one relies on inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) to understand that all phenomena abide in such a nature (*tathatā*).
By means of the analytical knowledge of language, one displays and explains based on conventional knowledge;
by means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence, one is well able to preach the Dharma based on ultimate knowledge.
"Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that the single principle is of an indestructible nature;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one enters into and practices skillfulness regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, truths, and dependent origination;
by means of the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one expounds [the Dharma] using beautiful sounds, words, and phrases that are easily understood by all worldly beings."

By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one further relies on the boundless illumination of wisdom that proceeds in succession, providing explanations according to the principles.
Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one thoroughly understands the distinctions among the gateways of the One Vehicle;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one knows how to skillfully differentiate the various vehicles.
By means of the analytical knowledge of language, they are skillfully able to expound the various vehicles without confusion;
by means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence, they explain each one through boundless illuminations of the Dharma.

"Furthermore, by means of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one is able to enter all bodhisattva practices, wisdom practices, and dharma practices, proceeding in accordance with wisdom;
by means of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one enters the distinctions established in the exposition of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);
and by means of the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one expounds and bestows the path of the various stages according to what is appropriate, without confusion."
By means of the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one can explain each stage of wisdom (*jñāna-bhūmi*) through infinite modes of expression.
